Reading the results
The summary table and trace plots give the full picture. Two results deserve comment: the GA pass and the random effects on travel time.
The GA pass as negative gate. The GA effect on Car is catastrophic (\(\gamma_z \approx -9.5\), HDI: \([-10.8, -8.1]\)): holders of the annual rail pass do not consider driving. The HDI excludes zero by a wide margin. The GA effect on Train, by contrast, is essentially zero (\(\gamma_z \approx 0.0\), HDI: \([-0.8, 0.7]\)). Once the consideration intercept absorbs the baseline, there is no additional boost from holding the pass. The commitment is already total. The pass does its strongest work not by promoting rail but by eliminating the car alternative. It is a negative gate, not a positive one. The remaining instruments (business trip, income, age) show a consistent pattern: negative slopes indicating narrower consideration sets, not wider ones. Habitual travellers have already decided.
Random effects on travel time. The per-individual random coefficient reveals massive heterogeneity: \(\beta_{tt,\mu} \approx -1.81\), \(\beta_{tt,\sigma} \approx 1.89\). The standard deviation is nearly as large as the mean. Individuals one standard deviation above the mean are barely time-sensitive (\(\mu + \sigma \approx 0.1\)); those one standard deviation below are extremely so (\(\mu - \sigma \approx -3.7\)). Without this random effect, the unmodelled heterogeneity bleeds into the consideration stage, attenuating the \(\gamma_z\) slopes. This is the aliasing problem described earlier. The per-individual parameterisation absorbs the heterogeneity where it belongs: in the utility stage.
The specification arrived through iteration, not foresight. The first model dropped consideration intercepts and had no random effects. The GA pass showed a flipped sign on Train. Dramatic but shallow: an artefact of uncentred instruments and missing intercepts. Adding per-individual random effects on travel time absorbed the heterogeneity that was bleeding into the consideration slopes. Restoring the consideration intercepts freed \(\alpha_j\) from doing double duty. Each perturbation changed the posteriors. What survived across all three specifications was the GA effect on Car: always catastrophically negative, always with an HDI excluding zero. What didn’t survive was the GA effect on Train. Its sign and magnitude shifted with the intercept specification. That asymmetry is the finding. The pass acts as a negative gate on alternatives, not a positive promoter of rail. Only the sensitivity analysis made this visible.
This is the core advantage over transformer attention. The consideration set model makes every modelling choice visible and arguable: the intercept specification, the exclusion restriction, the choice of which variables enter \(Z\) versus \(X\). When a multi-head model distributes mode preferences across anonymous subspaces, there is nothing to argue about.

title: The Architecture of Focus: Attention in Transformers and Discrete Choice
section: Part III: Where the Analogy Holds and Breaks
text:
Part III: Where the Analogy Holds and Breaks
We’ve argued that the structural analogies between these two technologies is deep and meaningful. Yet, the analogy is not perfect. The consideration set model is a stylised abstraction of discrete choice, just as transformer attention is a stylised abstraction of selective relevance weighting. Both are simplified models that capture key features while omitting others. We propose to use consideration set methologies to audit transformer attention. The differences are fruitful.






Where the Analogy Holds











Dimension
Transformer Attention
Consideration Set




Scoring
\(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\)
\(\tilde{z}_{nj}\gamma_j\)


Normalisation
Softmax: \(w_j = e^{s_j} / \sum_k e^{s_k}\)
Log-adjusted softmax: \(e^{\log\pi_{nj} + V_{nj}} / \sum_k (\cdots)\)


Signal/value separation
\(K\) and \(V\) are different projections of the same embeddings
\(z_{nj}\) (consideration) and \(x_{nj}\) (utility) are different variables


Identification requirement
\(K \neq V\): degenerate if the same projection is used for both
\(Z \neq X\): non-identified if the same covariates enter both stages


Context-sensitivity
\(Q\) changes per query
\(\pi_{nj}\) changes per person via \(z_{nj}\)


Bottleneck
Sequence → fixed-size context vector
Full alternative space → consideration set → choice











Where the Analogy Breaks











Dimension
Transformer
Consideration Set




Gate type
Soft: every token always contributes
Hard: alternatives are in or out


Independence
Softmax couples all tokens: \(\sum_j w_j = 1\)
Sigmoid decouples: \(\pi_j\) is independent


Uncertainty
Deterministic at inference
Stochastic: a latent discrete variable


Learning
Backpropagation from task loss
MCMC / VI from a likelihood


Output
A transformed representation
A discrete choice


Interpretability
Bias distributed across anonymous heads
Each \(\gamma_{zj}\) is named with a posterior





The most productive difference is the hard/soft divide. Transformer attention is a differentiable relaxation of discrete consideration. Consideration sets provide a Bayesian interpretation of what attention weights represent: the posterior probability that an alternative is decision-relevant.
Cross-pollination runs both ways:

From discrete choice to transformers: Attention weights are better read as “how likely is this token to be decision-relevant” than “how much does this token contribute.” This motivates sparsity-inducing variants (Sparsemax, \(\alpha\)-entmax) as continuous relaxations of hard consideration.
From transformers to discrete choice: The \(Q/K/V\) factorisation suggests consideration models could separate the signal that determines consideration from the utility that drives choice, rather than conflating them through shared covariates. Our Swiss Metro model takes a step in this direction.


Behavioural Audit, Not Mechanistic Explanation
Mechanistic interpretability (probing classifiers, causal tracing, activation patching) asks: where inside the model does the bias live? This is the streetlight question. It searches where the representations are visible. The consideration set approach asks something different: does the system’s observable screening behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? It does not need to find the keys under the lamppost. It applies to any screener, whether human, logistic regression, or transformer, without access to weights or architecture.
A clarification on what the audit recovers. Fitting a consideration set model to a screener’s decisions does not estimate the screener’s internal mechanism. It estimates a behavioural model. If the system’s input-output mapping were generated by a two-stage process (gating then evaluation), what would the gating parameters look like? The \(\gamma_z\) posteriors say the system’s decisions are consistent with a process where a given variable gates consideration with a given magnitude and uncertainty. This is a functional claim, not a mechanistic one. It has the same epistemic status as the infamous résumé audit studies, which surface discrimination without opening the hiring pipeline. The consideration model adds structure beyond a simple disparity test. It decomposes screening from conditional-on-screening evaluation. The exclusion restriction makes the decomposition identified.

Finding Instruments is the Hard Part
Everything rests on the exclusion restriction \(Z \neq X\). You need variation that shifts who gets considered without shifting who is attractive conditional on consideration. Without it, screening and evaluation are aliased and the model is unidentified.
The two demos illustrate the range. Hiring is the exemplary domain. Protected characteristics satisfy the exclusion restriction almost by definition. They gate whether a résumé is read but should not determine job performance conditional on reading. The “should not” is not a pious hope; it is the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets. Swiss Metro is harder. A GA pass plausibly shifts both consideration and utility. The model names this tension and invites scrutiny rather than burying it.
Other domains are harder still. In content recommendation, what feature shifts whether an item is considered without shifting its quality? In credit scoring? In triage? The framework does not pretend instrument discovery is easy. It makes the difficulty visible as a modelling assumption that must be defended. The same identification problem applies inside the transformer. Is a given attention head encoding screening bias, or a legitimate feature correlation, or both? Without exogenous variation that isolates the bias channel, internal attribution is underdetermined, for the same reason that a consideration model without valid instruments is unidentified.

title: The Architecture of Focus: Attention in Transformers and Discrete Choice
text:
Conclusion
Two metaphors, one problem. The streetlight effect: we search where the light is, not where the keys fell. The accountability sink: the architecture ensures there is no one to blame when the keys go missing. Multi-head attention is both at once. The bias is real, distributed across anonymous subspaces where it resists inspection, and no single head is responsible. Wrap the architecture in a vendor API and the sink deepens. The firm points to the model. The vendor points to the data. The data records past human decisions that nobody alive made. Accountability does not vanish. It is delegated into a void.
Consideration set models are the counter-architecture. They name the variables that gate access, estimate how strongly each one operates, and report their uncertainty. \(\gamma_z[\text{Car, GA}] \approx -9.5\) is not a diffuse activation pattern. It is a claim, with a sign, a magnitude, and a credible interval. You can show it to a regulator. You can argue about whether the instrument is valid. You can be wrong — and that is the point. A framework that can be wrong can also be held accountable.
Naming what you model is not a stylistic preference. It is audit infrastructure.

title: The Architecture of Focus: Attention in Transformers and Discrete Choice
section: What the Consideration Set Model Buys You
text:
What the Consideration Set Model Buys You
Three levels of attention, each making bias harder to locate. Human attention: biased by the conjunction fallacy, but experimentally detectable. Single-head attention: replicates the fallacy from training data, bias visible in one attention map. Multi-head attention: distributes the same bias across four anonymous heads, recombines through a GELU MLP. No single attention map tells the full story.
The consideration set model provides the structural contrast. Each screening variable gets a named parameter \(\gamma_z\) with a full posterior. You can compute \(P(\gamma_z > 0 \mid \text{data})\) and make a falsifiable claim about whether race or age gates consideration. The parameter has a name, a sign, a magnitude, and a credible interval. You can show it to a regulator.

Behavioural Audit, Not Mechanistic Explanation
Mechanistic interpretability (probing classifiers, causal tracing, activation patching) asks: where inside the model does the bias live? This is the streetlight question. It searches where the representations are visible. The consideration set approach asks something different: does the system’s observable screening behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? It does not need to find the keys under the lamppost. It applies to any screener — human, logistic regression, or transformer — without access to weights or architecture.
A clarification on what the audit recovers. Fitting a consideration set model to an LLM’s screening decisions does not estimate the transformer’s internal mechanism. It estimates a behavioural model, a reduced-form surrogate: if the system’s input-output mapping were generated by a two-stage process (gating then evaluation), what would the gating parameters look like?
The \(\gamma_z\) posteriors tell you the system’s decisions are consistent with a process where race gates consideration with a given magnitude and uncertainty. This is a functional claim, not a mechanistic one. It has the same epistemic status as Bertrand & Mullainathan’s résumé audit studies, which surface discrimination without opening the hiring pipeline. The consideration model adds structure beyond a simple disparity test: it decomposes screening from conditional-on-screening evaluation. The exclusion restriction makes the decomposition identified.


The Hard Part: Finding Instruments
Everything rests on the exclusion restriction \(Z \neq X\): you need variation that shifts who gets considered without shifting who is attractive conditional on consideration. Without it, screening and evaluation are aliased and the model is unidentified.
Hiring is the exemplary domain, not just a convenient one. Protected characteristics — name, race, age — satisfy the exclusion restriction almost by definition. They plausibly gate whether a résumé is read but should not determine job performance conditional on reading. The “should not” is not a pious hope; it is the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets.
Other domains are harder. In content recommendation, what feature shifts whether an item is considered without shifting its quality? In credit scoring? In triage? The framework does not pretend instrument discovery is easy. It makes the difficulty visible as a modelling assumption that must be defended, rather than hiding it inside an end-to-end loss. The same identification problem applies inside the transformer. Is a given attention head encoding screening bias, or a legitimate feature correlation, or both? Without exogenous variation that isolates the bias channel, internal attribution is underdetermined — for the same reason that a consideration model without valid instruments is unidentified.

Mechanistic interpretability (probing classifiers, causal tracing, activation patching) asks: where inside the model does the bias live? This is the streetlight question. It searches where the representations are visible. The consideration set approach asks something different: does the system’s observable screening behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? It does not need to find the keys under the lamppost. It applies to any screener, whether human, logistic regression, or transformer, without access to weights or architecture.
A clarification on what the audit recovers. Fitting a consideration set model to a screener’s decisions does not estimate the screener’s internal mechanism. It estimates a behavioural model. If the system’s input-output mapping were generated by a two-stage process (gating then evaluation), what would the gating parameters look like? The \(\gamma_z\) posteriors say the system’s decisions are consistent with a process where a given variable gates consideration with a given magnitude and uncertainty. This is a functional claim, not a mechanistic one. It has the same epistemic status as the infamous résumé audit studies, which surface discrimination without opening the hiring pipeline. The consideration model adds structure beyond a simple disparity test. It decomposes screening from conditional-on-screening evaluation. The exclusion restriction makes the decomposition identified.

Finding Instruments is the Hard Part
Everything rests on the exclusion restriction \(Z \neq X\). You need variation that shifts who gets considered without shifting who is attractive conditional on consideration. Without it, screening and evaluation are aliased and the model is unidentified.
The two demos illustrate the range. Hiring is the exemplary domain. Protected characteristics satisfy the exclusion restriction almost by definition. They gate whether a résumé is read but should not determine job performance conditional on reading. The “should not” is not a pious hope; it is the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets. Swiss Metro is harder. A GA pass plausibly shifts both consideration and utility. The model names this tension and invites scrutiny rather than burying it.
Other domains are harder still. In content recommendation, what feature shifts whether an item is considered without shifting its quality? In credit scoring? In triage? The framework does not pretend instrument discovery is easy. It makes the difficulty visible as a modelling assumption that must be defended. The same identification problem applies inside the transformer. Is a given attention head encoding screening bias, or a legitimate feature correlation, or both? Without exogenous variation that isolates the bias channel, internal attribution is underdetermined, for the same reason that a consideration model without valid instruments is unidentified.

title: The Architecture of Focus: Attention in Transformers and Discrete Choice
section: Part III: What the Analogy Buys You
text:
Part III: What the Analogy Buys You
The most productive difference is the hard/soft divide. Transformer attention is a differentiable relaxation of discrete consideration. Cross-pollination runs both ways: attention weights read better as “how likely is this token to be decision-relevant” than “how much does this token contribute,” motivating sparsity-inducing variants (Sparsemax, \(\alpha\)-entmax). In the other direction, the \(Q/K/V\) factorisation suggests consideration models could separate the signal that drives consideration from the utility that drives choice.
But the deeper difference is about what each framework makes arguable.

Behavioural Audit, Not Mechanistic Explanation
Mechanistic interpretability (probing classifiers, causal tracing, activation patching) asks: where inside the model does the bias live? This is the streetlight question. It searches where the representations are visible. The consideration set approach asks something different: does the system’s screening behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? It does not need to find the keys under the lamppost. It applies to any screener, human or algorithmic, without access to weights or architecture.
Internal attribution methods face a related problem. SHAP, LIME, and integrated gradients assume feature contributions are additive or locally linear. Multi-head attention violates both assumptions. The bias lives in the interaction of concatenated value vectors through the GELU MLP. A SHAP value for “applicant name” tells you the marginal contribution of that token holding other features fixed. It does not tell you whether the name gated consideration or shifted utility conditional on screening. The distinction matters: a blocked consideration funnel and a low utility score produce the same outcome (rejection) but require different interventions.
More sophisticated methods get closer. Concept erasure (LEACE) projects out the linear subspace encoding a protected attribute and checks whether performance drops. Causal abstraction tests whether a structural decomposition — “this component screens on race” — faithfully describes the network. Both ask the right question. Neither can answer it without the same assumption the consideration model makes explicit: an exclusion restriction that separates the screening channel from the utility channel. The identification problem is not a limitation of any particular method. It is the problem itself.
The consideration set model does not try to open the black box. It wraps a separate behavioural model around it. The \(\gamma_z\) posteriors say the system’s decisions are consistent with a process where a given variable gates consideration with a given magnitude and uncertainty. This is a functional claim. It describes behaviour, not mechanism, with the same epistemic status as résumé audit studies that surface discrimination without opening the hiring pipeline. The consideration model decomposes screening from conditional-on-screening evaluation, and the exclusion restriction makes that decomposition identified.

Finding Instruments is the Hard Part
Everything rests on the exclusion restriction \(Z \neq X\). The two demos illustrate the range. In hiring, protected characteristics satisfy it almost by definition. “Should not affect job performance” is not a pious hope but the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets. The Swiss Metro case is harder. The GA pass is an impure instrument, pulled between consideration and utility. The framework names this tension rather than hiding it.
Other domains are harder still. In content recommendation, what feature shifts whether an item is considered without shifting its quality? In credit scoring? In triage? The framework does not pretend instruments are easy to find. It makes the difficulty visible as a modelling assumption you must defend. The same identification problem applies inside the transformer. Without exogenous variation that isolates the bias channel, internal attribution is underdetermined, for the same reason that a consideration model without valid instruments is unidentified.

title: Prompting the Void: On Sustained Attention and Goal Discovery
text:
At my most cynical, I think the hype around AI-assisted work is largely driven by the revelatory power of simply writing things down. I’ve kept a personal blog and a suite of Obsidian notes for years. Writing has always been the most important step in developing quality work. That this is now marketed as a feature of AI tooling tells you how rarely it was practiced before. To test whether AI can improve work quality, I leaned into the workflow for a recent post: tracking every commit, prompt, response, and every revision. The question I wanted to answer was not whether the AI helps (it does) but under what conditions, and at what tasks.



An Obsidian style mind map of related notes


The companion post, The Architecture of Focus, took 15 days and 21 commits. It started as a technical comparison between transformer attention and econometric consideration sets, with bias detection as the motivating question. It came from the accumulated stock of reading and note-taking that the mind map above represents. It ended as an argument about accountability infrastructure: how multi-head attention functions as what Dan Davies calls an accountability sink, and how consideration set models provide a counter-architecture with named parameters, posteriors, and an exclusion restriction you can audit and argue about.
The core analogy was there from the first draft. What unfolded over the next two weeks was the rhetorical structure, the real-data empirical grounding, and the political framing. This emerged through iterative refinement with Claude. I have an instinct to call it dialogue, but it was less than that. More mechanical, less enriching, but an occasional spur to thought. This essay maps that evolution: a record of how an argument changes shape when you refine it with a system that can diagnose technical failures, recognise structural patterns, and execute editorial passes at speed.
Both writing and modelling are iterative processes of corrective refinement. The same dynamic played out in both domains across this project: a first attempt that was competent and inert, a corrective prompt that named what was wrong, and a second attempt that was actually useful. This pattern repeats. The tools make that repetition fast.



The argument evolved through seven phases, from technical analogy through accountability infrastructure to sensitivity analysis.

title: Prompting the Void: On Sustained Attention and Goal Discovery
text:
How the Argument Developed

The Initial Draft: Machinery Without Argument
My initial prompt:

You are an expert statistician and machine learning engineer. I want your help to craft a blog post about the analogies between the transformer self-attention mechanism in large language models, and the idea of attention or consideration sets in discrete choice modelling. The idea is to demonstrate the idea of attention is integral to efficient processing in the two statistical paradigms, and then stress how far each implementation serves as an analogy for the other. I will want your help to implement the consideration sets discrete choice model in pymc, while I’ll implement a simple transformer model with pytorch. I’ve attached the pymc-marketing code for a mixed logit implementation. The considerations set model should be implemented on top of this model. Let’s build a qmd file with a skeleton draft of a compelling blog post on this topic.

The skeleton took shape quickly. Claude produced a clean pytorch model about lexical ambiguity on the word “bank”: river vs money. The implementation of cross-attention mechanisms was technically correct but argumentatively inert. The first corrective prompt pushed for a more compelling example:

Good, but let’s restructure the transformer data example to give it a bit more bite about attention. Let’s replace the lexical ambiguity example with a vocabulary inspired by Tversky and Kahneman’s Linda the bank teller example. Instead of river and finance classification let’s classify the context as “feminist banker” or “bank teller.”

The initial prompting did a few things: it introduced a motivating example with genuine bite, and it oriented the modelling toward bias rather than lexical disambiguation. It also moved the argument to simpler attention mechanisms, rather than full-fledged self attention. The first commit landed on March 13 with ~1,200 lines: the Q/K/V to consideration set structural map, the Linda conjunction fallacy as motivating example, and four working transformer demos. Ranging from single-head to multi-head cross-attention mechanisms. We had technical content, and a human interest hook.
What was missing was not content but argument. I had working code and a clean analogy table but no rhetorical thread. No metaphor to carry the reader through. No real-world data to ground the synthetic validation. No political framing to connect the technical observation to anything a regulator would care about. This is practically often more important than the technical content. The code is the machinery; the argument is the purpose. It’s why anyone should listen to you, why the details matter.
Over the next five days I built out the econometric side. Starting from my earlier work on mixed-logit models using PyMC Marketing, the dialogue extended it to handle the consideration set decomposition. We refined the data generating process for a hiring case study, defined a PyMC consideration set model, interpreted parameter estimates and derived the implications. The first tightening pass removed 140 lines. By March 18 the post had both halves of the analogy working and a concrete bias-detection result. It still read like a technical report.



21 commits over 16 days. The Swiss Metro addition is the steepest spike; the tightening passes are the dips.




Finding the Through-Line: Rhetoric and the Streetlight
On March 23, I asked for an assessment of writing style and redundancy through the lens of Deirdre McCloskey, the economist whose Economical Writing argues that academics write badly because they hedge, pad, and refuse to commit to a claim.
The prose tightening was mechanical and fast: splitting run-on sentences, cutting throat-clearing, replacing passive constructions. The more interesting contribution was structural, and it came from a corrective prompt about a disconnected image.
The post contained a streetlight photograph that illustrated the interpretability problem but didn’t argue anything. I had gestured at the idea without making it land. The corrective prompt was simple: make this image do argumentative work. Once I named the problem, the response could thread it into a through-line

The old joke about searching under the streetlight applies here. Interpretability tools examine attention weights because they are visible, not because they are where the bias lives. Single-head attention is the lamppost: you can see the weights clearly, so you look there. Multi-head attention scatters the keys into the dark. Consideration set models do something different. They ask not where does the mechanism put the bias? but does the system’s behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? They bring their own light.

But this was still a claim without a demonstration. What made the streetlight image fully earn its place was the multi-head attention demo built earlier in the post. The demo trains a classifier to identify the Linda context, then shows the bias localised clearly in a single attention head. Add a second head: the same bias persists but is now split across both. Add more heads: the bias is distributed across anonymous subspaces and no single head is “the biased one.” You literally cannot find it by looking at any individual head. That progression is the streetlight effect made technical: the architecture does not hide the bias through malice but through aggregation. The metaphor and the demo were made for each other. Once the prompt surfaced the framing, the demo became the proof.
The streetlight was then threaded through three touch-points: the introduction (lamppost = single-head attention, where the bias is visible), the multi-head interpretability callout (the keys are in the dark), and the conclusion (consideration set models bring their own light). A disconnected image became a structural metaphor carried across the whole post.






Before and after



Before: “These systems encode bias. The real problem is detection: can we locate and quantify what they encode? Consideration set models separate ‘who gets noticed’ from ‘who gets chosen.’ They provide the audit infrastructure that transformer attention lacks.”
After: “These systems encode bias. They learn it from data that biased humans generated. The real problem is detection. Can we locate and quantify what they encode? Consideration set models separate ‘who gets noticed’ from ‘who gets chosen.’ They provide the audit infrastructure that transformer attention lacks.”
The colon becomes a full stop. “The real problem is detection” becomes a declaration, not a prelude. The question that follows lands as a challenge. McCloskey’s point: if you believe it, say it. The edit highlights the bias in the data too, which makes the model diagnostics more meaningful.


The sharpening of the prose and the threading of the metaphor were accompanied by technical model refinements too.


The Aliasing Discovery: Modelling as Iterative Correction
Applying the consideration model to real data was the next priority. The Swiss Metro dataset was added on March 23. The post needed real-world grounding: nobody hands you the true \(\gamma_z\) in the real world. The Swiss Metro survey provides three transport modes (Train, Swiss Metro, Car), mode-level attributes (time, cost), and person-level characteristics (GA pass, business trip, income, age). The question: which characteristics gate consideration of a mode, as distinct from the attributes that drive utility conditional on consideration?
The first model produced a flipped sign on the GA pass: a rail pass showed negative \(\gamma_z\) on rail modes. This looked dramatic but was not deep. The instruments were not mean-centred and the model had no consideration intercepts, so the slopes picked up a residual with a flipped sign. Fix the specification, fix the sign. A bad implementation, not a paradox.
What was worth writing about was why the bad implementation failed. The surrogate likelihood adds \(\log \pi_{nj}\) and \(V_{nj}\) inside the same softmax. If both components include intercept-like terms, a baseline consideration \(\gamma_0\) and a utility constant \(\alpha_j\), those terms compete during sampling. The sampler can shift probability mass between the two without changing the likelihood, because what matters is only their sum. This is the aliasing problem: multiple intercepts across the consideration and utility phases create competing degrees of freedom that are weakly identified.






The surrogate likelihood



The structural consideration set model says each alternative is independently in or out of the consideration set, generating \(2^J\) possible subsets. For three modes that is manageable. For ten it is not. The log-consideration-adjusted utility approximation collapses the combinatorial sum into a tractable single softmax: \(\log \pi_{nj}\) and \(V_{nj}\) simply add inside it. This preserves the two-stage interpretive structure while avoiding the combinatorial explosion. It also makes the transformer analogy precise: \(\log \pi_{nj}\) plays the role of the query-key dot product, and both enter a normalising function alongside a payload.


What followed was a discrete sensitivity analysis, not planned as such but recognisable in retrospect. Each modelling decision was a perturbation; the dialogue tracked what changed:

Drop consideration intercepts, let \(\alpha_j\) absorb both baselines. The slopes become identified from cross-person variation, but \(\alpha_j\) does double duty and is hard to interpret cleanly.
Add per-individual random effects on travel-time sensitivity. This absorbs person-level heterogeneity in the utility stage where it belongs, rather than letting it bleed into the consideration slopes. My first attempt put random effects per observation, not per individual: a subtle error that inflated the parameter count without modelling the right structure. The fix was an index lookup mapping each observation to its respondent, so the model learns one time sensitivity per person across their multiple choice scenarios.
Restore consideration intercepts alongside the random effects. The intercepts absorb baseline consideration for each mode, freeing \(\alpha_j\) to capture only utility preference and the slopes to capture only marginal instrument effects. The aliasing between \(\gamma_0\) and \(\alpha_j\) is not eliminated; it is managed by priors and the sigmoid nonlinearity. But the decomposition becomes interpretable.

Each step changed the posteriors. The GA effect on Car was robust across all specifications: always catastrophically negative, always with an HDI excluding zero by a wide margin. The GA effect on Train was fragile; its sign and magnitude shifted with the intercept specification. That asymmetry is the finding: the pass acts as a negative gate on alternatives, not a positive promoter of rail. Only the sensitivity analysis made this visible. This is exactly parallel to the writing process: the first draft requires a corrective pass, the second reveals what the argument actually is.

Identifying Restrictions: Comparing the Hiring and Transport Cases
The hiring case, by contrast, has clean instruments. Protected characteristics like race and age gate whether a résumé is read but should not determine job performance conditional on reading. The model recovers which firm screens on which variable and how strongly. The aliasing problem barely arises because the exclusion restriction holds by construction and, in practice, by law.

The “should not” is not a pious hope; it is the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets.

This contrast, clean instruments in hiring against impure instruments in transport, became the heart of the argument. Its status as the central modelling choice only emerged through iterative refinement. The most important idea in the post was latent for several drafts before the right framing surfaced it.



The Political Turn: Naming What Was Already There
The post had argued from the start that multi-head attention distributes bias across anonymous subspaces where it resists audit. That is already a claim about accountability; it just hadn’t been named as one. Dan Davies’s concept of an accountability sink gave the observation its proper name: an institutional structure that absorbs blame without assigning it. Calling multi-head attention an accountability sink is not adding a political frame from outside. It is following the technical observation to its logical conclusion.
The dialogue extended the logic. I pushed further:

Not only is the architecture at risk of obscuring information and responsibility. Eager adoption of these architectures via API calls to vendor LLMs is a pattern of off-loading responsibility to SOTA models rather than human actors or firms…

The response articulated the three-level nesting:

When a firm replaces its screening committee with an API call to a vendor LLM, it outsources the decision and the accountability. The vendor says: “we provide a tool, not a decision.” The firm says: “we used the best available technology.” The candidate has no one to appeal to. The architecture distributes blame internally across anonymous heads. The procurement structure distributes it externally across organisations.

The architecture (no single head), the procurement (no single firm), the history (no single decision-maker). Each layer is an accountability sink nested inside the next. The framing was new. The logic was already latent in the post’s technical claims. The dialogue surfaced it.
What the accountability sink prevents is not just blame assignment. It prevents the feedback that makes diagnosis possible. If no one is responsible for a discriminatory outcome, no one is obliged to investigate it, correct the model, or change the intake filter. The sink is not just a political problem; it is an epistemological one. It structurally blocks the corrective iteration that would improve the system. Consideration set models are the counter-architecture not only because they name the variables that gate access, but because they make the decomposition arguable: a named parameter can be challenged, a posterior can be updated, a specification error can be diagnosed and fixed. The accountability sink forecloses that loop. Consideration set models reopen it.

title: Writing with an AI: How an Argument Evolves
section: What It Tells You About AI Collaboration
text:
What It Tells You About AI Collaboration
So: is the AI adding something, or is it just the act of writing things down? Both, but unevenly. The prose tightening is mechanical: fast, somewhat reliable, and not interesting. What is interesting is what happened when the mechanical parts were done and there was something specific to push against.
The streetlight metaphor needed a corrective prompt and guided threading through the post’s structure. The political framing needed a corrective prompt and rhetorical positioning. The Swiss Metro model needed three corrective prompts before it said something true: drop the intercepts, fix the random effects to individuals, restore the intercepts. In each case the AI’s first response was competent. The work was in knowing what was wrong with it.
That is the honest description of the tool. It is not a collaborator in the sense of bringing independent insight. It is a respondent that scales with the quality of your prompts. Corrective prompting requires the domain knowledge the AI is simulating: knowing that a flipped sign is a specification error rather than a finding, knowing that random effects per observation and per individual are different models rather than different parameterisations of the same model, knowing that a disconnected image can be made argumentative rather than merely illustrative. Rhetorical positioning requires a point of view the AI will mirror back if you give it one. Model sensitivity analysis requires knowing what to perturb and what counts as a robust result. None of that can be delegated. What can be delegated is execution: drafting the paragraph once you know what it should say, running the model variant once you know what to change, threading the metaphor once you know where it should land.
Convergence on what matters took longer than convergence on how to say it. The prose was tight by Phase 3. The argument only landed in Phase 6. The style determines their arrangement. That gap, between writing that reads well and writing that resonates, is where the human work lives. A sharper initial prompt would have collapsed six phases into two. But writing that prompt requires knowing what you are arguing, and knowing what you are arguing is partly what the six phases produced.



Per-commit additions (green) and deletions (red). The best commits often remove material.


The core unit of progress here was not generation but diagnosis. Every useful step began with a diagnosis of what was wrong with the previous version: the Linda example replacing bank/river, the streetlight threaded across three sections, the GA pass identified as a negative gate rather than a rail promoter. The AI accelerated the subsequent execution. It did not originate the diagnosis or identify the need.
Branko Milanovic’s Capitalism, Alone argues that fear of the robot is misplaced:

“Fear of robotics and technology arise, I think, from two human frailties. One is cognitive: we simply do not know what future technological change will be and thus cannot tell what jobs will be created, what our future needs will be, or how raw materials will be used. The second is psychological: we get a thrill from the feat of the unknown…”

The cognitive frailty is the point. We do not know what our future needs will be because discovering what they are is an iterative process of diagnosis and correction. The essay began as a blog post exploring an analogy. The modelling work — extending my earlier PyMC Marketing mixed-logit implementation to handle the consideration set decomposition — turned out to be more than illustration. Working through the aliasing problem, the exclusion restriction, and the surrogate likelihood in prose clarified what the code needed to do. The essay culminated in a pull request to pymc-marketing combining consideration set modelling with mixed logit models. Writing the post was not a detour from the software work. It was the process by which the software design became clear. The AI made each cycle faster. It did not determine what the cycles were for. That remains the hard part — not because the mechanics of iteration resist automation, but because the goal itself is what the iteration discovers. You cannot prompt your way to a destination you have not yet found.

title: Prompting the Void: On Sustained Attention and Goal Discovery
section: The Notion of Style in Work
text:
The Notion of Style in Work
Style, in so far as I have one, is a function of the intention to say something true and well crafted. This intention is filtered through details of biography and taste. Style is not merely adornment, it constrains vision and focus. The Linda vignette rather than the river bank lexicon, the political dimension alongside the technical detail and consideration sets applied to hiring alongside transport modes. These constraints determine what I choose to attend to, what I notice, and how I connect things. Attention is all you need, sure. But the kind of attention matters. Labour and craft are a kind of sustained attention, not stateless. A writer’s style determines relevance in the way a transformer’s attention mechanism cannot: through accumulated commitment and refinement, not context-window-sized weighting. Proust has the line:

Style for the writer, no less than colour for the painter is a question not of technique but of vision: it is the revelation, which by direct and conscious methods would be impossible, of the qualitative difference, the uniqueness of the fashion in which the world appears to each one of us, a difference which, if there were no art, would remain forever the secret of every individual. - Proust, Time Regained

Your style of thought pervades your work-product. It determines what you attend to, and what you recognise as wrong, and therefore what you try to fix. The AI can help you express that vision more clearly, but it does not determine it. It lacks a way of seeing what matters. Most of the value of all work is in the act of fitting your vision to task at hand.

title: Working as a Data Scientist
text:
Key ideas

Data scientists perform three core activities: measurement (collecting data), counting (organizing and summarizing), and prediction (making informed guesses about unseen data)
Histograms and simple distributions help visualize patterns in measured data
Prediction requires looking at patterns in existing data to make educated estimates about new observations
Data science is an accessible, engaging field that can be explained through everyday activities like measuring heights

title: Survival Regression Models in PyMC
text: A talk on survival regression models in PyMC, with application to people analytics and employee attrition prediction. Covers two main approaches: Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) models using parametric distributions like Weibull, and Cox proportional hazards models using discrete interval hazards. Demonstrates how to handle censored data properly and extends both frameworks with frailty terms and stratified baseline hazards to capture individual heterogeneity and group-level differences in survival risk.

title: Survival Regression Models in PyMC
text:
Key ideas

Survival analysis is the proper framework for modeling time-to-event outcomes when data are censored; naive summaries bias results
Accelerated Failure Time models use parametric distributions (Weibull, log-logistic) with regression entering the scale parameter
Cox proportional hazards can be fit via the Poisson trick: likelihood decomposes into baseline hazard rates and covariate adjustments over discrete time intervals
The proportional hazards assumption requires that covariate effects on hazard remain constant over time
Frailty terms (random effects) capture unobserved individual heterogeneity; multiplicative frailties scale the baseline hazard
Stratified baseline hazards allow different baseline risk trajectories across subgroups (e.g., by gender)

title: Bayesian Structural Causal Inference
text: A talk on Bayesian Structural Causal Modeling using PyMC, framing causal inference as “world-building”: exploring the space of plausible causal structures that generated observed data. Contrasts design-based minimalism (natural experiments) with structural maximalism (explicit joint modeling of treatment assignment and outcomes). Focuses on how hidden confounding (correlation in unobserved errors) biases conventional OLS estimates, and how Bayesian variable selection priors and sensitivity analysis across confounding parameters enables robust causal conclusions despite model uncertainty.

title: Bayesian Structural Causal Inference
text: A talk on Bayesian Structural Causal Modeling using PyMC, framing causal inference as “world-building”: exploring the space of plausible causal structures that generated observed data. Contrasts design-based minimalism (natural experiments) with structural maximalism (explicit joint modeling of treatment assignment and outcomes). title: Bayesian Structural Causal Inference
text:
Key ideas

Causal effect estimates depend on the “world structure”—assumptions about hidden confounders and their relationships
Joint structural modeling estimates the correlation between unobserved treatment factors and outcome factors (rho parameter), making hidden confounding explicit rather than assumed away
The rho parameter quantifies selection bias: when rho=0 we have OLS-like assumptions; rho≠0 indicates unobserved confounding affecting both treatment and outcome
Variable selection priors (Spike-and-Slab, Horseshoe) eliminate implausible causal graphs by collapsing the multiverse of possible worlds
Outcome equation flexibility (BART, Gaussian processes) can absorb causal signals and destroy identification; treatment equation flexibility is safer as it models selection without obscuring effects
Parameter recovery via synthetic data validates whether a model can identify the true treatment effect in principle
Sensitivity analysis maps treatment effects across plausible values of rho, enabling robust decision-making under causal uncertainty

title: Skill Estimation, Agents and the Condorcet Jury Theorem
text: A talk on using Item Response Theory with PyMC to stress-test the Condorcet Jury Theorem in practice. The theorem promises that independent, slightly-above-chance decision-makers converge on truth as the group grows—but assumes equal competence, equal difficulty, and independence. Using synthetic IRT simulations with skill (θ), difficulty (δ), and block effects, the talk demonstrates how shared training, information, and incentives break independence. Key finding: “groupthink” agents show parameter collapse and flat scaling curves; even high-competence expertise can mask blind spots. Provides diagnostic vocabulary (effective ensemble size, error correlation heatmaps, relative log-odds gain) for evaluating any collective decision system.

title: Skill Estimation, Agents and the Condorcet Jury Theorem
text:
Key ideas

The Condorcet Jury Theorem holds only if agents are independent; shared structure (training, incentives, information) creates correlated errors that collapse effective ensemble size
Item Response Theory decomposes decisions into skill, case difficulty, block effects, and treatment effects, enabling precise diagnosis of why collectives fail
Block effects (structural alignment) can crush individual skill signal; “kappa compression” shows how groupthink reduces individual contribution to near-interchangeability
Parameter recovery under three scenarios reveals pathology: independent agents scale beautifully, grouped agents show parameter collapse, expert agents achieve high baseline accuracy but zero scaling
Error correlation heatmaps quantify structural coupling; clustered patterns indicate shared failure modes rather than independent errors
Effective ensemble size (N_eff) can be far smaller than headcount when errors are correlated; accuracy gains from adding members only occur with genuine independence
Treatment effects that overcome block effects require unrealistically large interventions, showing the strength of structural vs. individual drivers

title: Freedom, Hierarchies and Confounded Estimates
text: Explores how group-level confounding biases causal inference in Differences-in-Differences designs and hierarchical data structures. Compares estimation strategies (naive, fixed effects, multilevel, Mundlak) for recovering treatment effects when group effects confound covariates, showing that Mundlak regression—adding group means as covariates—offers a principled alternative to heavily parameterized fixed effects models. Uses simulation and real examples with pupils nested in classes in schools to illustrate how model specification shapes the parameter space and constrains causal identification.

title: The Architecture of Focus: Attention in Transformers and Discrete Choice
text: Reveals that transformer attention and econometric consideration set models share the same mathematical skeleton: selective relevance weighting. Compares how multi-head transformer attention distributes bias across anonymous subspaces (creating an “accountability sink”) versus how named consideration set parameters make gatekeeping bias explicit and auditable. Uses the Linda problem and synthetic hiring data to show how attention bias replicates conjunction fallacies from training data, and argues that consideration set models offer better infrastructure for detecting and fixing bias than interpretability methods trapped by architectural opacity.

title: Prompting the Void: Writing as Corrective Steering
text: Tracks the 15-day, 21-commit development of a technical post on attention mechanisms to understand when AI-assisted work adds value. Finds that the primary driver of quality is not generation but iterative correction: diagnosing what fails in a draft (wrong emphasis, weak metaphor, specification error, missing framing), then executing the fix at speed. Prose tightening is mechanical and fast; discovering what the argument actually is takes longer and requires domain knowledge the AI cannot supply. Contrasts mechanical execution with originative diagnosis—the human’s irreducible contribution—and reflects on how style (vision of what matters) determines both what we attend to and what we can fix.

title: Freire’s Pedagogy as Concrete Inferentialism
text:
Freire’s literacy method embodies Brandom’s inferentialism at the level of practice, and surpasses it. Freire grasped that the space of giving and asking for reasons must be created against systematic pressure, not merely described. He poses the prior question Brandom evades: whose practices of mutual recognition constitute the concepts we analyze as universal?



Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968) developed a theory of education as consciousness-raising through adult literacy programs in Northeast Brazil. His method begins with “generative words” from learners’ lived experience and proceeds by examining their full social and inferential context. Freire draws on Marx and Hegel without the mediation of analytic philosophy, yet arrives at structurally identical insights about meaning, recognition, and conceptual development.




Banking education #freire — teachers deposit knowledge into passive students; treats learners as objects; destroys the conditions for genuine conceptual grasp
Problem-posing education #freire — teachers and students investigate reality together as co-inquirers; constitutes the mutual recognition Brandom requires
Conscientização #freire — consciousness-raising through confronting contradictions between ideology and lived experience; Hegelian Aufhebung in a literacy circle
Generative words #freire — words drawn from learners’ experience (favela, trabalho) whose inferential web is examined collectively; inferentialism enacted before it was named






Freire does not teach reading as decoding marks. He begins with words whose inferential commitments are live for learners. To learn the word “oppression” is to gain the capacity to articulate commitments about one’s social situation, draw inferences about causes, and challenge others’ claims. That is Brandom’s account of concept acquisition, realized in a favela literacy circle.



Brandom analyzes the structure of conceptual content as though entry into the space of reasons were freely available. Freire shows it is not. The banking model is not merely inefficient pedagogy. It actively prevents the constitution of genuine conceptual content by denying learners standing as rational interlocutors. If concepts gain content through mutual justification, then systematic denial of that standing corrupts the content formed.

text: Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968) developed a theory of education as consciousness-raising through adult literacy programs in Northeast Brazil. Freire draws on Marx and Hegel without the mediation of analytic philosophy, yet arrives at structurally identical insights about meaning, recognition, and conceptual development.

title: Condorcet Aggregation and Social Objectivity
text:
The Condorcet Jury Theorem provides the formal mechanism Brandom’s social epistemology needs. Fallible individual reasoners converge on correct judgments through aggregation, without any individual possessing complete knowledge. Objectivity is a structural feature of aggregation under independence, not a metaphysical relation to mind-independent reality. Freire’s pedagogy creates the independence conditions that make the mechanism work.



The Condorcet Jury Theorem states: if \(n\) voters each have probability \(p > 0.5\) of choosing correctly between two options and vote independently, the probability of a correct majority verdict approaches 1 as \(n \to \infty\). Applied to scientific communities and social epistemology, the theorem suggests that reliable collective judgment can emerge from individually fallible reasoners. The independence condition must hold.




Condorcet Jury Theorem #condorcet — collective accuracy is a function of individual accuracy and independence; given \(p > 0.5\), majority accuracy converges to certainty as group size increases
Epistemic independence #social-epistemology — voters form judgments without systematic correlation; independence is violated by hierarchical authority, ideological conformity, or shared bias
Diversity Prediction Theorem #scott-page — collective accuracy depends on both individual ability and diversity of perspectives; adding diverse but less-skilled reasoners can improve collective judgment more than adding skilled but similar ones
Correlated error #social-epistemology — when group members share biases, aggregation amplifies rather than cancels error; the group converges on a wrong answer with high confidence






Brandom claims objectivity emerges from social practices of mutual challenge and justification but does not specify the mechanism. Condorcet supplies it. Each scientist has partial, fallible grasp of the concepts involved. Their independent assessments, aggregated through practices of peer review, replication, and debate, converge on increasingly reliable collective judgment. No individual needs God’s-eye access. The process does the epistemic work.
This is a purely procedural account of objectivity. Follow the practices, and convergence happens. The content of concepts like mass or entropy is what survives this process of challenge and aggregation, not what any individual correctly represents.



Condorcet convergence requires independence. If judgments are correlated, aggregating them does not increase accuracy. This maps directly onto Brandom’s requirement for genuine mutual recognition. For the space of reasons to generate objectivity rather than consensus, participants must form judgments from genuinely distinct perspectives.
Three systematic violations, all endemic to oppressive structures:
Exclusion. Excluding whole groups removes independent perspectives. If women scientists notice anomalies male scientists systematically miss, excluding women creates blind spots no number of additional male scientists can repair. The convergence achieved is parochial: correct from within the restricted jury, undetectable as inadequate without it.
Induced dependence. Hierarchy produces correlated judgments. Graduate students deferring to supervisors, colonized scientists working within imposed frameworks, and researchers constrained by funding incentives all reduce the effective independence of the jury. The group shrinks epistemically even as it grows numerically.
Shared bias. When all jury members share background assumptions, aggregation amplifies those assumptions. Peer review within a community with shared racist premises will converge confidently on conclusions those premises generate. The mechanism works, but on corrupted inputs.



Freire’s culture circles are institutions for generating epistemic independence. Problem-posing education does not transmit approved answers. It develops the capacity to form independent judgment: to notice contradictions, articulate one’s own perspective, challenge received claims from one’s own standpoint.
From a Condorcet perspective, Freire is increasing both jury size and the independence of its members. Peasants with critical consciousness are not merely more voters. They are voters whose perspectives are genuinely distinct from elite academic perspectives, drawn from different material positions and practical experiences. The Diversity Prediction Theorem explains why their inclusion improves collective judgment even when their formal training is limited: diversity of perspective is an independent contributor to collective accuracy.



The Condorcet framework explains why epistemic inclusion is an endless task. First, the relevant jury changes with the question. Physicists are the right jury for quantum calculations; local communities are the right jury for whether a development project serves local needs. Identifying who has standing for which questions is itself ongoing work. Second, independence is fragile. Power continuously generates new forms of dependence: funding pressures, institutional hierarchies, ideological conformity. The conditions for genuine aggregation must be actively maintained. Third, new perspectives are always possible. Each expansion of the jury can shift collective judgment in ways that reveal previous convergence as partial.




Let \(n\) voters each have accuracy \(p_i > 0.5\) and vote independently. The probability that the majority is correct is:
\[P(\text{majority correct}) = \sum_{k > n/2} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \to 1 \text{ as } n \to \infty\]
The Diversity Prediction Theorem: \(\text{Collective error} = \text{Average individual error} - \text{Diversity}\), where diversity measures the variance in individual predictions around the collective prediction.

[[Freire’s Pedagogy as Concrete Inferentialism]] — Freire’s culture circles realize the independence condition Condorcet requires; inclusion is epistemically necessary, not merely just
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — frequentist and Bayesian disagreements are a case study in whether diverse competing frameworks improve collective judgment; Feyerabend’s counter-induction says yes
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — missing perspectives in an epistemic community are structurally analogous to missing data in a statistical model; both bias conclusions in ways that aggregating available information cannot correct
[[Missing Perspectives as Missing Data]] — the full formal development of this connection; oppressive exclusion maps to MNAR, Freire’s culture circles map to instrumental variables





Can the diversity that improves Condorcet aggregation be operationalised? What makes two perspectives genuinely independent rather than superficially different?
The theorem requires \(p > 0.5\) for each voter. What is the analogue in concept formation? Can a perspective be “worse than random” and systematically harm collective judgment?
Is there a principled account of which questions require which juries, or is jury composition itself always politically contested?

title: Brandom’s Inferentialism and Hegelian Conceptual Content
text:
To grasp a concept is to master its inferential role: what it licenses, what commits you, what challenges it invites. Meaning is constituted by social practices of giving and asking for reasons, not by representation of objects or mental states.



Brandom’s Making It Explicit (1994) and Articulating Reasons (2000) rehabilitate Hegelian ideas within analytic philosophy. The central puzzle: if concepts get their content from social practices, how does objective content emerge? Brandom’s answer is that objectivity is a structural feature of any practice of mutual challenge and justification, not a metaphysical relation between mind and world.




Inferentialism #semantics — the meaning of a concept consists in its inferential relations: what follows from applying it, what entitles you to apply it, what it is incompatible with
Normative scorekeeping #brandom — linguistic practice involves tracking commitments and entitlements; to make a claim is to undertake a commitment others can hold you to
Recollective rationality #brandom — conceptual development is reconstructed retrospectively; later usage reinterprets earlier usage while maintaining rational continuity
Semantic holism #semantics — no concept has content in isolation; content depends on inferential relations to other concepts across the whole system






Brandom rejects representationalism. “Copper” means what it means not because it labels a kind of stuff, but because it licenses inferences (conducts electricity, reddish metal warrants its application, etc.). Mastery of a concept is mastery of its inferential role.



Recognition. Self-consciousness requires mutual recognition. Brandom translates this: conceptual normativity requires that others recognize you as a participant in reason-giving, and you recognize them as capable of assessing your reasons. Recognition is constitutive, not merely enabling.
Determinate negation. Hegel’s concept development through internal tension becomes, for Brandom, an account of how communities resolve incoherence in their inferential practices. Contradictions in our commitments force revision that preserves what worked while transforming what failed. Brandom calls this expressive rationalism: making implicit commitments explicit, then revising accordingly.
Priority of the whole. Hegel’s claim that truth belongs to the whole, not isolated judgments, becomes Brandom’s semantic holism. The content of any concept depends on the entire inferential web of the community employing it.



Concepts have careers. The concept of mass transformed from Newtonian to relativistic form through a rational process: later scientists could articulate why Einstein’s framework resolved incoherences in Newton’s, not merely assert that it replaced it. This is recollective rationality: the path of development is a rational reconstruction, not a mere sequence.





[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — Halvorson’s realism/antirealism reframing is itself an exercise in Brandomian expressive rationalism: making implicit equivalence commitments explicit
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — Feyerabend’s theoretical pluralism requires genuine independent perspectives; Brandom’s mutual recognition requires the same; both resist single-framework hegemony
[[Freire’s Pedagogy as Concrete Inferentialism]] — Freire enacts Brandom’s abstract framework in adult literacy work, and reveals what the abstract account misses about power





Can Brandom’s inferentialism handle empirical content without a representationalist residue? How does the inferential circle connect to the non-inferential world?
Is recollective rationality genuinely rational progress or a post-hoc narrative imposed on contingent historical sequences?
Does semantic holism make conceptual revision too conservative? If everything is connected, how does any revision propagate far enough to transform a framework?

title: Design and Analysis: Paradox of Bayesian Propensity Scores
text: Outlines the paradox of using propensity scores in Bayesian outcome regressions: while propensity scores should theoretically cancel out when conditioning on all relevant covariates, joint Bayesian models systematically misestimate treatment effects compared to two-stage approaches. The issue arises from violated causal ordering—allowing outcomes to reshape treatment assignment estimation. A modular, two-stage approach respects temporal precedence and recovers propensity score utility.

title: Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability
text:
Morita equivalence generates an unstable triad with Quinean ontological commitment. Two Morita-equivalent theories may quantify over entirely different objects, so formal equivalence does not track ontological sameness.



Morita equivalence permits richer translations than definitional equivalence by allowing new sort symbols to be introduced by definition. The standard example: a points-based geometry and a lines-based geometry are Morita equivalent, yet they appear to be about different things. The question is what this intertranslatability tells us about ontology.




Morita equivalence #model-theory — \(T\) and \(T'\) are Morita equivalent if each can be extended by definitional means to a common, richer theory; definitional equivalence generalised to permit new sort symbols
Quinean ontological commitment #quine — a theory is committed to those entities that must exist for it to be true, read off by existential quantification over a domain
Common Morita extension #model-theory — a richer theory quantifying over all sorts of both \(T\) and \(T'\), proposed as a shared ontological ground






Three claims jointly generate a contradiction: 1. Equivalent theories have the same ontological commitments. 2. A theory’s ontological commitments are what it existentially quantifies over (Quine). 3. A points-geometry and a lines-geometry are Morita equivalent but quantify over different things.
Accepting (3) forces rejection of (1) or (2).



One response: move to a common Morita extension quantifying over both points and lines. This is unstable. New extensions are trivial to generate: quantify over “parallels” (pairs of non-intersecting lines), “triangles” (triples of non-collinear points), and so on. The process iterates without a principled stopping point. There is no canonical most-basic extension.



Morita equivalence is a tool for identifying when two formulations can do the same theoretical work. It operates entirely within the space of formal structure. It does not determine which concrete domain a theory is about, or why one signature picks out real properties rather than gerrymandered ones. The formal equivalence is real; the ontological verdict is suspended.




\(T\) and \(T'\) are Morita equivalent if there exist Morita extensions \(T^+\) of \(T\) and \(T'^+\) of \(T'\) such that \(T^+\) and \(T'^+\) are definitionally equivalent.
A Morita extension of \(T\) adds new sort symbols \(S\), new function and relation symbols, and explicit definitions of \(S\) in terms of existing sorts, so all new entities are definable within \(T\).




[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — Morita equivalence sits one level above definitional equivalence in the liberality hierarchy; a realist resists its permissiveness
[[Button’s Realism Within Limits]] — Button’s semantic externalism is motivated by the same gap: formal equivalence does not fix reference; something pre-theoretical must
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — a cross-domain instance of the same structure: observable relations underdetermine an underlying ontology





Is there a principled criterion for preferring one Morita extension over others, or is the choice always pragmatic?
Does the instability of the common extension refute the structuralist program, or is it an artefact of working in first-order logic?
Does categorical equivalence dissolve or deepen the ontological instability in the points/lines case?

title: Button’s Realism Within Limits
text:
External realism and internal realism both fail. We must occupy the space between them, anchored by messy semantic externalism and conceptual cosmopolitanism, without a determinate answer to where exactly we stand. The book’s own parenthetical — “for what that is worth” — is the honest verdict.



The Limits of Realism (OUP, 2013) takes the model-theoretic argument as a genuine threat rather than reframing it. Part A shows the argument damages external realism. Part B shows that all alternatives fail. Part D stakes the qualified positive position. The vat variations — scenarios that shift gradually from internal to external realism without a sharp transition — demonstrate that the internal/external distinction is a continuum.




External realism #realism — there is a fully mind-independent world; radical deception is a coherent possibility
Internal realism #putnam — truth is relative to a conceptual scheme; reference questions only arise within a scheme
Semantic externalism #reference — reference is fixed by actual causal-semantic relations between speakers and world; a BIV’s “brain” does not refer to brains because the required causal relation is absent
Conceptual cosmopolitanism #realism — we can inhabit multiple conceptual schemes simultaneously; translation between schemes is genuine; no single scheme is uniquely privileged






Button modifies the brain-in-a-vat scenario through a series of steps: universes of shrinking radius, increasing insulation from the environment. At some point semantic externalism clearly fails, but no principled line marks where. The internal/external distinction is a continuum, not a binary.



Semantic externalism grounds reference in causal-semantic relations that pre-exist any theoretical formulation. It cannot be made fully precise without circular appeal to the reference relations it is meant to explain. Button treats this as an honest acknowledgement of complexity, not a defect.



Putnam’s internal realism implies conceptual relativism: different schemes determine different truths. Button’s cosmopolitanism replaces this. We inhabit multiple schemes simultaneously and can navigate between them. No scheme is uniquely correct, but genuine inter-scheme comparison is possible.



External realism is untenable: the model-theoretic argument erodes that faith. Internal realism is untenable: Cartesian angst re-emerges within any scheme. The result is realism within limits: reference is constrained by causal embeddedness, multiple conceptual frameworks are navigable, but no guarantee attaches that we are fully “at” the world rather than near it.

[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — Button’s cosmopolitanism and Feyerabend’s theoretical pluralism share the move of treating multi-scheme navigation as epistemically essential

Is there a principled criterion for where on the internal/external continuum scientific theories sit in practice?
Could Halvorson’s formal tools, applied to the theory-world interface rather than to inter-theory relations, bring rigour to Button’s position?

title: Button’s Realism Within Limits
text: External realism and internal realism both fail. We must occupy the space between them, anchored by messy semantic externalism and conceptual cosmopolitanism, without a determinate answer to where exactly we stand. The book’s own parenthetical — “for what that is worth” — is the honest verdict.

title: Button’s Realism Within Limits
text: The Limits of Realism (OUP, 2013) takes the model-theoretic argument as a genuine threat rather than reframing it. Part A shows the argument damages external realism. Part B shows that all alternatives fail. Part D stakes the qualified positive position. The vat variations — scenarios that shift gradually from internal to external realism without a sharp transition — demonstrate that the internal/external distinction is a continuum.

title: Button’s Realism Within Limits
text:
External realism #realism — there is a fully mind-independent world; radical deception is a coherent possibility
Internal realism #putnam — truth is relative to a conceptual scheme; reference questions only arise within a scheme
Semantic externalism #reference — reference is fixed by actual causal-semantic relations between speakers and world; a BIV’s “brain” does not refer to brains because the required causal relation is absent
Conceptual cosmopolitanism #realism — we can inhabit multiple conceptual schemes simultaneously; translation between schemes is genuine; no single scheme is uniquely privileged

title: Button’s Realism Within Limits
text:
Button modifies the brain-in-a-vat scenario through a series of steps: universes of shrinking radius, increasing insulation from the environment. At some point semantic externalism clearly fails, but no principled line marks where. The internal/external distinction is a continuum, not a binary.



Semantic externalism grounds reference in causal-semantic relations that pre-exist any theoretical formulation. It cannot be made fully precise without circular appeal to the reference relations it is meant to explain. Button treats this as an honest acknowledgement of complexity, not a defect.

External realism is untenable: the model-theoretic argument erodes that faith. Internal realism is untenable: Cartesian angst re-emerges within any scheme. The result is realism within limits: reference is constrained by causal embeddedness, multiple conceptual frameworks are navigable, but no guarantee attaches that we are fully “at” the world rather than near it.
