title: Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity
text:
Competing theories generate evidence unavailable within any single framework. Theoretical proliferation is therefore a logical requirement for maximising testability, not a counsel of permissiveness. Naturalness emerges from inter-theoretic friction; it is not a static metaphysical given.



The German title Wider den Methodenzwang (“Against Forced Methodological Constraint”) is a better guide to Feyerabend’s thesis than the English Against Method. His target is methodological uniformity enforced as a constraint. His commitment to rigour is not in question; his commitment to pluralism is epistemologically motivated.




Counter-induction #feyerabend — the rule to introduce hypotheses that contradict well-confirmed theories, not merely extend them; justified because the consistency condition preserves the older theory, not the better one
Theoretical proliferation #philosophy-of-science — maintaining multiple competing theories simultaneously so as to generate anomalies inaccessible within any single framework
Naturalness (emergent) #lewis — a verdict that emerges from inter-theoretic competition, not a pre-given feature of properties; contrast with Lewis’s static picture






Standard methodology demands that new hypotheses be consistent with existing well-confirmed theories. Feyerabend argues this preserves the institutionally entrenched theory, not the better one. Anomalies relevant to a theory often become visible only from the standpoint of a competing theory. Brownian motion and special relativity both illustrate this.



A theory’s content — what it actually says about the world — can only be fully articulated by contrast with alternatives. A theory tested only against evidence collected within its own framework will miss the anomalies that expose its limits. Pluralism is epistemologically necessary, not merely historically contingent.



Lewis treats natural properties as a static metaphysical given: the world has joints and reference is magnetically attracted to them. Feyerabend’s argument implies we cannot determine which theoretical properties are natural before the competitive process runs. Naturalness is what survives inter-theoretic friction. Halvorson treats naturalness as already encoded in a choice of signature; Feyerabend treats it as earned through testing.












Halvorson
Feyerabend




Level
Meta-level: criteria for comparing theories
Object-level: competing empirical theories


Grounding
Formal taxonomy of equivalence criteria
Epistemology of scientific practice and history


Naturalness
Encoded in signature choice
Emerges from inter-theoretic competition


Theory-world interface
Bracketed
Central: practice is the interface



Feyerabend’s philosophy is grounded in the historical practice of testing competing theories against phenomena. Halvorson’s is synchronic: a map of theoretical space with no account of how science moves through it, or why some directions have proved more fruitful.





[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — Halvorson’s pluralism is formally precise where Feyerabend’s is historically grounded; together they suggest that neither a purely formal nor a purely historical account suffices
[[Button’s Realism Within Limits]] — Button’s messy semantic externalism shares Feyerabend’s move of grounding epistemic authority in actual practice
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — Bayesian and frequentist frameworks are a live instance of the Feyerabendian point: genuine competitors that generate different evidence about the same phenomena





Can counter-induction be formalised as a constraint on the model space or a prior over alternative theories, or does formalisation domesticate it in a way that loses the point?
Is “naturalness emerges from friction” compatible with any version of Lewis’s reference magnetism, or does it require abandoning that picture?
A possible synthesis: use Halvorson’s tools to map theoretical space, and Feyerabend’s epistemology to navigate it. Is this coherent?

title: Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate
text:
The realist/antirealist dispute is a dispute about standards of theoretical equivalence. The realist adopts conservative standards; the antirealist adopts liberal ones.



Putnam’s model-theoretic argument holds that any consistent theory has many permuted models satisfying it equally well, so reference is radically underdetermined. Halvorson’s The Logic in Philosophy of Science (CUP, 2019) reframes this as a proposal about how liberally to individuate theories, not as a standalone semantic threat.




Theoretical equivalence #model-theory — a relation between theories; different criteria (definitional, Morita, categorical) give different verdicts on when two theories are “the same”
Liberal vs. conservative equivalence #realism — the antirealist counts many theories equivalent that the realist resists counting equivalent; the debate just is this disagreement
Permutation argument #putnam — any consistent theory T can have its predicates reassigned to different objects while preserving truth, which blocks determinate reference on naive realist accounts






Putnam presents the model-theoretic argument as showing that reference is indeterminate. Halvorson presents it as proposing an extremely liberal equivalence criterion: under minimal assumptions, all consistent theories collapse into equivalence. The realist’s response, that some predicates carve at natural joints, amounts to insisting on a more conservative criterion.



Halvorson surveys notions from definitional equivalence (same symbols, same theorems) through Morita equivalence (allows new sorts via definition) to categorical equivalence (identifies theories sharing the same category of models). Each criterion is more liberal than the last. No single criterion is uniquely correct; choice depends on purpose and context.



Realism is a commitment to conservative individuation of theories: differences in vocabulary and structure are treated as real differences. Antirealism collapses those differences. The reframing does not resolve the debate; it repositions it on formally tractable ground.




\(T\) and \(T'\) in signatures \(\Sigma\), \(\Sigma'\) are definitionally equivalent if translations \(\tau: \Sigma \to \Sigma'\) and \(\tau': \Sigma' \to \Sigma\) exist such that \(T \vdash \tau'(\tau(\phi)) \leftrightarrow \phi\) for all \(\phi\), and vice versa.




[[Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability]] — the next level of the hierarchy; liberality creates ontological instability
[[Button’s Realism Within Limits]] — Button takes the model-theoretic threat at face value and anchors realism in causal embeddedness rather than formal structure
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — Feyerabend’s pluralism about theories runs parallel to Halvorson’s pluralism about equivalence criteria, but is grounded in the epistemology of practice





Can Lewis’s naturalness do the stabilising work Halvorson gestures at, or does pluralism about criteria dissolve the magnetic link entirely?
If scientific practice is the arbiter of equivalence, does it pick out a preferred criterion? If so, the pluralism is unstable.
Can Halvorson’s formal precision be applied to Button’s theory-world interface problem rather than to inter-theory relations?

title: The Journey Is the Model: Dynamic Path Analysis in PyMC
text: Demonstrates Aalen’s Additive Model for dynamic path analysis—a method to decompose time-varying causal effects in survival data. Shows how to implement fully Bayesian dynamic path models in PyMC using B-splines and the Poisson bridge, tracking mediation effects that evolve over time rather than assuming constant interventional effects. Contrasts with proportional hazards assumptions that mask how treatment effects wax, wane, or reverse across the study period, using the metaphor of an odyssey to illustrate how consequences emerge through time.

title: Heuristics in Latent Space: VAEs and Bayesian Inference
text: Compares machine learning and Bayesian approaches for imputation in missing-data problems, focusing on their ability to preserve latent correlation structures. Examines Variational Autoencoders (standard and mask-aware) versus transparent Bayesian multivariate models in PyMC for reconstructing job satisfaction survey data. Demonstrates that while VAEs can recover latent structures with sufficient data, simpler Bayesian models with explicit prior specifications on covariance recover structure more efficiently and encode inductive biases transparently rather than architecturally.

title: GAMs and GPs: Flexibility and Calibration
text: This post explores the tension between flexibility and interpretability in statistical function approximation, examining Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) and Gaussian Processes (GPs) as complementary abstractions for nonlinear modelling. The author demonstrates how these methods balance the discovery of patterns in data against the imposition of theoretical constraints, illustrating the interplay through motorcycle crash data, insurance loss curves, and educational outcomes. Hierarchical Bayesian spline models are shown to avoid overfitting while improving predictive accuracy by borrowing strength across multiple curves.

title: Condorcet Juries and Incentivised Legibility
text: Uses the Condorcet Jury Theorem to analyze how organizational standardization undermines collective intelligence. Stress-tests Condorcet’s independence assumptions through Item Response Theory (IRT), modeling how “blocks”—groups of employees aligned through training and culture—introduce systematic correlations in errors. Demonstrates that legibility (the drive to standardize and centralize control) and value capture (outsourcing reasoning to KPIs) manufacture exactly the statistical homogeneity that predicts organizational failure, and explores whether interventions like red teaming can restore epistemic diversity.

title: Bayesian Workflow with SEMs
text: A talk at PyCon Ireland 2025 presenting Bayesian workflow methodology applied to Structural Equation Models (SEMs). Emphasizes that statistical modeling is iterative craft rather than checklist compliance, using a job satisfaction dataset to build from Confirmatory Factor Analysis through hierarchical SEM with residual covariance structures. Demonstrates parameter recovery and sensitivity analysis as validation techniques, arguing that careful iteration between theory and data—disciplined by probabilistic programming—yields robust, justifiable scientific conclusions.

title: Bayesian Workflow with SEMs
text:
Key ideas

Bayesian workflow is a craft: iterative exploration guided by theory and data, not checkbox compliance
SEMs formalize scientific theory as systems of statistical relationships with latent constructs and measurement error
Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) validates that observed indicators reliably represent latent constructs through factor loadings
Structural paths between latent variables capture direct and indirect effects (mediation), requiring careful model layering

title: Missing Perspectives as Missing Data
text:
Excluding perspectives from an epistemic community is structurally identical to generating missing-not-at-random data: both produce biased conclusions that aggregating available information cannot repair.



Collective objectivity requires independent perspectives; [[Condorcet Aggregation and Social Objectivity]] shows why. Missing data mechanisms determine whether imputation recovers the true quantity of interest; [[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] shows how. The structural parallel between these two domains is not merely analogical. It identifies a shared formal problem.




MCAR / MAR / MNAR #missing-data — data is missing completely at random, missing at random given observed covariates, or missing not at random (i.e., missingness depends on the unobserved value itself)
Correlated error #condorcet — when jury members share biases, aggregation amplifies rather than cancels error; this is the epistemic analogue of MNAR
Strong ignorability #causal-inference — treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes given observed covariates; the causal analogue of MAR
Non-ignorable missingness #missing-data — missingness depends on the missing value itself; no amount of reweighting by observed covariates recovers the true distribution






In missing data analysis, three regimes differ by what drives the gap between observed and complete data. Under MCAR, absence is unrelated to value: the observed sample is a random draw from the full population, and naive estimation is unbiased. Under MAR, absence depends on observed covariates but not on the unobserved value: conditional on covariates, the observed sample is unbiased, and imputation succeeds. Under MNAR, absence depends on the unobserved value itself: no conditioning on observed covariates can recover the distribution, because the very cases most informative about the gap are the ones missing.
Epistemic communities exhibit the same three regimes. MCAR: some perspectives are absent for reasons uncorrelated with the questions at stake. This is epistemically benign. MAR: some perspectives are absent for reasons correlated with observable features of the community (geography, training, funding access), but not with the substantive conclusions those perspectives would reach. Conditioning on these features partially restores reliability. MNAR: the perspectives most likely to challenge dominant conclusions are systematically excluded precisely because they would challenge them. Oppressive structures generate MNAR epistemic communities. No amount of reweighting within the surviving sample repairs this, because the absent perspectives are not a random or conditionally random draw from the space of possible viewpoints.



The inverse probability weighting (IPW) estimator re-weights observed units by the inverse of their probability of observation, to recover population-level quantities. It works under MAR. Under MNAR, the propensity score is a function of the unobserved outcome itself, so the weights cannot be consistently estimated from observed data alone.
The epistemic parallel: if a scientific community systematically excludes the perspectives of those whose findings would be most disruptive, no diversity program that re-weights the remaining researchers by observable characteristics (field, institution, demographic background) can replicate the missing signal. The absent contribution is absent because of its content, not its correlates.



Missing data analysis handles MNAR through sensitivity analysis, external constraints, and structural assumptions about the missingness mechanism. Causal inference handles non-ignorable treatment assignment through instrumental variables and natural experiments that supply identifying variation from outside the selection process.
The epistemic analogue is Freire’s culture circles and Feyerabend’s counter-induction. Both introduce identifying variation from outside the established inference process: perspectives formed in material conditions and practical experiences that are independent of the dominant framework. They are instruments in the econometric sense: correlated with the question, but excluded from the biased selection mechanism.




Missing data propensity: \(p_R(\mathbf{x}) = P(R = 1 \mid X = \mathbf{x})\)
IPW estimator: \(E[Y] = E\left[\dfrac{YR}{p_R(\mathbf{x})}\right]\)
This recovers \(E[Y]\) under MAR. Under MNAR, \(p_R\) depends on \(Y\) itself: \(p_R(\mathbf{x}, y) = P(R = 1 \mid X = \mathbf{x}, Y = y)\), and the weights are unidentified from observed data alone.
The Diversity Prediction Theorem supplies the positive condition: \(\text{Collective error} = \text{Average individual error} - \text{Diversity}\), where diversity is variance in individual predictions around the collective prediction. MNAR exclusion destroys diversity by exactly removing the perspectives that diverge from the collective prediction.




[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — the source formal framework; this note extends it into the epistemic domain
[[Condorcet Aggregation and Social Objectivity]] — the epistemic problem this note formalises; correlated error maps to MNAR, independence maps to MAR
[[Freire’s Pedagogy as Concrete Inferentialism]] — Freire’s culture circles function as instruments, supplying identifying variation from outside the biased selection process
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — the broader argument that statistical reasoning and social epistemology share deep structure
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — counter-induction as the methodological strategy for introducing MNAR-breaking variation





Can sensitivity analysis techniques from missing data (e.g. Rosenbaum bounds, pattern mixture models) be adapted to measure the severity of epistemic MNAR in a given scientific community?
The IPW analogy breaks down if the excluded perspectives would not have higher individual accuracy but only greater diversity. Does the Diversity Prediction Theorem handle this, or does the Condorcet theorem’s \(p > 0.5\) requirement resurface?
Is there an epistemic analogue of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)? What would it mean for a perspective to be “stable” in the relevant sense?

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text:
Marketing mix models are underidentified in precisely the way Manski’s partial identification framework describes: observational data define a wide identified set, and each additional source of design information (lift tests, cross-validation, functional form assumptions) narrows that set along specific parameter directions while leaving others untouched.



Manski’s programme distinguishes what the data tell you from what your assumptions tell you. Standard econometric practice imposes enough structure (functional forms, independence, exclusion restrictions) to point-identify parameters. Remove those assumptions and the estimated point becomes an identified set: a range of values all consistent with the observed data distribution. This framing applies directly to marketing mix models, where severe collinearity and limited spend variation leave the likelihood surface flat in important directions.




Identified Set #identified-set — the range of parameter values consistent with the data under the weakest defensible assumptions
Point Identification #point-identification — occurs when the identified set collapses to a single value, typically requiring strong (often untestable) assumptions
Lift Test #lift-test — a randomised experiment measuring the incremental causal effect of a marketing channel at a specific spend level
Saturation Curve #saturation-curve — the function describing diminishing marginal returns to advertising spend, often parameterised as a Hill curve with half-saturation \(K\) and slope \(n\)
Adstock #adstock — the temporal carryover of advertising effect; a decay structure applied to spend before it enters the response function






The question shifts from “what is the estimate of \(\theta\)?” to “what values of \(\theta\) are consistent with what we can observe, under the weakest assumptions we are willing to defend?” If the identified set is narrow, the data are informative. If it is wide, that width represents genuine uncertainty that point estimates were papering over.



Manski identifies a hierarchy. Raw data variation provides the loosest bounds. Monotonicity assumptions (e.g. treatment effects are non-negative) tighten them. Independence assumptions (random assignment, selection on observables) can collapse the set to a point, at the cost of strong untestable commitments. Instrumental variables narrow the set under weaker conditions than full independence, but achieve point identification only with additional homogeneity or monotonicity (the LATE framework of Imbens and Angrist).



The observational time series defines a wide identified set over saturation parameters, adstock parameters, and baseline sales. Many parameter combinations generate essentially the same predicted sales trajectory. Lift tests narrow the set for saturation parameters by providing locally identified causal estimates at specific spend levels. They do not speak to adstock (tests are too short for carryover to manifest), they do not speak to baseline (no experiment takes spend to zero in most cases), and they do not resolve the attribution share problem.
Repeated lift tests at varying spend levels trace out the response curve empirically, sharpening the posterior over saturation parameters conditional on the chosen functional form. The Hill curve assumption remains: you are fitting a parametric form to a handful of experimental points, not nonparametrically identifying the curve. Uncertainty about functional form does not show up in the posterior unless you explicitly do model comparison.



Three diagnostics triangulate different failure modes of the likelihood specification:

Repeated lift tests at varying spend check whether saturation identification is consistent across experimental contexts. Inconsistency signals a wrong functional form or unmodelled heterogeneity.
Time-series cross-validation (TSCV) parameter stability checks whether the full model is stable once saturation curves are anchored. If calibrated parameters are stable across rolling windows but uncalibrated parameters drift, the lift tests are identifying something real.
Predictive TSCV performance checks whether the joint model is coherent as a generative model. This is necessary but not sufficient for structural validity, because a model can predict well and decompose badly.




Manski’s analysis of extrapolation applies directly. MMM attribution asks: what fraction of sales would have occurred at zero spend on channel \(k\)? This counterfactual requires extrapolating the response function to zero, almost always outside the support of the observational data. The curve’s behaviour near zero is governed by the functional form, not the data. Lift tests help only at the spend levels actually tested. The identified set expands dramatically in this extrapolation region.



A calibrated MMM should present a posterior where widths vary systematically across parameters: tight for lift-calibrated saturation parameters, moderate for time-series-identified dynamics, wide for weakly identified quantities like long-run adstock or the zero-spend counterfactual. Confusing “the posterior has finite width because of my prior” with “the posterior has finite width because the data identified this parameter” is the central error Manski’s framework guards against.




For a Hill saturation curve: \[f(s) = \frac{s^n}{K^n + s^n}\] where \(K\) is the half-saturation point and \(n\) controls steepness. A lift test at spend level \(s_0\) identifies \(f'(s_0)\) locally. The full curve shape at \(s \to 0\) remains extrapolated from the parametric form.




[[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]] — the ecumenical framing that motivates asking “what does the likelihood actually identify?”
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — Manski’s bounds framework originated in the same intellectual milieu as missing-data and causal-inference formalisms
[[Missing Perspectives as Missing Data]] — partial identification resonates with the idea that excluded perspectives create non-ignorable gaps in the evidence base

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text: Marketing mix models are underidentified in precisely the way Manski’s partial identification framework describes: observational data define a wide identified set, and each additional source of design information (lift tests, cross-validation, functional form assumptions) narrows that set along specific parameter directions while leaving others untouched.
crumbs: Manski's Partial Identification and MMM Calibration

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text: Manski’s programme distinguishes what the data tell you from what your assumptions tell you. Standard econometric practice imposes enough structure (functional forms, independence, exclusion restrictions) to point-identify parameters. Remove those assumptions and the estimated point becomes an identified set: a range of values all consistent with the observed data distribution. This framing applies directly to marketing mix models, where severe collinearity and limited spend variation leave the likelihood surface flat in important directions.
crumbs: Manski's Partial Identification and MMM Calibration

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text:
Identified Set #identified-set — the range of parameter values consistent with the data under the weakest defensible assumptions
Point Identification #point-identification — occurs when the identified set collapses to a single value, typically requiring strong (often untestable) assumptions
Lift Test #lift-test — a randomised experiment measuring the incremental causal effect of a marketing channel at a specific spend level
Saturation Curve #saturation-curve — the function describing diminishing marginal returns to advertising spend, often parameterised as a Hill curve with half-saturation \(K\) and slope \(n\)
Adstock #adstock — the temporal carryover of advertising effect; a decay structure applied to spend before it enters the response function
crumbs: Manski's Partial Identification and MMM Calibration

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text:
The question shifts from “what is the estimate of \(\theta\)?” to “what values of \(\theta\) are consistent with what we can observe, under the weakest assumptions we are willing to defend?” If the identified set is narrow, the data are informative. If it is wide, that width represents genuine uncertainty that point estimates were papering over.



Manski identifies a hierarchy. Raw data variation provides the loosest bounds. Monotonicity assumptions (e.g. treatment effects are non-negative) tighten them. Independence assumptions (random assignment, selection on observables) can collapse the set to a point, at the cost of strong untestable commitments. Instrumental variables narrow the set under weaker conditions than full independence, but achieve point identification only with additional homogeneity or monotonicity (the LATE framework of Imbens and Angrist).



The observational time series defines a wide identified set over saturation parameters, adstock parameters, and baseline sales. Many parameter combinations generate essentially the same predicted sales trajectory. Lift tests narrow the set for saturation parameters by providing locally identified causal estimates at specific spend levels. They do not speak to adstock (tests are too short for carryover to manifest), they do not speak to baseline (no experiment takes spend to zero in most cases), and they do not resolve the attribution share problem.
Repeated lift tests at varying spend levels trace out the response curve empirically, sharpening the posterior over saturation parameters conditional on the chosen functional form. The Hill curve assumption remains: you are fitting a parametric form to a handful of experimental points, not nonparametrically identifying the curve. Uncertainty about functional form does not show up in the posterior unless you explicitly do model comparison.



Three diagnostics triangulate different failure modes of the likelihood specification:

Repeated lift tests at varying spend check whether saturation identification is consistent across experimental contexts. Inconsistency signals a wrong functional form or unmodelled heterogeneity.
Time-series cross-validation (TSCV) parameter stability checks whether the full model is stable once saturation curves are anchored. If calibrated parameters are stable across rolling windows but uncalibrated parameters drift, the lift tests are identifying something real.
Predictive TSCV performance checks whether the joint model is coherent as a generative model. This is necessary but not sufficient for structural validity, because a model can predict well and decompose badly.




Manski’s analysis of extrapolation applies directly. MMM attribution asks: what fraction of sales would have occurred at zero spend on channel \(k\)? This counterfactual requires extrapolating the response function to zero, almost always outside the support of the observational data. The curve’s behaviour near zero is governed by the functional form, not the data. Lift tests help only at the spend levels actually tested. The identified set expands dramatically in this extrapolation region.



A calibrated MMM should present a posterior where widths vary systematically across parameters: tight for lift-calibrated saturation parameters, moderate for time-series-identified dynamics, wide for weakly identified quantities like long-run adstock or the zero-spend counterfactual. Confusing “the posterior has finite width because of my prior” with “the posterior has finite width because the data identified this parameter” is the central error Manski’s framework guards against.
crumbs: Manski's Partial Identification and MMM Calibration

title: Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration
text: For a Hill saturation curve: \[f(s) = \frac{s^n}{K^n + s^n}\] where \(K\) is the half-saturation point and \(n\) controls steepness. A lift test at spend level \(s_0\) identifies \(f'(s_0)\) locally. The full curve shape at \(s \to 0\) remains extrapolated from the parametric form.

title: The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive
text:
The likelihood principle, read ecumenically, is a directive to encode all available design information into the likelihood rather than a partisan claim favouring one inferential framework. This reading shifts the question from “does all evidence live in the likelihood?” to “how should we encode what we know into the likelihood?”



Birnbaum’s likelihood principle states that all evidence about an unknown parameter \(\theta\) provided by observation \(x\) is contained in the likelihood function \(L(\theta \mid x)\). In its strong form, this favours Bayesian and likelihoodist inference over frequentist methods, because frequentist inference depends on features outside the likelihood: the sample space, the stopping rule, the set of experiments not performed. The ecumenical reading proposed here sidesteps that debate. It treats the principle as a design standard for statistical models rather than a theorem about evidential content.




Likelihood Principle #likelihood-principle — the thesis that \(L(\theta \mid x)\) contains all the evidential content of an observation
Design Information #design-information — knowledge about the data-generating mechanism (randomisation, selection, assignment) that can be encoded in the model
Propensity Score #propensity-score — \(e(x) = P(\text{treatment} \mid \text{covariates})\), a summary of the assignment mechanism in observational studies






Instead of deploying the likelihood principle as a weapon in the Bayesian-frequentist wars, read it as: the likelihood is the primary locus of modelling judgment. The statistician’s job is to formulate it well for the question at hand. This preserves the principle’s emphasis on the likelihood without legislating which inferential machinery you attach to it.



In observational studies, incorporating a propensity score into a regression enriches the likelihood with information about the assignment mechanism. The modelling judgment is about how to represent treatment assignment. Getting that right matters more than whether you compute a confidence interval or a posterior. This example works across frameworks: you can use propensity scores in frequentist or Bayesian regression.



A critic could argue this reading deflates the principle to near-triviality. “Formulate your likelihood carefully” is good advice, but Birnbaum, Edwards, and Royall meant something stronger: that design features living outside the likelihood are irrelevant. The ecumenical reading inverts this by saying design information is important, so put it inside the likelihood. The distinctive content of the original principle drops out. A fair response: call this a successor principle, a “modelling principle,” which preserves everything useful while being honest that it makes a broader claim.



Frequentist concerns about coverage and error control operate at a different level from likelihood specification. They ask: if we ran this procedure many times under various true parameter values, does inference reliably track the truth? These concerns act as an external diagnostic on whether the likelihood has been well specified, not as an alternative to it. Bayesian coherence gives internal consistency. Frequentist simulation gives external validation. The two are complementary.





[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — propensity scores connect the assignment mechanism to missing-data theory
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — broader reflections on the relationship between statistical frameworks
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — the natural continuation: what happens when design information only partially identifies the model
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — methodological pluralism in statistics echoes Feyerabend’s argument against method-monism in science





Can the “modelling principle” be stated with enough precision to be falsifiable, or does it collapse into “be a good modeller”?
Does the boundary between likelihood and prior become load-bearing here? In Bayesian MMM calibration, lift test results often enter through priors rather than the likelihood proper.
Are there cases where design information genuinely resists likelihood encoding (network interference, adaptive experiments)?

href: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation.html
title: Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation
text:
Preemption cases reveal that causation is a many-faced concept. Productive continuity, counterfactual dependence, responsibility, and explanatory relevance can deliver conflicting verdicts. No single analysis captures all of them because they track genuinely different features of causal situations.



Billy and Suzy both throw rocks at a bottle. Suzy’s arrives first and shatters it. Billy’s would have shattered it had Suzy not thrown. Lewis’s counterfactual analysis (in its original form) says Suzy did not cause the shattering, because the counterfactual “if Suzy hadn’t thrown, the bottle wouldn’t have shattered” is false. This is plainly the wrong verdict.




Preemption #preemption — a cause fires first, rendering a backup cause redundant; the backup’s presence blocks simple counterfactual analysis
Productive causation #productive-causation — continuous physical process connecting cause to effect (Salmon, Dowe, Glennan)
Dependence causation #dependence-causation — outcome varies with input; the framework of Pearl’s DAGs and Rubin’s potential outcomes
Causal pluralism #causal-pluralism — the view that “cause” tracks multiple distinct relations, not one






Lewis revised his analysis repeatedly: chains of counterfactual dependence, fragility of events, then “Causation as Influence” (2000) with patterns of counterfactual variation. Each revision added complexity while chasing the same quarry: the single correct counterfactual analysis. The revisions grew baroque.



When we say “Suzy caused the shattering,” we might track: (1) productive continuity from her throw to the breaking, (2) counterfactual dependence of the outcome on the input, (3) responsibility and blame, (4) explanatory relevance. In the preemption case these come apart. The concept feels difficult precisely because it serves multiple roles simultaneously.



Both Pearl’s structural causal models and Rubin’s potential outcomes are dependence accounts. Pearl’s do-calculus asks what happens to \(Y\) when you set \(X\) to a value. Rubin compares potential outcomes under treatment versus control. Both track whether and how much an outcome varies with an input. Neither represents the physical process connecting them.
A DAG’s arrows encode functional dependencies, not mechanisms. Two DAGs can be structurally identical while representing utterly different physical processes. The dependence framework treats all instances of the same structural relation as equivalent. A production-oriented account insists they are fundamentally different.



Mechanism knowledge enables generalization in ways pure dependence knowledge does not. Knowing the RCT showed efficacy in population A says little about population B unless you understand the pathway. The multiplicity of causal concepts reflects a real multiplicity in the questions we need causation to answer.





[[Lewis’s Unification Programme as Nested Idealization]] — preemption as the stress point of Lewis’s programme
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — dependence frameworks underlie both missing data theory and causal inference
[[Competing Risks as Causal Preemption]] — preemption instantiated in survival analysis
[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — an attempt to encode process within dependence frameworks





Can a formal framework represent both productive and dependence causation without collapsing one into the other?
Is causal pluralism stable, or does it invite an unprincipled eclecticism?
crumbs: Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation

title: Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary
text:
Aalen’s additive hazard model introduces time as a constitutive dimension of causal structure, encoding process information within a dependence framework. The additive functional form is the price of admission: it captures temporal dynamics only for processes whose productive structure is well-approximated by additive hazard contributions.



Standard Pearlian DAGs represent dependencies as static. Arrows encode functional relationships that hold, full stop. Odd Aalen’s dynamic path analysis lets the strength and direction of causal influence change as a process evolves. Risk factors that matter early may become irrelevant later. Mediating pathways may switch on after a threshold.




Time-varying coefficients #time-varying-coefficients — in Aalen’s additive model, regression coefficients are functions of time \(t\), not constants. Formally: \(h(t) = \beta_0(t) + \beta_1(t)X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p(t)X_p\)
Dynamic path analysis #dynamic-path-analysis — a sequence of time-indexed DAGs where causal structure evolves
Functional form constraint #functional-form — the additive assumption shapes what dynamics the model can express; it is a modelling choice, not a discovery about nature






By letting coefficients vary with time, Aalen captures something Pearl and Rubin cannot: the evolution of causal structure during a process. You can watch the causal graph change and infer something about the dynamics of the underlying mechanism from the pattern of change. This goes further toward accommodating productive causation than anything in standard causal inference.



The additive assumption is strong. Hazard contributions combine as \(h(t) = \sum_k \beta_k(t)X_k\). This is imposed for mathematical tractability, not derived from biological knowledge. A multiplicative model (Cox regression) or something with thresholds and feedback would yield a different picture of evolving causal structure.
Real biological mechanisms often violate additivity. Feedback loops, threshold effects, nonlinear interactions, and phase transitions resist capture in any fixed functional form. Aalen gets closer to the mechanism, but the gap between model and process relocates from the structural level (which arrows exist) to the parametric level (what form the influence takes).



Classical thermodynamics treats equilibrium states as static snapshots. Non-equilibrium thermodynamics captures dynamics of heat flow and entropy production, but achieves tractability through its own assumptions: linear response, local equilibrium, specific transport equations. The refinement is real. The escape from idealization is not.



The trajectory from Pearl’s static DAGs to Aalen’s dynamic paths is a trajectory from one idealization to a richer one that captures more phenomena at the cost of different assumptions. The question is not “which is right” but “which serves which purposes.” For estimating an average treatment effect, Rubin suffices. For evolving causal structure in disease, Aalen gives something neither Pearl nor Rubin can. For actual molecular biology, you leave the statistical framework altogether.




Aalen’s additive hazard model: \[h_i(t) = \beta_0(t) + \beta_1(t)X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p(t)X_{ip}\]
The cumulative regression functions \(B_k(t) = \int_0^t \beta_k(s) \, ds\) are estimable nonparametrically via least-squares at each event time.




[[Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation]] — Aalen’s model as a partial reconciliation of dependence and production
[[Competing Risks as Causal Preemption]] — the additive constraint becomes especially limiting in competing risks with non-additive interactions
[[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]] — functional form choices shape the likelihood and determine what the data can identify
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — partial identification applies here: the additive form identifies certain dynamics while leaving others in a wide identified set





Can nonparametric or semiparametric extensions of Aalen’s model relax the additivity constraint while preserving interpretability?
Does the analogy to non-equilibrium thermodynamics suggest a principled hierarchy of causal idealizations ordered by what dynamics they can represent?
See [[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] for how a Bayesian PyMC implementation sidesteps the additivity constraint by treating the path decomposition as diagnostic rather than as the estimand itself
See [[Hernán’s Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes]] for the interventionist critique of treating time-varying coefficients as primary causal objects

title: Lewis’s Unification Programme as Nested Idealization
text:
Lewis’s philosophical programme (possible worlds, counterfactual causation, best-system laws, the Principal Principle) is simultaneously the strongest evidence for Appiah’s thesis about productive idealization and the most ambitious attempt to do what Appiah counsels against: collapsing productive ambiguities into a single unified framework.




Principal Principle #principal-principle — rational credence in a proposition should equal the believed objective chance, absent inadmissible information
Best-system account #best-system — laws and chances are optimal summaries of the Humean mosaic, balancing simplicity and strength
Counterfactual analysis of causation #counterfactual-causation — A caused B iff, had A not occurred, B would not have occurred (evaluated via nearest possible worlds)
Modal realism #modal-realism — possible worlds are as real as the actual world






The Principal Principle bridges subjective credence and objective chance. It manages probability’s Janus face by introducing an idealized rational agent who perfectly calibrates belief to chance. Appiah would observe: this bridge is itself an idealization. The ideal agent is no more real than the frictionless plane. The unification is achieved within the model, not in the world.



Lewis systematically analyses causation, chance, law, and counterfactual dependence within one framework. Causation reduces to counterfactual dependence. Counterfactuals are evaluated via possible worlds. Laws are best-system summaries. Chances fall out of laws. The Principal Principle ties chances to credence. Everything interlocks.



First: the ambition of unification is itself an idealization about idealization. Lewis treats his analytical tools as if they belong to a single metaphysical picture. Each tool was developed for a particular domain. Forcing them together may sacrifice the productive looseness that made each useful alone.
Second, more sympathetic: Lewis’s programme magnificently demonstrates the generative power of “as if” reasoning. The possible worlds framework transformed modal logic, philosophy of language, decision theory, and metaphysics. Most philosophers who use it reject modal realism. They reason “as if,” and it works.



Lewis: the world has determinate structure, and properly analysed concepts can mirror it. Appiah: concepts are tools whose power partly depends on flexibility and imprecision. The search for perfect mirroring is itself an idealization to hold lightly.





[[Appiah’s As If and Productive Idealization]] — the framework applied here
[[Probability’s Janus Face and Productive Ambiguity]] — the Principal Principle as attempted resolution
[[Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation]] — where Lewis’s unification breaks down
[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — Lewis’s realism about possible worlds vs. instrumentalist alternatives
[[Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability]] — formal tools for assessing when two frameworks are equivalent





Is Lewis’s modal realism the honest destination of his programme, or can the framework survive without it?
Does “as if all the way down” lead to a regress, or does it stabilize at the pragmatic level?

title: Appiah’s As If and Productive Idealization
text:
Kwame Anthony Appiah argues that idealization (reasoning “as if” known falsehoods were true) is constitutive of theorizing across science, ethics, and practical life. The power of idealizations often derives from their ambiguity and flexibility, not from their precision.



Appiah’s As If: Idealization and Ideals (2017) builds on Hans Vaihinger’s Philosophy of “As If” (1911). Vaihinger catalogued useful fictions across intellectual life. Appiah pushes further: idealizations are not convenient shortcuts but necessary structural features of reasoning itself.




Idealization #idealization — treating the world as if it matched a simplified or perfected model, knowing it does not
Productive ambiguity #productive-ambiguity — the feature of successful idealizations that lets them serve multiple communities and answer different questions simultaneously
As-if reasoning #as-if — deploying a framework you know to be literally false because it generates useful inferences




Appiah connects the “as if” strategy across theoretical and practical domains. Scientists treat surfaces as frictionless. Economists treat agents as perfectly rational. These models are known falsehoods, yet reasoning proceeds through them rather than despite them.
The key move extends this to moral and political life. Our ideals of justice, equality, and democracy function like idealizations in physics. No society perfectly realizes justice, just as no surface is frictionless. Reasoning as if these ideals could be realized, and measuring reality against them, drives moral and political progress.
Appiah remains attentive to risks. Idealizations mislead when we forget they are idealizations. The more entrenched a framework becomes, the more vigilance we need. The philosophical error is mistaking the model for reality.
This connects to Feyerabend’s methodological pluralism. Where Feyerabend argues that counter-induction prevents theoretical monocultures, Appiah argues that we should hold any single idealization lightly precisely because its power comes from being one tool among many.




[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — if idealizations are tools rather than mirrors, theoretical equivalence becomes expected rather than troubling
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — Feyerabend’s pluralism and Appiah’s “hold lightly” share a common structure
[[Probability’s Janus Face and Productive Ambiguity]] — probability as a case study of Appiah’s thesis
[[Lewis’s Unification Programme as Nested Idealization]] — Lewis as Appiah’s foil





Does Appiah’s view collapse into pragmatism? What distinguishes “productive fiction” from “true enough”?
Can the idealization framework account for its own status? Is “idealizations are constitutive of reasoning” itself an idealization?

title: Probability’s Janus Face and Productive Ambiguity
text:
Probability’s simultaneous epistemic and aleatory character is not a defect awaiting resolution but a structural feature that explains the concept’s extraordinary reach. Appiah would treat this duality as a paradigm case of productive idealization.



Ian Hacking’s The Emergence of Probability (1975) traces how the modern concept of probability arose in the mid-seventeenth century from the convergence of two traditions: one about credibility of testimony (epistemic), another about stable frequencies in games of chance (aleatory). The concept was born dual, and the duality persists through every Bayesian-frequentist debate since.




Epistemic probability #epistemic-probability — degree of rational belief given evidence
Aleatory probability #aleatory-probability — stable frequency or propensity in nature
Janus-faced concept #janus-faced — Hacking’s term for probability’s irreducible duality
Conceptual genealogy #conceptual-genealogy — Hacking’s method of tracing conditions of possibility for a concept






Hacking argues that probability required specific preconditions before it could be thinkable. Changes in European thought about evidence, testimony, and the relation between knowledge and opinion had to occur first. His method is archaeological: he reveals that what feels natural and inevitable is historically contingent.



Appiah would read the duality differently. An idealization that serves only one purpose has limited reach. An idealization that operates in multiple registers, adaptable to different purposes, proves indispensable. The same mathematics describes your uncertainty about rain and the decay rate of uranium. This versatility is the mark of a deeply successful idealization.



The dual reading lets practitioners slide between interpretations without noticing. A scientist invokes objective frequencies when justifying a method, then shifts to subjective credence when interpreting a result. The flexibility that makes probability powerful also makes it harder to track one’s commitments. Appiah would say: this is precisely the moment to press the question hardest.



If a theoretical idealization succeeds partly through ambiguity, the same may hold for moral ideals. “Equality” and “freedom” are Janus-faced: formal versus substantive equality, negative versus positive freedom. Their productive ambiguity lets diverse communities orient toward them while disagreeing about exact content. The flexibility is load-bearing.





[[Appiah’s As If and Productive Idealization]] — the parent thesis that this note instantiates
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — earlier reflections on the philosophical status of statistical reasoning
[[Lewis’s Unification Programme as Nested Idealization]] — Lewis’s Principal Principle as an attempt to resolve the duality
[[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]] — another case where a foundational statistical principle admits multiple readings





Does every successful idealization exhibit Janus-faced character, or is probability special?
Hacking’s genealogical method and Appiah’s functional method give different explanations for the duality. Are they compatible or rival accounts?

title: Competing Risks as Causal Preemption
text:
Competing risks models in survival analysis handle exactly the structural situation that philosophical preemption creates. Their response to it is epistemically more honest than Lewis’s: they explicitly mark which causal questions the data can and cannot answer.



A patient faces simultaneous risk of death from cancer, heart disease, and stroke. If cancer kills first, we never observe what heart disease would have done. The other causes are preempted. This is Billy-and-Suzy made flesh.




Cause-specific hazard #cause-specific-hazard — among those still alive at time \(t\), the instantaneous rate of dying from cause \(k\). Explicitly conditional on not yet having been preempted.
Cumulative incidence function #cumulative-incidence — probability of failing from cause \(k\) by time \(t\), accounting for the presence of competing risks
Non-identifiable counterfactual #non-identifiable-counterfactual — the question “what would heart disease have done without cancer?” may lack a coherent answer because the causes share a body and interact






The competing risks framework refuses the question in Lewis’s form. Fine and Gray emphasize that removing one cause of death can change the entire biological landscape. The causes share metabolic pathways, inflammatory processes, and vascular biology. They are not independent mechanisms sitting side by side.
The framework characterizes the joint structure of competing processes: cause-specific hazards, cumulative incidence functions, copula structures for dependence. It accepts that this characterization is what causal knowledge looks like here. There is no hidden fact about what heart disease would have done in a cancer-free world.



Pearl would draw a DAG, specify structural equations, and evaluate the do-intervention. Rubin would define potential outcomes under each cause. Both retain the ambition of answering the counterfactual question. The competing risks tradition acknowledges that some counterfactuals are not well-defined. The processes are not separable in the way the counterfactual presupposes.



From Appiah’s perspective, the competing risks framework builds into its structure an acknowledgment of the limits of idealization. It models the causal situation while flagging which questions it cannot answer. Lewis’s programme, with its ambition for a complete analysis of causation, lacks this structural modesty.



The reason competing risks are difficult is that the underlying processes are physically entangled. Cancer treatment may increase cardiac risk through cardiotoxic chemotherapy. The competing risks framework captures the statistical shadow of this entanglement in the form of dependent censoring and non-identifiable joint distributions. The entanglement itself exceeds what any dependence framework can represent.





[[Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation]] — the philosophical framework that competing risks instantiate
[[Sorites Paradox and Survival Analysis]] — another connection between philosophical puzzles and survival analysis
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — competing risks create a specific missing data pattern (what would the preempted cause have done?)
[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — an attempt to capture dynamics within this framework





Can we formalize when a counterfactual is “not well-defined” versus merely hard to identify?
Do competing risks models suggest a general principle: the more physically entangled causal processes are, the less useful counterfactual reasoning becomes?

title: Scale Dependence in Causal Decomposition
text:
Additive path decomposition in survival mediation holds on the latent predictor scale (\(\eta\)) but breaks on the hazard scale. If the hazard determines patient outcomes, then the scientific relevance of a latent-scale decomposition requires justification, not just acknowledgment.



Dynamic path analysis decomposes a latent predictor additively: \(\eta(t) = \alpha_1(t) X + \alpha_2(t) M\). A link function (softplus, exponential, logistic) maps \(\eta\) to the hazard \(\lambda(t)\). The link is nonlinear, so additivity on \(\eta\) does not imply additivity on \(\lambda\). The direct and indirect contributions to \(\lambda\) interact through the curvature of the link. G-computation propagates uncertainty through this nonlinearity to produce marginal contrasts, but the path decomposition itself is approximate on the outcome scale.




Latent predictor #latent-predictor — the linear combination \(\eta(t)\) before the link function; the scale on which structural coefficients are additive
Link function #link-function — the monotone transformation from \(\eta\) to \(\lambda\); softplus, exponential, and logistic are common choices in discrete-time survival
Scale dependence #scale-dependence — the property that a causal decomposition’s form depends on which scale you compute it on; additive on one scale, interactive on another






The structural model specifies \(\eta(t) = \alpha_1(t) X + \beta(t) L + \alpha_2(t) M\). On this scale, the direct contribution of \(X\) is \(\alpha_1(t)\) and the indirect contribution through \(M\) is the product \(\beta(t) \cdot \alpha_2(t)\). The decomposition is exact. The two paths sum.



Apply softplus: \(\lambda(t) = \log(1 + \exp(\eta(t)))\). The hazard is a nonlinear function of \(\eta\), so the direct and indirect contributions to \(\lambda\) do not sum. The marginal effect of \(X\) on \(\lambda\) through the direct path depends on the value of \(M\), and vice versa. The decomposition is no longer additive on the scale that determines survival probabilities.



Two positions are available. First: the latent predictor is the natural object. The coefficients measure causal influence in the structural sense, and the link function is merely a device for ensuring the hazard stays positive. On this view, the decomposition is exact where it matters. Second: the hazard determines when patients die. A decomposition that is only additive on a transformed scale is scientifically incomplete. The interaction induced by the link function is real. If \(\alpha_1(t)\) and \(\alpha_2(t)\) are both large and positive, the softplus’s near-linearity breaks down, and the cross-path interaction on \(\lambda\) becomes substantial.



G-computation resolves the scale issue for marginal estimands. Simulate counterfactual survival curves under different intervention regimes (set \(M\) to its natural value under control, then under treatment) and compute contrasts on the survival probability scale. These contrasts absorb the link function’s nonlinearity. The NDE and NIE computed via g-computation are scale-free in the sense that they compare survival probabilities, not latent predictors. The coefficient decomposition and the g-computation decomposition agree qualitatively (same sign, same temporal pattern) but diverge quantitatively when \(\eta\) is far from zero.

[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — Aalen’s original additive model avoids this problem by keeping the hazard itself additive, at the cost of allowing negative hazards





Is there a natural metric for how badly the link function breaks additivity at a given point in \(\eta\)-space? The second derivative of the link evaluated at typical posterior values of \(\eta\) might serve.
Would a log-link (exponential hazard) be preferable to softplus for interpretability, since the decomposition becomes multiplicative on the hazard scale and additive on the log-hazard scale?
Does the distinction between latent-scale and hazard-scale decomposition matter in practice when \(\eta\) values are small (where softplus is approximately linear)?

title: Non-Collapsibility of Hazard Ratios
text:
Hazard ratios are non-collapsible: the marginal hazard ratio differs from a weighted average of stratum-specific hazard ratios, even without confounding. This mathematical property makes hazard ratios poor causal estimands. Survival curves and their contrasts are the correct target.



Cox proportional hazards models remain the default in applied survival analysis. Analysts report hazard ratios as if they were risk ratios. The non-collapsibility problem means that adjusting for a covariate changes the hazard ratio even when the covariate is not a confounder. This is a property of the measure, not a data problem.




Non-collapsibility #non-collapsibility — a measure is non-collapsible when the marginal value is not a weighted average of stratum-specific values. Odds ratios and hazard ratios share this property. Risk differences do not.
Built-in selection bias #survivorship-bias — at time \(t\), the hazard ratio compares survivors in each arm. If treatment works, the treated arm retains its frail members while the control arm has already lost theirs. The comparison groups become non-comparable through the passage of time itself.
Restricted mean survival time (RMST) #rmst — the area under the survival curve up to horizon \(\tau\). A collapsible, interpretable causal estimand: the expected time spent alive (or as a customer) within a fixed window.






Hernán and Robins identify three interrelated problems. First, the hazard at time \(t\) conditions on survival to \(t\), which is a post-treatment variable. Even in a perfect RCT, this induces selection bias that grows over time. Second, the proportional hazards assumption masks treatment-effect heterogeneity. If the treatment delays events for one subgroup but not another, the apparent hazard ratio changes over time as the risk set composition shifts. Third, the hazard ratio at any time point lacks a clean counterfactual interpretation. “The rate of events among survivors” does not map to a well-defined potential-outcome contrast.



The survival function \(S(t)\) under each treatment condition yields collapsible, interpretable contrasts. The survival probability difference at a fixed horizon gives a risk-difference interpretation. The RMST gives an expected-duration interpretation:
\[\text{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^{\tau} S(t) \, dt\]
The difference in RMST between treatment arms has a direct counterfactual meaning: the expected additional time spent in the desired state if assigned to treatment rather than control.



Three approaches recover causal survival curves from observational data. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) creates a pseudo-population where treatment is independent of confounders, then estimates weighted Kaplan-Meier curves. G-computation fits a conditional outcome model and averages predicted curves over the confounder distribution. Doubly robust methods combine both, requiring only one of the two models to be correct.



Competing-risks settings raise a sharper version of this issue. Fine-Gray regression models the cumulative incidence function directly, through the subdistribution hazard, which looks like a fix for the causal estimand problem in [[Competing Risks as Causal Preemption]]. It is not. The subdistribution hazard ratio is non-collapsible for the same reason the ordinary Cox hazard ratio is: it is not a weighted average of stratum-specific subdistribution hazard ratios, even absent confounding. The correct use of Fine-Gray (or of cause-specific hazard models) is to construct the cumulative incidence function through standardization and read the CIF contrast as the causal quantity. Interpreting the regression coefficient itself as a causal effect repeats the original mistake in a new model.




The causal RMST difference:
\[\Delta \text{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^{\tau} [S(t \mid A=1) - S(t \mid A=0)] \, dt\]
For economic applications with time-varying revenue \(r(t)\):
\[\Delta \text{LTV}(\tau) = \int_0^{\tau} r(t) \cdot [S(t \mid A=1) - S(t \mid A=0)] \, dt\]




[[Competing Risks as Causal Preemption]] — competing risks inherit the same problems with hazard-based estimands; the cumulative incidence function is the competing-risks analogue of the survival curve
[[Hernán’s Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes]] — the target trial framework operationalizes the shift from hazard ratios to survival curve contrasts
[[Two-Stage Survival Models for Freemium Economics]] — the LTV application that motivates preferring survival curves
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — g-computation is one of the key estimation strategies for causal survival curves





When (if ever) is a hazard ratio acceptable as a summary? Possible answer: only under genuine proportional hazards with no interest in the absolute scale.
How sensitive is the RMST to the choice of horizon \(\tau\)? Can sensitivity analysis over \(\tau\) be standardised?

title: IPW for Time-Varying Confounding in Survival Mediation
text:
Inverse probability weighting handles the treatment-confounder feedback problem by reweighting rather than conditioning. Standard regression adjustment fails when a time-varying mediator is simultaneously on the causal pathway and a confounder of later mediator-outcome relationships. IPW creates a pseudo-population where this feedback is broken.



In survival settings with a time-varying mediator \(M_t\), the mediator at time \(t\) is a consequence of treatment (and thus on the causal pathway) and a confounder of the \(M_{t+1} \to Y\) relationship. Conditioning on \(M_t\) blocks the indirect effect you want to estimate while being necessary to remove confounding. This is the classic Robins problem that motivates marginal structural models.




Treatment-confounder feedback #feedback — the structure where a post-treatment variable (here \(M_t\)) affects both future treatment/mediator values and the outcome, making standard adjustment invalid
Stabilised weight #stabilised-weight — the ratio of the marginal treatment probability to the conditional treatment probability, reducing variance compared to unstabilised weights
Pseudo-population #pseudo-population — the reweighted sample in which time-varying confounders are balanced, enabling simple marginal models






At each time point \(t\): treatment \(A\) affects mediator \(M_t\). Mediator \(M_t\) affects the hazard at time \(t\). Mediator \(M_t\) also confounds the relationship between \(M_{t+1}\) and the hazard at \(t+1\), because \(M_t\) predicts both future mediator values and future outcomes. Conditioning on \(M_t\) removes confounding but also blocks the indirect pathway. Not conditioning on \(M_t\) leaves the confounding intact.



Fit a model for the probability of the observed treatment and mediator history given covariates. This yields the stabilised weight:
\[w_{it} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{P(A_s \mid \bar{A}_{s-1}, V)}{P(A_s \mid \bar{A}_{s-1}, \bar{M}_{s-1}, \bar{L}_{s-1})}\]
where \(\bar{L}\) is time-varying confounder history, \(\bar{M}\) is mediator history, and \(V\) is baseline covariates. The numerator stabilises; the denominator adjusts for confounding. In the reweighted pseudo-population, the time-varying confounders are balanced without conditioning on the mediator.



Correct specification of the treatment and mediator assignment models (the weights). The outcome model can be simple: a weighted Cox or weighted pooled logistic regression. The key advantage over structural equation approaches is that only the weight models need correct specification, not the outcome model. Weight models concern observable quantities and can be checked against observed patterns.



IPW with many time points is notoriously unstable. Weights become extreme when positivity is violated (some confounder configurations make treatment nearly deterministic). Truncation and stabilisation are standard but introduce bias. The method does not naturally produce time-varying coefficient trajectories. You get a single marginal effect estimate, not a picture of how the mechanism evolves over time.



A dynamic path analysis (Aalen-style) handles temporal confounding implicitly through the structural equations. If the equations are correctly specified, no reweighting is needed. The cost is that misspecification of functional form propagates through the entire decomposition. IPW is robust to outcome model misspecification but fragile to weight model misspecification. The structural approach is robust to weight model issues but fragile to structural misspecification. Neither dominates.




For mediation specifically, separate weights for treatment mechanism and mediator mechanism:
\[w^A_{it} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{P(A_s \mid \bar{A}_{s-1}, V)}{P(A_s \mid \bar{A}_{s-1}, \bar{M}_{s-1}, \bar{L}_{s-1})}\]
\[w^M_{it} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{P(M_s \mid \bar{M}_{s-1}, A_s, V)}{P(M_s \mid \bar{M}_{s-1}, A_s, \bar{L}_{s-1})}\]
The combined weight \(w^A \cdot w^M\) creates a pseudo-population where both treatment and mediator paths are exchangeable conditional on baseline \(V\) alone.




[[Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects]] — the general MSM framework of which mediation IPW is a special case
[[Separability as the Potential Outcomes Alternative to Cross-World Counterfactuals]] — IPW handles the confounding; separability handles the estimand definition; together they form the full PO mediation toolkit
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — g-computation is the parametric alternative to IPW for the same estimands
[[Hernán’s Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes]] — the target trial framing motivates why these weights correspond to a specific experimental design




The potential outcomes school’s full mediation strategy has two components that handle distinct problems. Separability (Robins, Richardson, Stensrud) defines the estimand. IPW handles the confounding. Together they form a complete alternative to structural equation mediation.
Separability redefines direct and indirect effects so that no quantity involves cross-world counterfactuals. It decomposes the treatment into components \((X_M, X_Y)\) that can in principle be administered independently. Each estimand maps to a single-world intervention.
IPW then identifies those estimands in observational data by reweighting to break the treatment-confounder feedback. The combined weight \(w^A \cdot w^M\) creates a pseudo-population where both treatment and mediator paths are exchangeable given baseline covariates alone.
The architectural contrast with process models is sharp. A dynamic path analysis (Aalen-style) uses a single structural model to simultaneously define the estimand (the path decomposition) and handle confounding (through correct specification of the structural equations). The process model is a unified object. The PO toolkit is modular: swap in different estimand definitions without changing the identification strategy, or swap in different confounding adjustments without changing the estimand.
The process model’s advantage is temporal specificity. It produces coefficient trajectories that show when and where to intervene. The PO toolkit’s advantage is modularity and robustness. Each component can be checked independently, and failure of one does not invalidate the other.




In discrete-time survival with many intervals, is there a threshold number of time points beyond which IPW weight instability makes the method practically unusable?
Can doubly-robust estimators (combining IPW with outcome modelling) rescue the approach when both models are slightly wrong?
How does the Bayesian structural approach (posterior predictive checks on the mechanism) compare epistemically to checking IPW weight models against observed treatment patterns?
Can the PO toolkit’s modularity be imported into the process framework? Could one use separability to define the estimand but g-computation (instead of IPW) to identify it, gaining both clean experimental interpretation and temporal trajectories?

Separability redefines direct and indirect effects so that no quantity involves cross-world counterfactuals. It decomposes the treatment into components \((X_M, X_Y)\) that can in principle be administered independently. Each estimand maps to a single-world intervention.
IPW then identifies those estimands in observational data by reweighting to break the treatment-confounder feedback. The combined weight \(w^A \cdot w^M\) creates a pseudo-population where both treatment and mediator paths are exchangeable given baseline covariates alone.
The architectural contrast with process models is sharp. A dynamic path analysis (Aalen-style) uses a single structural model to simultaneously define the estimand (the path decomposition) and handle confounding (through correct specification of the structural equations). The process model is a unified object. The PO toolkit is modular: swap in different estimand definitions without changing the identification strategy, or swap in different confounding adjustments without changing the estimand.
The process model’s advantage is temporal specificity. It produces coefficient trajectories that show when and where to intervene. The PO toolkit’s advantage is modularity and robustness. Each component can be checked independently, and failure of one does not invalidate the other.

Can doubly-robust estimators (combining IPW with outcome modelling) rescue the approach when both models are slightly wrong?
How does the Bayesian structural approach (posterior predictive checks on the mechanism) compare epistemically to checking IPW weight models against observed treatment patterns?

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Hernán's Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Hernán's Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes.html
title: Hernán’s Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes
text:
Hernán’s framework for causal inference with survival outcomes rests on five principles: define the question as a target trial before touching data; avoid conditioning on post-treatment variables; use g-methods when treatment varies over time; report survival-scale contrasts as primary estimands; and distinguish statistical models from causal models. The hazard ratio is not a reliable causal estimand even in a perfectly randomized trial.



Hernán (with Robins) has been one of the most vocal critics of conventional survival analysis in causal settings. The programme is interventionist: causation is defined by what would happen under manipulation. This positions it in direct tension with Aalen’s processual approach, where time-varying coefficients are the primary causal objects.




Target trial #target-trial — every causal analysis of observational data emulates a hypothetical randomized experiment. You must specify eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, outcome, causal contrast, and analysis plan before modelling
Hazard ratio problem #hazard-ratio — even under perfect randomization, the hazard ratio at time \(t\) conditions on survival to \(t\), which is a post-treatment event. The risk sets at each time point are no longer exchangeable. Selection bias from depletion of susceptibles can produce HR = 1.0 when treatment is genuinely harmful
Treatment-confounder feedback #treatment-confounder-feedback — when a time-varying covariate simultaneously predicts future treatment and is affected by past treatment. Standard regression cannot handle both confounding adjustment and path-blocking simultaneously. This is a structural impossibility, not a matter of functional form






If treatment kills the frailest individuals early, treated survivors at time \(t\) are healthier than control survivors. The hazard ratio compares non-comparable groups. A HR that changes over time may reflect real effect modification or nothing more than differential selection. The proportional hazards assumption is causally incoherent as a general model because selection almost guarantees non-proportionality even when the causal effect is constant.
The alternative: work with survival probabilities directly. The risk difference \(\Pr[T > t \mid \text{do}(X=1)] - \Pr[T > t \mid \text{do}(X=0)]\) compares the same population under two counterfactual interventions and does not condition on post-treatment events.



When treatment varies over time and affects future confounders, no single regression model can handle both confounding adjustment and causal path preservation. Hernán and Robins advocate three solutions:
The parametric g-formula models the full joint distribution of treatment, confounders, and outcome at each time point. Simulate forward under hypothetical interventions. Closest to the PyMC implementation in the Aalen article.
Inverse probability weighting of marginal structural models separates confounding adjustment (in the weights) from the causal model (in the outcome regression). Creates pseudo-populations where treatment is independent of confounders.
G-estimation of structural nested models directly estimates causal effects at each time point as a function of treatment history. Removes treatment effects to recover counterfactual outcomes under no treatment.



Hernán prefers controlled direct effects: \(\Pr[Y(a, m)] - \Pr[Y(a^*, m)]\), fixing mediator at level \(m\). This requires only standard sequential exchangeability. Natural direct/indirect effects require cross-world independence (untestable), do not correspond to any single experiment, and fail when treatment induces confounders of the mediator-outcome relationship.
For time-varying mediation, interventional disparity measures offer a middle ground — stochastic interventions on the mediator that avoid cross-world assumptions while still permitting decomposition.



Hernán treats regression coefficients as means to an end. The causal estimand is defined in potential outcomes; the model estimates it. Aalen treats time-varying coefficients as the primary objects of interest. Hernán would say: the coefficients are interpretable as causal quantities only under identification assumptions, and even then you should prefer survival contrasts because they directly answer the clinical question.





[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — the framework Hernán’s critique addresses; the additive model as a special case of the structures g-methods handle
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — shows how the Bayesian implementation satisfies both Hernán’s interventionist requirements and Aalen’s processual goals
[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the philosophical framing of this disagreement
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — Hernán treats censoring and competing risks as missing data problems, not as special survival machinery





Does the target trial framework apply cleanly to observational settings where treatment is continuous and time-varying, or does it become a stretched metaphor?
Can Hernán’s critique of hazard ratios be formally reconciled with the practical reality that most clinical trial reporting uses them?
Is the g-formula’s sensitivity to model specification (modelling the full joint distribution) a fatal weakness or a feature that forces transparency about assumptions?
