objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand.html
title: G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand
text:
A full Bayesian implementation of Aalen-style dynamic path analysis achieves something neither the processual nor the interventionist tradition delivers alone. The process model is the estimation engine. The counterfactual contrast is the estimand. G-computation is where they meet. This is the article’s real contribution: showing that Aalen’s process model is a good estimation engine for interventionist estimands.



The dpasurv R package implements frequentist dynamic path analysis with step-function estimators and bootstrap confidence intervals. It stops at the path decomposition. It does not produce counterfactual survival curves. The Bayesian implementation in PyMC goes further: the same model that decomposes the mechanism also generates the interventionist estimand via posterior predictive simulation.




G-computation #g-computation — simulate counterfactual outcomes by intervening on the treatment equation while letting confounders evolve naturally through the full joint model. Interventionist in definition (\(\text{do}(X=x)\)), processual in implementation (model the full joint trajectory)
Joint likelihood #joint-likelihood — estimating mediator and hazard equations simultaneously, treating the system as a unified mechanism rather than separate estimation steps. Information flows bidirectionally; the posterior over mediator effects is informed by event data and vice versa
Symmetry argument #symmetry — modeling choices that distort absolute survival curves (softplus, carry-forward, constant-hazard extrapolation) apply identically under both counterfactual interventions. The distortions cancel in the causal contrast. The survival difference is robust to projection assumptions






First: a working Bayesian implementation of dynamic path analysis in PyMC that did not previously exist. Smooth spline-based coefficient paths, full posterior uncertainty, posterior predictive checks, LOO model comparison. Directly usable for time-varying mediation in survival data.
Second: the g-computation bridge from process to estimand. The path decomposition shows how the treatment works. The counterfactual survival contrast shows that it works. The Bayesian generative approach makes the connection operationally seamless.
Third: diagnostic transparency. Spline sensitivity analysis, LOO comparison, posterior predictive checks on both mediator and event outcomes. The frequentist version offers none of this. A practitioner can verify whether conclusions are robust to modeling choices.



Aalen’s original model uses the identity link because the decomposition is the estimand. Fidelity to the additive scale is load-bearing. The PyMC model uses the processual structure differently. The time-varying coefficients are internal mechanics of a generative model whose purpose is to produce counterfactual survival curves. The decomposition plots are diagnostic — they show the qualitative structure of the mechanism. The causal quantity lives on the survival probability scale, where the softplus has already been applied and the path algebra need not hold exactly.
This is not a Bayesian Aalen model. It is a Bayesian generative survival model inspired by Aalen’s dynamic path structure, whose internal architecture borrows his additive decomposition for mechanistic insight, but whose causal output is defined interventionally on the survival scale. The softplus is the right choice for this object.



The carry-forward projection for censored subjects, the softplus transformation, the constant-hazard extrapolation — all apply identically under \(\text{do}(X=1)\) and \(\text{do}(X=0)\). Whatever distortion they introduce to absolute survival curves cancels in the difference. The causal contrast is robust to the projection assumption. For the population quantity (the absolute survival curve) the distortion is real. But the estimand is the contrast, and the contrast is clean.



The lagged mediator in the hazard equation enforces strict temporal ordering: \(X(t) \to M(t) \to \lambda(t+1)\). The autoregressive mediator component (\(\rho \cdot M_{\text{lag}}\)) captures the momentum of the mediating process. The random walk prior on spline coefficients encodes the processual assumption that causal effects don’t jump discontinuously. Each of these is a philosophical commitment with statistical consequences.




The joint model:
\[M_i(t) = \beta(t) X_i + \rho M_i(t-1) + \epsilon_i(t)\]
\[\lambda_i(t) = \text{softplus}\big(\alpha_0(t) + \alpha_1(t) X_i + \alpha_2(t) M_i(t-1)\big)\]
G-computation survival curves:
\[\hat{S}(t \mid \text{do}(X=x)) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \exp\!\Big(-\sum_{s=1}^{t} \hat{\lambda}_i(s \mid \text{do}(X=x))\Big)\]




[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — the underlying framework; this note describes the Bayesian extension
[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the philosophical argument that motivates treating g-computation as a bridge
[[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]] — the joint likelihood embodies the principle that all information about the mechanism is in the likelihood; the Bayesian approach takes this seriously
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — the softplus link partially identifies the path decomposition on the hazard scale while fully identifying the survival contrast





Would a model-consistent forward simulation for censored subjects (evolving the mediator via the AR(1) equation at future time bins) meaningfully change the survival contrast, or does the symmetry argument guarantee robustness?
Can the NDE be replaced with the controlled direct effect without losing the processual narrative? The CDE is more philosophically consistent with the process view (it describes a conceivable experiment) and avoids cross-world assumptions
What are the formal conditions under which the softplus decomposition approximates the identity-link decomposition? This would be needed for a methods paper
crumbs: G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text:
When a baseline treatment propagates through a multi-state survival process, intermediate variables are simultaneously mediators, time-varying confounders, and collider-induced selection variables. The correct causal estimand is the total effect on the full outcome trajectory, estimated via marginal structural models or g-computation without conditioning on intermediates.



Freemium programmes assign treatment once, at baseline. The effect then propagates through a competing-risks stage (convert vs. churn from free) and a sequential stage (churn from paid). Between these stages, time-varying behaviours (engagement, feature adoption, support usage) accumulate. These intermediate variables create a triple identification problem that standard regression cannot solve.




Time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment #treatment-confounder-feedback — a variable \(L(t)\) that predicts future outcomes and is itself shaped by past treatment. Conditioning on \(L(t)\) blocks the mediated causal path. Ignoring \(L(t)\) leaves downstream transitions confounded.
Estimand taxonomy #estimand-taxonomy — total effect (all downstream consequences of baseline assignment), controlled direct effect (effect holding intermediates fixed), conditional transition effect (effect among those who reach a given state). Each requires different methods and answers a different question.
Principal strata #principal-strata — latent subgroups defined by joint potential outcomes: always-converters, never-converters, freemium-induced converters. The induced-converter stratum drives the economics, but membership is never directly observed.






During the free tier, customer engagement \(L(t)\) plays three roles simultaneously. It mediates the freemium effect: the programme works by building habits and demonstrating value through \(L(t)\). It confounds downstream transitions: \(L(t)\) predicts both future conversion and future churn. It creates collider-induced selection: conditioning on survival to time \(t\) (or conversion at time \(s\)) opens non-causal paths between previously independent factors.
Standard Cox regression with time-varying covariates conditions on \(L(t)\). This blocks the mediated pathway and biases the total effect estimate downward. The analyst who adjusts for engagement to “control for confounding” inadvertently removes part of the treatment’s own effect.



The total effect of freemium assignment compares the full outcome trajectory (conversion timing, post-conversion retention, revenue) under freemium versus paid. Identification requires only baseline confounder adjustment. Build a propensity score \(P(A = 1 \mid W)\) and use IPTW or standardisation to estimate counterfactual survival curves for each stage jointly. Do not decompose into “effect on conversion” times “effect on retention”: the stages share common causes and the product decomposition is invalid.
The controlled direct effect asks whether freemium changes retention through channels other than engagement. Interventional direct and indirect effects require the full mediation analysis machinery and stronger assumptions.
The conditional transition effect (e.g., “among converters, does freemium history improve retention?”) conditions on a post-treatment event. The set of freemium converters is a selected subpopulation. The comparison group of “paid converters” is ill-defined because paid customers were never at risk of conversion. This estimand requires principal stratification or bounds rather than standard adjustment.



When time-varying confounders \(L(t)\) are affected by treatment and predict future transitions, marginal structural models restore consistent estimation. The weights account for baseline confounding of treatment assignment and the time-varying confounding that arises because \(L(t)\) sits on the causal pathway. The weighted cause-specific hazard models produce causal CIFs that can be combined into causal economic summaries.



The causal effect of baseline treatment on late outcomes genuinely attenuates. Post-baseline events (product changes, market shifts, personnel turnover) intervene and dilute the initial condition’s influence. The survival curve framework encodes this: \(S(t \mid \text{freemium}) - S(t \mid \text{paid})\) can narrow over time, and this is a real feature of the causal process.
The CIF handles attenuation more cleanly than the hazard. Early conversion under freemium locks in customers in the paid tier. The CIF at later time points still carries the trace of this early effect. The hazard at a late time point does not.




The multi-state structure: Free \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{convert}}(t)}\) Paid \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{churn}}(t)}\) Gone, with a direct exit Free \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{churn-free}}(t)}\) Gone.
IPTW weights for the time-varying case:
\[W_i(t) = \prod_{k=0}^{t} \frac{P(A_i \mid \bar{L}_i(k-1))}{P(A_i \mid \bar{L}_i(k))}\]
where \(\bar{L}_i(k)\) is the covariate history through time \(k\).




[[Two-Stage Survival Models for Freemium Economics]] — the economic application motivating this identification problem
[[Competing Risks as Causal Preemption]] — the philosophical grounding for why competing-risks counterfactuals are difficult
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — g-computation as an alternative to IPTW for the same estimand
[[Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects]] — the general MSM framework applied here

Under what conditions do principal stratification bounds for the induced-converter stratum become informative enough to guide decisions?

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text: When a baseline treatment propagates through a multi-state survival process, intermediate variables are simultaneously mediators, time-varying confounders, and collider-induced selection variables. The correct causal estimand is the total effect on the full outcome trajectory, estimated via marginal structural models or g-computation without conditioning on intermediates.
crumbs: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text: Freemium programmes assign treatment once, at baseline. The effect then propagates through a competing-risks stage (convert vs. churn from free) and a sequential stage (churn from paid). Between these stages, time-varying behaviours (engagement, feature adoption, support usage) accumulate. These intermediate variables create a triple identification problem that standard regression cannot solve.
crumbs: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text:
Time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment #treatment-confounder-feedback — a variable \(L(t)\) that predicts future outcomes and is itself shaped by past treatment. Conditioning on \(L(t)\) blocks the mediated causal path. Ignoring \(L(t)\) leaves downstream transitions confounded.
Estimand taxonomy #estimand-taxonomy — total effect (all downstream consequences of baseline assignment), controlled direct effect (effect holding intermediates fixed), conditional transition effect (effect among those who reach a given state). Each requires different methods and answers a different question.
Principal strata #principal-strata — latent subgroups defined by joint potential outcomes: always-converters, never-converters, freemium-induced converters. The induced-converter stratum drives the economics, but membership is never directly observed.
crumbs: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text:
During the free tier, customer engagement \(L(t)\) plays three roles simultaneously. It mediates the freemium effect: the programme works by building habits and demonstrating value through \(L(t)\). It confounds downstream transitions: \(L(t)\) predicts both future conversion and future churn. It creates collider-induced selection: conditioning on survival to time \(t\) (or conversion at time \(s\)) opens non-causal paths between previously independent factors.
Standard Cox regression with time-varying covariates conditions on \(L(t)\). This blocks the mediated pathway and biases the total effect estimate downward. The analyst who adjusts for engagement to “control for confounding” inadvertently removes part of the treatment’s own effect.



The total effect of freemium assignment compares the full outcome trajectory (conversion timing, post-conversion retention, revenue) under freemium versus paid. Identification requires only baseline confounder adjustment. Build a propensity score \(P(A = 1 \mid W)\) and use IPTW or standardisation to estimate counterfactual survival curves for each stage jointly. Do not decompose into “effect on conversion” times “effect on retention”: the stages share common causes and the product decomposition is invalid.
The controlled direct effect asks whether freemium changes retention through channels other than engagement. Interventional direct and indirect effects require the full mediation analysis machinery and stronger assumptions.
The conditional transition effect (e.g., “among converters, does freemium history improve retention?”) conditions on a post-treatment event. The set of freemium converters is a selected subpopulation. The comparison group of “paid converters” is ill-defined because paid customers were never at risk of conversion. This estimand requires principal stratification or bounds rather than standard adjustment.



When time-varying confounders \(L(t)\) are affected by treatment and predict future transitions, marginal structural models restore consistent estimation. The weights account for baseline confounding of treatment assignment and the time-varying confounding that arises because \(L(t)\) sits on the causal pathway. The weighted cause-specific hazard models produce causal CIFs that can be combined into causal economic summaries.



The causal effect of baseline treatment on late outcomes genuinely attenuates. Post-baseline events (product changes, market shifts, personnel turnover) intervene and dilute the initial condition’s influence. The survival curve framework encodes this: \(S(t \mid \text{freemium}) - S(t \mid \text{paid})\) can narrow over time, and this is a real feature of the causal process.
The CIF handles attenuation more cleanly than the hazard. Early conversion under freemium locks in customers in the paid tier. The CIF at later time points still carries the trace of this early effect. The hazard at a late time point does not.
crumbs: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models

title: Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models
text:
The multi-state structure: Free \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{convert}}(t)}\) Paid \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{churn}}(t)}\) Gone, with a direct exit Free \(\xrightarrow{h_{\text{churn-free}}(t)}\) Gone.
IPTW weights for the time-varying case:
\[W_i(t) = \prod_{k=0}^{t} \frac{P(A_i \mid \bar{L}_i(k-1))}{P(A_i \mid \bar{L}_i(k))}\]
where \(\bar{L}_i(k)\) is the covariate history through time \(k\).

title: The PO Critique of Structural Mediation
text:
The potential outcomes school’s objection to structural equation mediation is not a single criticism but a five-step argument. Each step targets a distinct assumption. Together they claim that process-model decompositions are model artifacts, not discoveries about causal structure.



A PyData talk on dynamic path analysis (Aalen-style survival mediation) prompted a systematic review of where the Rubin/Robins/Richardson tradition would push back. The objections form a logical chain, each building on the last.




Model-dependent decomposition #model-dependency — a path decomposition that follows from parametric assumptions rather than nonparametric identification
Cross-world counterfactual #cross-world — a quantity like \(Y(1, M(0))\) requiring two incompatible intervention regimes
Sequential unconfoundedness #sequential-unconfoundedness — the assumption that at every time point, all common causes of treatment, mediator, and hazard are observed and adjusted for






The path decomposition (direct \(= \alpha_1(t)\), indirect \(= \beta(t) \cdot \alpha_2(t)\)) follows from the assumed additive separability of the latent predictor. A nonparametric model would not necessarily decompose the effect into two clean paths. The model does not discover the decomposition. It assumes one and estimates the weights.
The ATE, by contrast, is nonparametrically identified under standard ignorability conditions. The decomposition into direct and indirect components requires additional structure. The PO objection is that this structure is the modeller’s invention.



The natural direct effect requires computing \(Y(1, M(0))\). A generative model can simulate this quantity. The PO school never doubted the computability. Their objection targets meaning: no experiment could produce this quantity. The model computes a number, but the number has no experimental referent without structural assumptions that are themselves unverifiable.



Posterior predictive checks test fit, not causal structure. A well-fitting model with the wrong causal direction passes the same checks as a correctly specified one. The modularity assumption concerns invariance under intervention: \(\alpha_2(t)\) acts on \(M\) the same way regardless of which intervention generated \(M\). Observational data cannot verify this claim. See [[Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models]] for the full argument.



In survival mediation with time-varying confounders, sequential unconfoundedness requires that at every time point, all common causes of treatment, mediator, and hazard are observed. The structural model handles confounding implicitly through correct specification of the equations. If the equations are wrong, the confounding adjustment fails silently. The Robins tradition handles this explicitly through IPW, where the weight models are separately checkable against observed treatment patterns.



The hardest-nosed version: the process framing adds philosophical narrative but no methodological advantage. What you have is a parametric Bayesian survival model with time-varying coefficients and a mediation structure. The parameters face the same identification problem they always did. Calling the coefficients “process” does not change whether they are identified.



The five objections connect: the decomposition depends on the model (1), the model computes cross-world quantities (2), fit cannot validate the causal structure (3), the confounding adjustment is implicit and uncheckable (4), and the “process” label adds interpretation but not identification (5). The conclusion: structural mediation produces numbers whose causal interpretation rests entirely on unverifiable structural commitments.





[[Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models]] — Objection 3 in full detail
[[Separability as the Potential Outcomes Alternative to Cross-World Counterfactuals]] — the PO school’s constructive alternative to cross-world counterfactuals
[[IPW for Time-Varying Confounding in Survival Mediation]] — the PO school’s explicit confounding adjustment, contrasting with the structural model’s implicit one
[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the philosophical framing that Objection 5 targets
[[Temporal Trajectory as the Process Model’s Comparative Advantage]] — the strongest counter-argument to this critique





Can the five objections be ranked by severity? Objection 1 (model dependency) seems foundational: if the decomposition is an artifact, the other objections become moot.
Is there a version of structural mediation that addresses Objection 4 by incorporating explicit weight-based confounding adjustment while preserving the process decomposition?
Does the “metaphysics not methodology” charge apply equally to the PO school’s own commitments? The “no experimental referent” criterion is itself a philosophical position about what counts as a valid estimand.

href: notes/certain_things/Public/Philosophy/Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis.html
title: Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis
text:
Aalen’s dynamic path analysis and Hernán’s g-computation framework instantiate two genuinely different philosophies of causation — processual and interventionist — that map onto a long-standing divide between Salmon/Dowe process theories and Lewis/Woodward counterfactual theories. They are not competing statistical methods. They are different answers to the question of what causation is.



Reviewing the causal interpretation latent in Aalen’s work through Hernán’s lens reveals a philosophical disagreement dressed in statistical formalism. The tension surfaces concretely in mediation analysis, where path decomposition and counterfactual contrasts pull in different directions.




Processual causation #process-causation — causation is the transmission of influence along a continuous spatiotemporal path. You understand a cause by tracing the mechanism. The journey is the explanation. (Salmon, Dowe, and statistically: Aalen)
Interventionist causation #interventionist-causation — causation is counterfactual dependence under manipulation. You understand a cause by comparing worlds. The outcome contrast is the explanation. (Lewis, Woodward, and statistically: Rubin, Robins, Hernán)
Cross-world independence #cross-world — the assumption required for natural direct/indirect effects: potential mediator under one treatment is independent of potential outcome under a different treatment. Untestable and conceptually strange under interventionism; coherent under the process view as a question about channel flow






Aalen treats cumulative regression coefficients as the causal objects themselves. They say: here is how this covariate has been pushing the system, incrementally, over time. The additive hazard model mirrors the ontology — causes accumulate, layer on each other, and the system at time \(t\) is the integral of everything acting on it up to \(t\).
Hernán defines causal effects as contrasts between possible worlds under manipulation. The survival probability under \(\text{do}(X=1)\) versus \(\text{do}(X=0)\) is a clean, manipulation-defined quantity. The path through which the effect travels is secondary — interesting perhaps, but not constitutive of the causal claim.



When Aalen decomposes the total effect into direct and indirect paths, he traces the flow of influence through the system. The decomposition is meaningful because the paths are real features of the mechanism. From Hernán’s standpoint, the decomposition is only meaningful if each path corresponds to a possible intervention. Can you intervene on the mediator independently of the treatment? If not, the “indirect effect” doesn’t correspond to any experiment.
This is why Hernán prefers controlled direct effects over natural effects. The CDE corresponds to a joint intervention (set \(X=1\), set \(M=m\)) that is at least conceivable. The natural indirect effect asks: “what if I treat you but magically hold your mediator at its untreated value?” — not an experiment anyone can run.
For Aalen, the question is perfectly coherent. You are asking how much of the causal process flowed through a particular channel.



Hernán tells you whether to act. Aalen tells you why it works. Knowing that treatment reduces mortality by 17% is actionable. Knowing that the effect is protective early, then partially undermined by a mediator after day 100, is explanatory in a way the marginal contrast cannot be. Neither fully substitutes for the other.





[[Preemption and the Many Faces of Causation]] — processual vs dependence causation instantiated in a different setting; preemption cases also separate these two faces
[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — the technical framework where this philosophical tension plays out
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — Otsuka’s analysis of frequentist reliabilism and Bayesian coherentism as epistemological programmes; the processual/interventionist split is a parallel divide at the level of causal ontology
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — the synthesis point where both views meet





Is the processual view formally expressible without committing to a specific functional form (additivity, proportionality), or does the ontology always come with a parametric price?
Can interventional disparity measures (stochastic interventions on mediators) genuinely split the difference, or do they collapse into one camp?
crumbs: Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Philosophy/Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Philosophy/Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models.html
title: Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models
text:
Making a structural assumption “inspectable” through posterior predictive checks is not the same as making it testable. Observational fit cannot distinguish a correctly specified causal model from a well-fitting but causally wrong one. The modularity assumption concerns invariance under intervention, which no amount of observational model checking can verify.



Bayesian structural models (dynamic path analysis, generative BLP, structural equation models with priors) claim an advantage over algebraic SCMs: their assumptions are inspectable. You can simulate from the model, compare to data, check posterior predictive distributions. The potential outcomes school’s sharpest objection is that this inspectability does not constitute testability of the causal structure.




Posterior predictive check #ppc — simulating data from the fitted model and comparing to observed data; tests whether the model can reproduce observable patterns
Modularity #modularity — the assumption that intervening on one structural equation leaves others invariant; e.g., changing how treatment affects the mediator does not alter how the mediator affects the outcome
Observational equivalence #observational-equivalence — multiple causal structures can produce identical observed data distributions; fit alone cannot distinguish them






A Bayesian generative model makes its structural commitments visible. The coefficient \(\alpha_2(t)\) governing the mediator-outcome pathway is an explicit object with a posterior distribution. You can ask: does the model reproduce the observed survival curves? Does it capture the treatment-mediator association? Do posterior predictive intervals cover the data? If yes, the structural assumptions are at least consistent with observation.



Posterior predictive checks test fit, not causal structure. A model that fits because of confounding rather than genuine mediation passes the same checks. The modularity assumption states that \(\alpha_2(t)\) acts on \(M\) the same way regardless of which intervention generated \(M\). This is a claim about what would happen under interventions we have not performed. No observational check can verify it.
Consider: a model with the wrong causal direction (outcome causes mediator) might fit the observed joint distribution perfectly. Posterior predictive checks would pass. The causal conclusions would be entirely wrong.



Testing for treatment-mediator interactions is a partial check on modularity. If \(\alpha_2(t)\) differs by treatment arm, modularity is violated. Absence of detected interaction is consistent with modularity but does not confirm it. The interaction might exist in untested subgroups or at untested time points.



Structural assumptions in causal models occupy a distinctive epistemological position. They are stronger than statistical assumptions (they concern interventions, not just distributions). They are weaker than logical truths (they can be wrong). They cannot be verified from data alone. They require external knowledge: scientific theory, mechanistic reasoning, prior experimental evidence.
The Bayesian framework does not change this. It makes the assumptions explicit and checkable for internal consistency. It does not make them checkable for causal correctness. This is a genuine limitation, not a failure of execution.



The process modeler’s best response concedes the point and shifts the ground. The structural model is not proven correct by fit. It is useful because it produces temporally indexed recommendations that no single-number estimand can deliver. “Intervene on the mediator after day 100” is actionable in a way that “the total effect is -0.3” is not. The structural commitments are the price of this specificity. The PO school’s cleaner estimands come at the cost of less actionable answers.





[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the broader philosophical framing of what these two schools are asking
[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — observational equivalence of causal models parallels theoretical equivalence in philosophy of science
[[Button’s Realism Within Limits]] — limits on what observation can tell us about structure
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — structural models that contradict dominant methodology can still be epistemically productive





Is there a formal characterisation of what posterior predictive checks can and cannot tell you about causal structure? A “testable implications” theorem for Bayesian structural models?
Can sensitivity analysis (varying the modularity assumption parametrically) substitute for direct testing?
Does the distinction between inspectability and testability apply equally to non-causal structural assumptions, like the random coefficient distribution in BLP?

text:
A Bayesian generative model makes its structural commitments visible. The coefficient \(\alpha_2(t)\) governing the mediator-outcome pathway is an explicit object with a posterior distribution. You can ask: does the model reproduce the observed survival curves? Does it capture the treatment-mediator association? Do posterior predictive intervals cover the data? If yes, the structural assumptions are at least consistent with observation.



Posterior predictive checks test fit, not causal structure. A model that fits because of confounding rather than genuine mediation passes the same checks. The modularity assumption states that \(\alpha_2(t)\) acts on \(M\) the same way regardless of which intervention generated \(M\). This is a claim about what would happen under interventions we have not performed. No observational check can verify it.
Consider: a model with the wrong causal direction (outcome causes mediator) might fit the observed joint distribution perfectly. Posterior predictive checks would pass. The causal conclusions would be entirely wrong.



Testing for treatment-mediator interactions is a partial check on modularity. If \(\alpha_2(t)\) differs by treatment arm, modularity is violated. Absence of detected interaction is consistent with modularity but does not confirm it. The interaction might exist in untested subgroups or at untested time points.



Structural assumptions in causal models occupy a distinctive epistemological position. They are stronger than statistical assumptions (they concern interventions, not just distributions). They are weaker than logical truths (they can be wrong). They cannot be verified from data alone. They require external knowledge: scientific theory, mechanistic reasoning, prior experimental evidence.
The Bayesian framework does not change this. It makes the assumptions explicit and checkable for internal consistency. It does not make them checkable for causal correctness. This is a genuine limitation, not a failure of execution.



The process modeler’s best response concedes the point and shifts the ground. The structural model is not proven correct by fit. It is useful because it produces temporally indexed recommendations that no single-number estimand can deliver. “Intervene on the mediator after day 100” is actionable in a way that “the total effect is -0.3” is not. The structural commitments are the price of this specificity. The PO school’s cleaner estimands come at the cost of less actionable answers.

title: Two-Stage Survival Models for Freemium Economics
text:
Freemium customer journeys have a natural two-stage survival structure: a competing risks process (convert to paid vs. churn from free) followed by a sequential churn process (time-to-churn from paid). The economics of freemium depend on the joint distribution of these stages, not on summary statistics computed from either stage alone.



The standard business metric, LTV/CAC, conceals deep identification problems. Naive calculations multiply conversion rate by average post-conversion LTV. This decomposition is invalid because conversion timing matters, the two stages are dependent (early converters may retain differently from late converters), and the cost of supporting free users accumulates over the full free-tier duration.




Competing risks (Stage 1) #competing-risks — free-tier customers face two simultaneous events: conversion (free \(\to\) paid) and churn (free \(\to\) gone). The cumulative incidence function correctly accounts for the fact that churned customers are no longer available to convert.
Cure fraction #cure-fraction — the plateau of the conversion CIF as \(t \to \infty\), representing customers who will never convert. Typically 90-98% for freemium products.
Sequential churn (Stage 2) #sequential-churn — post-conversion retention, modelled as a standard survival process with time measured from conversion.
RMST as LTV #rmst-ltv — the restricted mean survival time, scaled by revenue rate, gives expected customer lifetime value within a fixed horizon.






During the free tier, treat conversion and churn as competing terminal events. This is cleaner than the two-stage sequential decomposition because it respects the joint structure: a customer simultaneously at risk of both events, with correlated hazards. The cause-specific hazards \(h_{\text{convert}}(t \mid X)\) and \(h_{\text{churn}}(t \mid X)\) are defined on the same risk set.
The cumulative incidence functions \(F_{\text{convert}}(t)\) and \(F_{\text{churn}}(t)\) sum to less than 1 at any finite \(t\). The remainder, \(1 - F_{\text{convert}}(t) - F_{\text{churn}}(t)\), is the probability of still being a free user.



Expected cost of a free user:
\[\text{Cost} = c \cdot \int_0^{\tau} [1 - F_{\text{convert}}(t) - F_{\text{churn}}(t)] \, dt\]
Expected revenue, integrating over the conversion time distribution and post-conversion retention:
\[\text{Revenue} = \int_0^{\tau} r \cdot \left[\int_0^{\tau - s} S_2(u) \, du \right] dF_{\text{convert}}(s)\]
where \(dF_{\text{convert}}(s)\) is the sub-distribution density and \(S_2(u)\) is post-conversion survival. The net value per free user is Revenue minus Cost minus CAC.



Three reasons block the naive decomposition. First, conversion timing determines the revenue window. A month-1 converter generates nearly a full horizon of revenue. A month-11 converter generates almost nothing. The distribution of conversion times, not just the rate, drives economics. Second, selection effects link the stages: quick converters may also retain longer, making the joint economics more favourable than marginal numbers suggest. Third, cost accumulates linearly during the free period. Each additional month of free usage pushes the payback period further out.



The total effect of freemium assignment on the full value trajectory is the policy-relevant estimand. Adjust for baseline confounders via IPTW or g-computation. Do not separately estimate causal effects on conversion and retention and multiply them: the two stages are not causally independent.
Time-varying confounders (engagement metrics shaped by the free experience that also predict conversion and churn) require marginal structural models. Standard Cox regression with time-varying covariates conditions on these intermediates and biases the total effect estimate.



Customers partition into always-converters, never-converters, and freemium-induced converters. The economics depend on the size of the induced-converter stratum and their post-conversion LTV. If most conversions are always-converters, freemium gives away free usage to people who did not need it. Bounds on stratum proportions follow from monotonicity assumptions under the principal stratification framework.

[[LTV-CAC as Counterfactual Decision Rule]] — the economic decision framework that consumes this model’s output

How should the dependence between conversion time and post-conversion retention be modelled? A joint frailty model with shared latent variable is one option. What are alternatives?
Can the principal stratum bounds be informative enough to guide the freemium/paid-only decision, or are they typically too wide?
The “leaky bucket” diagnostic: the area between the churn CIF and conversion CIF, weighted by economic consequences. Can this be formalised as a single summary statistic for free-tier health?

title: Scale Invariance and Parameter Comparability Across Studies
text:
Utility coefficients in discrete choice models are scale-dependent: multiplying price by a constant divides the price coefficient by the same constant, leaving economic behaviour unchanged. Comparing \(\alpha\) across studies without accounting for price units is meaningless. Elasticities are the scale-invariant quantities suitable for cross-study comparison.



A Bayesian BLP implementation on Nevo’s cereal data produced \(\alpha_\text{pop} = -0.30\) with prices in cents. Nevo (2000) reports \(\alpha\) between \(-0.8\) and \(-2.5\). The apparent discrepancy looks like a factor-of-six disagreement in price sensitivity. It is not. The resolution turns on measurement units.




Scale dependence #scale-dependence — if \(U = -\alpha \cdot p\), then rescaling \(p' = cp\) requires \(\alpha' = \alpha/c\) to preserve the same utility level. The parameter absorbs the units of its argument.
Elasticity as invariant #elasticity-invariance — own-price elasticity \(\epsilon_{jj} = (p_j/s_j) \int \alpha_i \, s_{ij}(1-s_{ij}) \, dF(\alpha_i, \beta_i)\) is dimensionless. The price-times-coefficient product is unit-free regardless of whether price is in cents or dollars.
Measurement equivalence #measurement-equivalence — two models with different \(\alpha\) values describe identical consumer behaviour if their implied elasticities match. The models are observationally and behaviourally equivalent despite different parameterisations.






Utility is linear in price: \(U_j = -\alpha \cdot p_j + x_j'\beta + \xi_j\). If prices are measured in cents, \(p = 250\) for a $2.50 box of cereal. If measured in dollars, \(p = 2.50\). The disutility from price is the product \(\alpha \cdot p\). With \(\alpha = -0.30\) and \(p = 250\) (cents): disutility \(= 75\). With \(\alpha = -30\) and \(p = 2.50\) (dollars): disutility \(= 75\). Same number. Same choice probabilities. Same market shares. Same elasticities.



Applied researchers routinely compare coefficient magnitudes across studies. “Nevo gets \(\alpha = -2\), we get \(\alpha = -0.3\), so our model underestimates price sensitivity.” This reasoning is invalid unless both studies use identical price scales. The literature rarely documents whether prices enter in dollars, cents, or standardised units. The only valid comparison is at the level of implied elasticities or willingness-to-pay measures, both of which cancel the units.



Any coefficient attached to a continuous variable inherits the variable’s units. Standardising the variable (dividing by its standard deviation) produces a coefficient interpretable as “effect per standard deviation,” which is comparable across datasets. But standardisation changes the coefficient’s economic interpretation. The cleanest solution is to report both the raw coefficient (for structural interpretation within the model) and the implied elasticities or marginal effects (for cross-study comparison).



The [[Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox]] compounds this confusion. A hierarchical model’s \(\alpha_\text{pop}\) is already difficult to compare to a pooled estimate. Adding scale differences between studies makes naive comparison doubly misleading. The diagnostic must always be: compute the implied economic quantity (elasticity, substitution pattern, welfare measure) and compare those.





[[Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models]] — unit choice is another pragmatic decision within the Berry framework that affects parameter magnitudes without affecting economic conclusions
[[Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox]] — scale confusion compounds the pooling paradox when comparing hierarchical to pooled estimates across studies
[[BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking]] — BLP’s innovation was the preference distribution, not any particular parameterisation; scale invariance reflects this





Should the BLP literature adopt a convention (e.g., always report in dollars, always standardise) to reduce cross-study confusion?
For random coefficient models where \(\alpha_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_\text{pop}, \tau_\alpha)\), does rescaling price change the relative magnitude of heterogeneity \(\tau_\alpha / |\alpha_\text{pop}|\)? The ratio should be invariant, but numerical optimisers may behave differently at different scales.
Is there an analogue in survival analysis? Hazard ratios are unit-free, but baseline hazard scales with time units. Coefficient comparability across studies with different time granularity faces a similar issue.

title: LTV-CAC as Counterfactual Decision Rule
text:
The standard LTV > CAC decision rule is a causal estimand, not an accounting identity. Naive LTV calculations from observed retention confound the causal effect of the acquisition strategy with selection into it.



SaaS heuristics prescribe LTV/CAC > 3 and CAC payback under 12-18 months. These rules encode reasonable discounting for uncertainty and time value. They break down when the underlying LTV calculation ignores who the strategy attracts and whether those customers would have converted anyway.




CAC (fully loaded) #cac — total spend per acquired customer, including infrastructure costs of free-tier support, marketing, and the opportunity cost of foregone revenue during the free period. For a 3% conversion rate, each paying customer carries the cost of roughly 33 free users.
Counterfactual LTV #counterfactual-ltv — the expected lifetime value a customer generates under a given acquisition strategy, compared to the value under the alternative. Observed LTV conflates the causal effect of the freemium experience with pre-existing characteristics of customers who select into it.
Incrementality #incrementality — the fraction of conversions caused by the freemium programme. Always-converters (who would have paid anyway) receive free usage at a pure cost. The value of freemium lives in the induced-converter stratum.






Define LTV via the survival function:
\[\text{LTV} = \int_0^{\tau} r(t) \cdot S(t) \cdot e^{-\delta t} \, dt\]
where \(r(t)\) is revenue rate, \(S(t)\) is retention, and \(\delta\) is a discount rate. The causal question replaces \(S(t)\) with counterfactual survival curves: \(S(t \mid \text{freemium})\) versus \(S(t \mid \text{paid})\), estimated for the same population via IPTW or g-computation.



Selection into freemium correlates with price sensitivity, willingness to pay, and buying-journey stage. Customers who choose free plans differ systematically from those who pay upfront. Naive LTV attributes these baseline differences to the programme.
Revenue trajectories differ qualitatively between arms. Freemium customers contribute zero during the free period, then convert, then generate expansion revenue. Paid customers start generating revenue immediately. Comparing LTV at a snapshot conflates programme effects with trajectory shape.
The incrementality gap means the “conversion rate” overstates the programme’s value. Some converters would have paid regardless. The true benefit is the marginal customer the programme brings in, plus any retention uplift for inframarginal customers.



LTV/CAC ratios degrade as a programme scales. CAC stays roughly flat (infrastructure costs scale sub-linearly). Marginal customer quality declines: the programme saturates high-value segments first, then increasingly attracts users with lower conversion propensity and lower post-conversion LTV. The relevant ratio for the marginal investment decision is the LTV/CAC of the next cohort, not the historical average.



The payback time \(t^*\) solves:
\[\int_0^{t^*} r \cdot S(u) \, du = \text{CAC}\]
A distant \(t^*\) means financing a long-duration asset with uncertain cash flows. The discount rate should reflect this duration risk. Causal survival curves give the correct \(S(u)\) for this calculation.





[[Two-Stage Survival Models for Freemium Economics]] — the survival structure that feeds into LTV integration
[[Non-Collapsibility of Hazard Ratios]] — aggregate LTV/CAC ratios across segments are misleading for the same reason hazard ratios are non-collapsible: heterogeneous subpopulations mix in ways that obscure segment-level economics
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — partial identification of the incrementality fraction parallels the bounds problem in marketing mix models
[[Segment-Level Freemium Decisions]] — enterprise LTV/CAC may be 10 while SMB is below 1; aggregate blends hide value-destroying segments





How should the discount rate \(\delta\) relate to the uncertainty in the survival curve estimate? Longer-horizon LTV carries more estimation error.
Can the dynamic deterioration of LTV/CAC be modelled as a function of market penetration, giving an optimal stopping rule for programme investment?

Marginal customer quality declines: the programme saturates high-value segments first, then increasingly attracts users with lower conversion propensity and lower post-conversion LTV. The relevant ratio for the marginal investment decision is the LTV/CAC of the next cohort, not the historical average.



The payback time \(t^*\) solves:
\[\int_0^{t^*} r \cdot S(u) \, du = \text{CAC}\]
A distant \(t^*\) means financing a long-duration asset with uncertain cash flows. The discount rate should reflect this duration risk. Causal survival curves give the correct \(S(u)\) for this calculation.

href: notes/certain_things/Public/Economics/Ecological Fallacy and BLP's Inversion of Inference.html
title: Ecological Fallacy and BLP’s Inversion of Inference
text:
BLP demand estimation reverses the direction of the ecological fallacy. Instead of inferring individual behaviour from aggregate data (invalid), it asks: what distribution of individual preferences would generate the observed aggregate shares? This inversion makes aggregate data informative about distributional shape in a way that individual data cannot match.



The ecological fallacy is a standard warning in statistics: you cannot infer individual-level relationships from group-level data. Cities with higher average income and higher crime rates do not imply that richer individuals commit more crime. Textbooks teach the fallacy as a prohibition. BLP (1995) constitutes the valid exception, but this framing rarely appears in textbook treatments.




Ecological fallacy #ecological-fallacy — inferring individual behaviour from aggregate patterns; logically invalid because compositional effects confound the inference
BLP inversion #blp-inversion — proposing a candidate distribution of individual preferences \(F(\theta)\) and checking whether it generates the observed market shares; inference runs from distribution to aggregate, not aggregate to individual
Halton draws #halton-draws — low-discrepancy quadrature points used to approximate the integral \(s_j = \int P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta) \, dF(\theta)\); not simulated consumers but numerical integration nodes






Ecological fallacy logic runs: “Aggregate data shows X, therefore individuals must do Y.” This is deductively invalid. The aggregation function is many-to-one. Multiple individual-level distributions produce the same aggregate statistic.



BLP does not infer from aggregate to individual. It proposes a parametric family for individual preferences \(F(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta, \Sigma)\) and computes the implied aggregate shares:
\[s_j = \int P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta) \, dF(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta, \Sigma)\]
The model searches for the parameters \((\alpha, \beta, \Sigma)\) that make the predicted shares match the observed shares. The direction of inference is: candidate distribution \(\to\) predicted aggregates \(\to\) comparison with data. No step involves deducing individual behaviour from a group statistic.



Observing aggregate market shares is like viewing a blurry photograph of a crowd. You cannot identify individual faces. The Halton/quadrature approach proposes 100 hypothetical face templates and asks: if the crowd were composed of people drawn from this distribution of templates, would the blurry photograph match what we observe?
Each Halton draw is a template, not a person. The integration approximation \(s_j \approx (1/R) \sum_r P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta_r)\) uses these templates as quadrature nodes. The approximation error scales as \(O(\log(N)^D / N)\) for Halton draws versus \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\) for random Monte Carlo. One hundred Halton draws give accuracy comparable to roughly one thousand random draws.



A productive paradox sits at the core. Observing individual choices gives you one draw from the preference distribution. Each consumer reveals their own type but tells you little about the distribution’s shape. Observing aggregate shares gives you the expected value of the choice function integrated over the entire preference distribution. Each market provides a data point about the shape of the distribution, not just one point within it.
Individual data is precise about individuals but noisy about the distribution. Aggregate data is silent about individuals but informative about distributional parameters. BLP exploits the second property. Cross-market variation in prices and product characteristics traces out how the distribution responds to different choice environments.



Three factors explain the gap. First, BLP (1995) focused on establishing computational feasibility for random coefficient models without micro data. Halton sequences were a numerical footnote, not the conceptual centrepiece. Second, the GMM tradition trains economists to think in moments, not distributions. The connection between aggregate shares and distributional shape is obscured by moment-condition notation. Third, the ecological fallacy warning is taught as a prohibition. The valid exception requires a structural model that specifies the aggregation function, and textbooks rarely frame structural estimation as “the ecological fallacy done right.”





[[Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration]] — the numerical machinery that makes the share integral tractable
[[BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking]] — the decade-long lag between publication and adoption reflects the conceptual barrier described here
[[Effective Sample Size as Implicit Regularization]] — another case where a BLP modelling choice is epistemically defensible despite looking “wrong”
[[Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models]] — the Normal likelihood approximation is a second pragmatic compromise in the same model





Does the aggregate-data advantage extend to richer distributional families (e.g., mixtures of normals for preferences)? At what point does the data lose identifying power over the distribution’s shape?
How many markets are needed before cross-market variation identifies the preference distribution reliably? The 8-city subset of Nevo’s data gives weak identification; the 47-city panel is adequate. Where is the threshold?
Can the BLP inversion logic be applied outside demand estimation, for example to aggregate voting data or aggregate health outcomes?

href: notes/certain_things/Public/Economics/BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking.html
title: BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking
text:
BLP (1995) took over a decade to become standard practice in industrial organization because the profession’s training in GMM and moment-based thinking obscured the model’s generative logic. The key insight was distributional, not computational. Textbooks presented Halton draws as a numerical trick rather than the mechanism enabling a conceptual shift.



Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes published in Econometrica in 1995. The paper combined three contributions: a contraction mapping to invert shares to mean utilities, instrumental variables for price endogeneity, and the recognition that aggregate scanner data identifies preference distributions. Adoption was slow despite the method’s elegance and the data’s ubiquity.




GMM training #gmm — the generation of econometricians trained on Hansen (1982) thought in terms of moment conditions and orthogonality restrictions, not distributions and generative processes
Generative model #generative-model — a complete probabilistic specification from latent parameters through to observed data, enabling forward simulation
Ecological fallacy caution #ecological-fallacy — the methodological warning that aggregate data cannot support individual-level inferences, which is correct in general but wrong for BLP’s specific inversion






The profession understood BLP through the lens it had: moment conditions, instruments, and asymptotic theory. The generative logic (posit a distribution, simulate forward, match predictions to data) was foreign to the GMM toolkit. Researchers could implement the estimator without grasping why it worked.
The ecological fallacy warning compounded the problem. Economists trained to distrust aggregate-to-individual inference reasonably asked: how can market shares identify individual preferences? The answer requires understanding distributional inference as distinct from individual inference. BLP identifies the shape of \(F(\theta)\), not any particular \(\theta_i\). This distinction is subtle and was not emphasized in early presentations.



The Halton sequences were a computational footnote in the original paper. The real contributions were conceptual. First, the contraction mapping showed that mean utilities are recoverable from shares without parametric distributional assumptions. Second, the IV strategy handled the fundamental identification problem (firms set prices knowing \(\xi\)). Third, the generative framing showed that aggregate data is sufficient for distributional identification.
Scanner data existed everywhere. The model unlocked it. The bottleneck was not data or computation. It was the conceptual framework for thinking about what aggregate data can tell you.



BLP is most clearly understood as a story: Nature draws preferences from \(F(\alpha, \beta)\). A random sample of consumers enters each market. They choose products given preferences and characteristics. We observe only aggregate shares. Estimation reverse-engineers step one from step four.
This framing makes explicit what the GMM formulation leaves implicit. The GMM approach specifies moment conditions that the true parameters satisfy. The generative approach specifies the entire data-generating process and asks: which parameters make the simulated data look like the real data? The two are mathematically equivalent but pedagogically different. The generative version communicates why the model works.





[[BLP as Ecological Reverse-Engineering]] — the epistemological content of what BLP achieves
[[Feyerabend’s Counter-Induction as Epistemic Necessity]] — BLP’s distributional approach contradicted the dominant ecological-fallacy intuition, yet proved correct
[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — GMM and Bayesian BLP are theoretically equivalent formulations with different heuristic power





Are there other cases in economics where a methodological insight took a decade to diffuse because the profession’s standard toolkit obscured the conceptual content?
Does the Bayesian formulation of BLP (posterior over preference distributions) make the generative logic more transparent than the classical GMM version?
How much of applied IO’s current practice still treats Halton draws as a computational trick rather than the mechanism enabling distributional identification?

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Economics/Identification Power and Cross-Market Variation in BLP.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Economics/Identification Power and Cross-Market Variation in BLP.html
title: Identification Power and Cross-Market Variation in BLP
text:
BLP identification of preference heterogeneity requires substantial cross-market variation in prices and product characteristics. With too few markets (e.g. 8 cities), key parameters become weakly identified because instruments lack power. This is not merely a statistical precision issue. It is a fundamental constraint on what the data can reveal about the preference distribution.



A Bayesian BLP implementation on Nevo’s cereal data used 8 cities. The random coefficient distribution \(\alpha_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_\text{pop}, \tau_\alpha)\) was identified but with wide posterior uncertainty on \(\tau_\alpha\). Expanding to 47 cities provides roughly 6x more cross-sectional variation, strengthening the first-stage regression and tightening inference on heterogeneity parameters.




Cross-market variation #cross-market — differences in prices, product availability, and demographics across geographic markets that provide the identifying variation for demand parameters
First-stage power #first-stage — the strength of the relationship between instruments (rival characteristics, cost shifters) and endogenous price. Weak first stages produce biased and imprecise second-stage estimates.
Identification vs. estimation #identification — a parameter is identified if in principle the data can pin it down as the sample grows. It is well-estimated if the current sample provides enough variation to do so with acceptable precision.






BLP uses instruments to isolate exogenous price variation. Standard BLP instruments include characteristics of rival products in the same market (which shift markups through competitive pressure) and cost shifters that affect supply but not demand directly. These instruments must vary across markets to generate identifying variation. If all markets face similar competitive conditions and similar costs, the instruments have no cross-sectional bite.



With 8 cities and 24 products over 4 quarters, the model has roughly 768 share observations. Each city contributes one draw from the random coefficient distribution. Eight draws from a Normal distribution cannot precisely identify both the mean and the variance. The posterior on \(\tau_\alpha\) reflects this: it is wide and sensitive to the prior.
With 47 cities, you get 47 draws from the random coefficient distribution. The mean and variance become well-identified from the data. Instruments have more variation to exploit. The first-stage F-statistic rises. Price sensitivity estimates tighten.



The deeper point is that cross-market variation is what makes the preference distribution identifiable at all. BLP’s inversion asks: “what distribution of preferences is consistent with these market shares?” Each market provides one integral equation constraining the distribution. With few markets, the system is underdetermined. Many distributions could produce the same 8 share vectors. With many markets facing different price-characteristic configurations, the system becomes increasingly constrained. The preference distribution is pinned down by the diversity of market conditions, not by the volume of data within any single market.



More markets increase computational cost. Each market requires Halton integration over the preference distribution to compute predicted shares. With 47 markets, 24 products, 4 quarters, and 100 Halton draws, the share computation involves \(47 \times 24 \times 4 \times 100 = 451{,}200\) utility evaluations per MCMC step. The gain in identification must be weighed against iteration speed, especially in a Bayesian framework where thousands of posterior samples are needed.





[[BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking]] — the generative structure makes the identification requirement transparent: you need enough diverse “experiments” (markets) to reverse-engineer the distribution
[[Ecological Fallacy and BLP’s Inversion of Inference]] — each market provides a moment of the preference distribution; more markets provide more moments and tighter identification
[[Temporal Structure in Panel Demand Models]] — temporal variation is a second axis of identifying variation, but exploiting it requires modelling temporal dynamics in \(\xi\)
[[Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox]] — with 8 cities, the hierarchical model leans heavily on the prior for \(\tau_\alpha\); with 47, the data speaks





Is there a minimum number of markets below which BLP heterogeneity parameters are effectively prior-determined? Can this threshold be characterised analytically?
Does the instrument strength vary systematically with geographic scope? National datasets may have less price variation than datasets spanning regulatory environments.
Can sequential experimental design principles (choosing which markets to add next) improve identification efficiency in BLP?

title: Identification Power and Cross-Market Variation in BLP
text:
BLP uses instruments to isolate exogenous price variation. Standard BLP instruments include characteristics of rival products in the same market (which shift markups through competitive pressure) and cost shifters that affect supply but not demand directly. These instruments must vary across markets to generate identifying variation. If all markets face similar competitive conditions and similar costs, the instruments have no cross-sectional bite.



With 8 cities and 24 products over 4 quarters, the model has roughly 768 share observations. Each city contributes one draw from the random coefficient distribution. Eight draws from a Normal distribution cannot precisely identify both the mean and the variance. The posterior on \(\tau_\alpha\) reflects this: it is wide and sensitive to the prior.
With 47 cities, you get 47 draws from the random coefficient distribution. The mean and variance become well-identified from the data. Instruments have more variation to exploit. The first-stage F-statistic rises. Price sensitivity estimates tighten.



The deeper point is that cross-market variation is what makes the preference distribution identifiable at all. BLP’s inversion asks: “what distribution of preferences is consistent with these market shares?” Each market provides one integral equation constraining the distribution. With few markets, the system is underdetermined. Many distributions could produce the same 8 share vectors. With many markets facing different price-characteristic configurations, the system becomes increasingly constrained. The preference distribution is pinned down by the diversity of market conditions, not by the volume of data within any single market.



More markets increase computational cost. Each market requires Halton integration over the preference distribution to compute predicted shares. With 47 markets, 24 products, 4 quarters, and 100 Halton draws, the share computation involves \(47 \times 24 \times 4 \times 100 = 451{,}200\) utility evaluations per MCMC step. The gain in identification must be weighed against iteration speed, especially in a Bayesian framework where thousands of posterior samples are needed.

title: Non-Collapsibility in Hierarchical Demand Models
text:
In hierarchical BLP models, the population mean price coefficient \(\alpha_{\text{pop}}\) does not equal the “effective” price sensitivity governing elasticities. The nonlinear mixed-logit integral makes marginal and conditional quantities non-collapsible, just as in survival analysis with hazard ratios.



A Bayesian BLP model with city-level price coefficients uses a hierarchical prior: \(\alpha_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_{\text{pop}}, \tau_\alpha)\). The estimated \(\alpha_{\text{pop}}\) often looks small compared to published non-hierarchical estimates. This mismatch prompts the question: is the model underestimating price sensitivity? The answer is no. Elasticities depend on \(\alpha_r\) values through a nonlinear integral, and the marginal effect cannot be read off the population mean.




Partial pooling #partial-pooling — Bayesian hierarchical technique shrinking group-level parameters toward a common mean, with data-determined shrinkage
Own-price elasticity #elasticity — \(\epsilon_{jj} = \frac{p_j}{s_j} \int \alpha_i \cdot s_{ij}(1 - s_{ij}) \, dF(\alpha_i, \beta_i)\)
Non-collapsibility #non-collapsibility — the property that a marginal effect parameter differs from the conditional effect parameter, even absent confounding




The elasticity formula integrates over consumer heterogeneity:
\[\epsilon_{jj} = \frac{p_j}{s_j} \int \alpha_i \cdot s_{ij}(1 - s_{ij}) \, dF(\alpha_i, \beta_i)\]
This integral is nonlinear in \(\alpha_i\). Jensen’s inequality guarantees that \(E[f(\alpha)] \neq f(E[\alpha])\) for the convex/concave share function. A population mean of \(\alpha_{\text{pop}} = -0.30\) can produce average elasticities of \(-3.17\). The naive calculation using \(\alpha_{\text{pop}}\) directly in the share formula gives \(-72\), demonstrating why the full integration over consumer types is essential.
The heterogeneous consumers who actually choose a product have different effective price sensitivities than the population mean implies. Consumers with high \(\alpha_i\) avoid expensive products. The selected sample has systematically different \(\alpha\) values than the population.
This is structurally identical to [[Non-Collapsibility of Hazard Ratios]]. The hazard ratio changes when you condition on covariates, even without confounding, because the Cox model is nonlinear. Here the logit share model is nonlinear, and the population-level \(\alpha_{\text{pop}}\) differs from the “average conditional” effect for the same mathematical reason.


The hierarchical and pooled models can produce identical elasticities while having different \(\alpha\) values. The models are empirically equivalent in elasticity space but ontologically distinct in parameter space. This connects to [[Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability]]: the parameter \(\alpha_{\text{pop}}\) is a theoretical entity whose interpretation shifts depending on the model structure surrounding it.




Hierarchical prior: \(\alpha_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_{\text{pop}}, \tau_\alpha)\)
Elasticity: \(\epsilon_{jj} = \frac{p_j}{s_j} \cdot \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} \alpha_r \cdot s_{rj}(1 - s_{rj})\)
Non-collapsibility: \(\frac{1}{R}\sum_r f(\alpha_r) \neq f\left(\frac{1}{R}\sum_r \alpha_r\right)\)




[[Non-Collapsibility of Hazard Ratios]] — the same mathematical phenomenon in survival analysis
[[Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability]] — empirical equivalence in elasticities despite different parameter values
[[BLP as Ecological Reverse-Engineering]] — the broader framework within which this non-collapsibility operates





How should one report hierarchical BLP results to make them comparable with the GMM literature? Is there a canonical “effective alpha” summary statistic?
Does the degree of non-collapsibility increase with the variance of the preference distribution \(\tau_\alpha\)?
Could rescaling prices (dollars vs. cents) interact with the non-collapsibility in misleading ways?

title: Temporal Structure in Panel Demand Models
text:
Standard BLP implementations treat time as a batch dimension with no temporal hierarchy. This is defensible with short panels (2-3 periods) but becomes increasingly untenable as the panel lengthens, because unobserved product quality \(\xi_{jmt}\) is almost certainly autocorrelated.



The typical BLP specification decomposes unobserved quality as \(\xi_{jmt} = \xi_j + \tilde{\xi}_{jmt}\), where \(\xi_j\) is a product fixed effect and \(\tilde{\xi}_{jmt}\) is an iid residual. This assumes that conditional on the product intercept, quality shocks are independent across quarters. The assumption simplifies estimation and is standard in the literature, but it imposes substantive restrictions on how demand evolves.




Batch-dimension time #batch-time – treating each market-period as an exchangeable draw, with no ordering or dependence across periods. The likelihood factors as a product over \((j, m, t)\) triples with no temporal links.
Autocorrelated unobservables #autocorrelated-xi – if a product receives favourable reviews in Q1, its unobserved quality in Q2 is likely still elevated. An AR(1) structure \(\tilde{\xi}_{jmt} = \rho \tilde{\xi}_{jm,t-1} + \epsilon_{jmt}\) captures this persistence.
Factor structure #factor-structure – a richer alternative where \(\xi_{jmt} = \lambda_j' f_t + \epsilon_{jmt}\), allowing time trends to load heterogeneously across products (e.g. electric vehicles gain unobserved appeal faster than sedans).






With only two time periods, an AR(1) structure has one autocorrelation parameter and one lagged observation per product-market. The model cannot distinguish temporal persistence from estimation noise. The iid assumption is the honest specification: it acknowledges ignorance rather than imposing structure the data cannot identify.



With four or more periods, the data can speak to temporal dependence. Ignoring it has two costs. First, the standard errors on demand parameters are too small because the effective sample size is overstated. Observations within a product-market series are not independent information. Second, instruments that exploit cross-period variation (e.g. cost shifters that change gradually) may be weak conditional on autocorrelated \(\xi\), because the identifying variation is confounded with persistent unobserved quality.



Three approaches add temporal structure with increasing complexity. The AR(1) on \(\xi\) is the simplest: it adds one parameter \(\rho\) and requires lagged residuals. Time-varying coefficients let price sensitivity or brand preferences drift, which matters if the consumer population changes (e.g. income growth shifts willingness to pay). The factor structure is the most flexible, allowing each product’s unobserved quality to follow its own trajectory, but requires enough periods to identify the factors.



For applied work with short panels, time fixed effects (an intercept for each period) capture aggregate time trends without imposing temporal dependence on \(\xi\). Add temporal hierarchy only when the panel is long enough to identify it. The threshold is roughly four periods for AR(1), eight or more for factor models.





[[BLP and the Decade-Long Diffusion of Generative Thinking]] – the generative framing makes the temporal assumption explicit: Nature draws \(\xi_{jmt}\) iid across periods
[[Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models]] – the temporal structure is another pragmatic modelling choice where parsimony trades off against realism
[[Non-Collapsibility in Hierarchical Demand Models]] – the hierarchical structure across markets is spatial; the temporal structure is the analogous problem across time
[[Effective Sample Size as Implicit Regularization]] – autocorrelated \(\xi\) reduces the effective sample size, paralleling the ESS concept in the likelihood approximation





At what panel length does ignoring autocorrelation in \(\xi\) produce materially biased elasticity estimates?
Can the AR(1) structure be integrated into the Bayesian BLP framework without breaking the contraction mapping, or does it require a fully joint specification?
How does temporal structure in \(\xi\) interact with the IV strategy? If cost instruments are themselves autocorrelated, the exclusion restriction may hold period-by-period but fail in the time-series dimension.
