title: BLP as Ecological Reverse-Engineering
text:
BLP demand estimation avoids the ecological fallacy by inferring preference distributions from aggregate data, rather than individual preferences. This inversion is logically valid: it asks which population distribution generates the observed market shares.



The ecological fallacy arises when analysts infer individual-level relationships from aggregate correlations. Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) proposed a demand model that works with aggregate market share data yet recovers the distribution of consumer preferences. The question: does this commit the ecological fallacy? The answer reveals something deep about the epistemology of aggregate inference.




Ecological fallacy #ecological-fallacy — the error of deducing individual behaviour from group-level statistics
Halton sequence #halton-draws — a low-discrepancy quasi-random sequence that fills a unit hypercube more uniformly than pseudo-random draws, with convergence rate \(O(\log(N)^D / N)\)
Generative model #generative-model — a probabilistic specification of the full data-generating process, from latent variables to observations
Distributional inference #distributional-inference — learning the shape of \(F(\theta)\) rather than specific \(\theta_i\) values






The ecological fallacy runs deductively from aggregate to individual. BLP runs inductively in the opposite direction: posit a distribution of individual preferences, integrate forward to predict aggregate shares, then compare predictions to data. The logic is:
\[s_{jm} = \int P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta) \, dF(\theta) \approx \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta_r)\]
Each candidate distribution \(F(\theta)\) generates predicted shares. Estimation finds the \(F\) whose predictions match observed shares. Individual preferences remain unidentified. The distribution is identified.



Observing individual choices reveals one draw from the preference distribution. Observing aggregate shares reveals the expected value of the choice function integrated over the entire distribution. Each market provides a data point about the shape of \(F\), not just one point within it. Aggregation destroys individual information but creates distributional information.



The Halton draws that represent “consumer types” in the integral are quadrature nodes. They are not estimates of real individuals. They function as preference personas: computational devices that efficiently represent the continuous distribution. Their ontological status is ambiguous. The model requires them for computation, yet they correspond to no actual person.
This parallels the status of theoretical entities in scientific realism. The Halton consumers are indispensable for prediction yet ontologically fictional. They are a concrete instance of the instability that [[Morita Equivalence and Ontological Instability]] identifies in formally equivalent theories.



The BLP share integral is structurally identical to the G-computation formula:
\[E[Y(a)] = \int E[Y \mid A=a, L=l] \, dF(l)\]
Both integrate a conditional model over a distribution of unobserved variables to obtain a marginal quantity. The Halton draws play the same role as the covariate distribution in [[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]]. Unobserved individual preferences are structurally analogous to missing data, connecting to [[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]].




Consumer \(i\)’s preference parameter: \(\alpha_i = \alpha_{\text{pop}} + \sigma_\alpha \cdot \Phi^{-1}(v_i)\), where \(v_i\) is a Halton draw on \([0,1]\).
Market share prediction: \(s_{jm} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{\exp(x_j \beta_r - \alpha_r p_j + \xi_j)}{1 + \sum_k \exp(x_k \beta_r - \alpha_r p_k + \xi_k)}\)




[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — identical integral structure for marginalizing over unobserved heterogeneity
[[Analogies between Missing Data and Causal Inference]] — unobserved preferences as missing data
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — BLP achieves point identification through parametric assumptions where Manski’s nonparametric approach yields only bounds
[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — if two distributional assumptions yield identical elasticities, are they theoretically equivalent?
[[LTV-CAC as Counterfactual Decision Rule]] — BLP counterfactual price simulations use the estimated distribution for forward-looking decisions, the same pattern





What are the limits of distributional identification from aggregates? Under what conditions does aggregate data fail to pin down the preference distribution?
How sensitive is identification to the parametric assumption of Normal preferences? Could nonparametric mixtures-of-logit achieve the same without distributional commitments?
The “lovely paradox” that aggregation creates distributional information while destroying individual information: does this generalize beyond discrete choice to other settings?

title: Model-Dependency and the PO Objection to Process Decomposition
text:
The potential outcomes school’s deepest objection to process-based causal decomposition (Aalen, Pearl, dynamic path analysis) is that the decomposition is a property of the model, not a property of the data. The model does not discover that an effect splits into direct and indirect paths. It assumes the split and estimates the weights.



A talk on dynamic path analysis in survival models prompted a systematic inventory of PO objections. Five distinct objections emerged, ordered from technical to philosophical. The model-dependency objection sits at the foundation. It claims that additive separability in the latent predictor guarantees a clean path decomposition regardless of whether the true data-generating process decomposes that way.




Model-dependency #model-dependency — the property that a causal conclusion depends on the parametric structure of the model rather than being identifiable from the data under weaker assumptions
Additive separability #additive-separability — the structural assumption \(\eta(t) = \alpha_1(t) X + \alpha_2(t) M\) that makes direct and indirect contributions readable from coefficients
Nonparametric identification #nonparametric-identification — the PO school’s gold standard: a causal quantity is identified if it can be expressed as a functional of the observed data distribution without parametric assumptions






The PO school’s objections to process-based mediation in survival models form a logical chain. Each builds on the previous one.
First: the decomposition is parametric. The direct effect \(\alpha_1(t)\) and indirect effect \(\beta(t) \cdot \alpha_2(t)\) are readable from the structural equations because the model assumes additive separability. In a nonparametric world, the total effect need not decompose into two additive components. The decomposition is the model talking to itself.
Second: the NDE remains a cross-world counterfactual. Computing \(Y(1, M(0))\) from a generative model does not resolve the PO objection that the quantity has no experimental referent. The objection was never about computability. It was about meaning. No trial can produce \(Y(1, M(0))\) without structural assumptions that are themselves unverifiable.
Third: inspectability is not testability. Posterior predictive checks test whether the model fits the observed data. They cannot distinguish a correctly specified causal model from a well-fitting but causally wrong one. See [[Inspectability Is Not Testability in Causal Models]] for the full argument.
Fourth: sequential unconfoundedness is extremely demanding. In survival contexts with time-varying confounders, the assumption requires that at every time point, all common causes of treatment, mediator, and hazard are observed and adjusted for. The structural model handles confounding implicitly through the equations, but only if the equations are correctly specified. This circles back to the first objection.
Fifth: “process” is metaphysics, not methodology. A hard-nosed PO critic will say: methodologically, you have built a parametric Bayesian survival model with time-varying coefficients. The “process” interpretation is a story told about the coefficients. Any parametric model with time-varying effects tells a process story. The identification question is unchanged.



The response concedes the model-dependency point and shifts the ground to practical payoff. The structural model produces temporally indexed recommendations: “intervene on the mediator after day 100.” No single-number estimand delivers this. The PO school’s cleaner estimands (average treatment effect, separable direct effect) collapse the time dimension. They say how much but not when or through what.
The Bayesian framework adds a second advantage: sensitivity analysis over the structural assumptions. You can vary the modularity assumption parametrically and watch how the decomposition responds. This does not make the assumption testable. It makes the conclusion’s dependence on the assumption transparent.



Model-dependency is not unique to process models. The ATE itself depends on SUTVA, positivity, and unconfoundedness. IPW depends on correct specification of the treatment mechanism. Every causal quantity rests on assumptions that cannot be verified from data alone. The relevant question is not “does the conclusion depend on assumptions?” but “does the assumption buy something worth having?”
Process models buy temporal specificity. The cost is structural commitment. PO models buy nonparametric identification of total effects. The cost is silence about mechanism and timing.

[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the philosophical framing that motivates the process approach
[[Theoretical Equivalence as the Core of the Realism Debate]] — model-dependency in causal inference parallels underdetermination in philosophy of science; multiple models fit the same data but support different causal stories





Is there a formal sense in which the process decomposition converges to a nonparametric quantity as the model becomes more flexible (e.g., Gaussian processes for time-varying coefficients)?
Can the five objections be ranked by how much they reduce the practical value of the decomposition? The first and fifth seem fundamental; the second through fourth seem resolvable in principle.
Does the process modeler’s “temporal specificity” argument hold up when the time-varying coefficients are estimated with wide uncertainty bands? Specificity without precision may be worse than silence.

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Philosophy/Temporal Trajectory as the Process Model's Comparative Advantage.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Philosophy/Temporal Trajectory as the Process Model's Comparative Advantage.html
title: Temporal Trajectory as the Process Model’s Comparative Advantage
text:
The strongest defence of structural mediation against the PO critique is not philosophical but practical. Time-varying coefficient trajectories produce recommendations that no single-number estimand can deliver. The recommendation “intervene on the mediator after day 100” requires knowing when the indirect path dominates, and neither separability nor IPW produces this temporal resolution.



The PO school’s five-pronged critique of structural mediation concludes that the causal interpretation of path coefficients rests on unverifiable assumptions. Grant the epistemological point. The question becomes pragmatic: what kind of answers does each framework produce?




Coefficient trajectory #coefficient-trajectory — the time-indexed path \(\alpha_2(t)\) showing how the mediator’s effect on the hazard evolves; the structural model’s distinctive output
Marginal estimand #marginal-estimand — a single-number summary like the ATE or the separable direct effect; the PO school’s preferred output
Actionable specificity #actionable-specificity — the property of a recommendation that tells you not just whether to act but when and on what






A dynamic path analysis with time-varying coefficients yields \(\alpha_1(t)\) (direct hazard effect of treatment), \(\alpha_2(t)\) (effect of mediator on hazard), and \(\beta(t)\) (effect of treatment on mediator). The indirect contribution at each time point is \(\beta(t) \cdot \alpha_2(t)\). This is a curve, not a number.
The curve reveals temporal structure: the direct effect may dominate early while the indirect effect grows over time, or vice versa. The crossing point identifies when the mediator becomes the primary channel. G-computation propagates these trajectories through the nonlinear link function to produce marginal survival contrasts at each time horizon.



Separability defines the estimand. IPW identifies it. The output is a marginal contrast: the separable direct effect is one number, the separable indirect effect is another. These numbers have clean experimental interpretations. They answer: “how much of the total effect flows through the mediator?”
They do not answer: “when does the mediator channel become dominant?” or “at what time point should a clinician shift attention from the treatment itself to the mediator?” For policy, timing matters as much as magnitude.



The process modeller concedes three points. The decomposition depends on the structural equations. The NDE is a cross-world quantity. Posterior fit does not validate causal structure. These are genuine limitations.
The counter-claim: structural commitments are the price of temporal specificity. A weighted MSM with separability gives a defensible single number. A time-varying coefficient model gives a trajectory that tells practitioners what to do and when. “Intervene on the mediator after day 100” is actionable in a way that “the indirect effect is 30% of the total” is not.



The two approaches answer different questions. The PO school asks: “what is the effect, defined without structural commitments?” The process school asks: “how does the mechanism evolve, and when should we intervene?”
A practitioner needs both. The PO framework’s clean total effect serves the binary decision (treat or not?). The process framework’s trajectory serves the follow-up decision (given treatment, what to monitor and when to adjust?).





[[The PO Critique of Structural Mediation]] — the critique this note responds to
[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — the technical framework producing the coefficient trajectories
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — how structural parameters translate into marginal estimands the PO school would accept
[[Separability as the Potential Outcomes Alternative to Cross-World Counterfactuals]] — the PO school’s clean estimand definition, which lacks temporal resolution





Can the PO toolkit be extended to produce time-varying estimands? A separable direct effect defined at each time horizon would bridge the gap.
Does the temporal trajectory’s actionability depend on the structural assumptions being approximately correct, or is it robust to moderate misspecification?
Is there a formal sense in which the trajectory contains “more information” than the marginal estimand, analogous to a sufficient statistic containing more information than a point estimate?

title: Effective Sample Size as Implicit Regularization
text:
In Bayesian BLP models, the notional market size \(n\) entering the Berry (1994) variance approximation functions as a regularization parameter, not a literal population count. Setting it below the true market size is epistemically defensible because structural error dominates sampling noise.



Berry (1994) derived an approximate variance for log-share-ratios under multinomial sampling. This variance enters the Normal likelihood as observation noise. The parameter \(n\) controls how tight the likelihood is. Larger \(n\) means smaller variance, steeper likelihood, and harder MCMC sampling. The question: what value of \(n\) should a Bayesian modeler use?




Berry variance approximation #berry-variance — \(\text{Var}(\log(s_j/s_0)) \approx (1 - s_j)/(n \cdot s_j)\), the heteroskedastic noise under multinomial sampling
Structural error (\(\xi\)) #structural-error — unobserved product-market demand shocks capturing quality variation beyond observables
Posterior geometry #posterior-geometry — the shape of the log-posterior surface as it affects NUTS/HMC sampling efficiency




The BLP model contains two sources of variation: multinomial sampling noise (governed by \(n\)) and structural shocks \(\xi_{jt}\). In real market data, structural shocks dominate. A product’s market share deviates from the model prediction primarily because of unobserved quality, advertising, or brand effects, not because of sampling variability in consumer choices.
Setting \(n\) equal to the true market size (say, millions of consumers) produces a near-degenerate likelihood. The variance \((1-s_j)/(n \cdot s_j)\) becomes tiny. MCMC samplers struggle with the resulting steep curvature.
Setting \(n\) to a moderate value (say, 1000) widens the likelihood. This acknowledges that \(\xi\) explains most variation, not sampling noise. The model puts variance where it belongs: in the structural error term. Point estimates remain unbiased. Posterior geometry improves. Sampling efficiency rises by orders of magnitude.
The choice of \(n\) is a modeling decision about where uncertainty lives. It parallels the broader theme in [[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]]: the likelihood specification encodes substantive assumptions, not just mathematical convenience.



\[\text{Var}(\log(s_j/s_0)) \approx \frac{1 - s_j}{n \cdot s_j}\]
\[\log(s_j/s_0) \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\delta_j, \frac{1-s_j}{n \cdot s_j}\right)\]
where \(\delta_j = x_j\beta - \alpha p_j + \xi_j\) is the mean utility.




[[The Likelihood Principle as Modeling Directive]] — \(n\) is a case where likelihood specification encodes assumptions about the location of uncertainty
[[Manski’s Partial Identification and MMM Calibration]] — the tradeoff between computational tractability and theoretical correctness echoes Manski’s point that tighter assumptions are not always better
[[Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models]] — the Normal approximation itself is the broader pragmatic choice; \(n\) is a parameter within it





Could \(n\) be estimated as a free parameter? What would the posterior over \(n\) reveal about the relative importance of sampling vs. structural variation?
How does the choice of \(n\) interact with formal model comparison criteria (WAIC, LOO)?
Is there a principled calibration procedure, or is \(n\) inevitably a tuning knob?

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Halton sequences achieve near-\(O(1/N)\) convergence for numerical integrals in moderate dimensions by exploiting coprimality of prime bases. Each new draw fills the largest remaining gap in the unit hypercube. This makes them vastly more efficient than pseudo-random Monte Carlo for computing mixed-logit share integrals.



BLP demand estimation requires evaluating integrals of the form \(s_{jm} = \int P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta) \, dF(\theta)\). With \(D\) random coefficients, this is a \(D\)-dimensional integral with no closed form. The computational method for approximating this integral determines both accuracy and feasibility of estimation.




Low-discrepancy sequence #low-discrepancy — a deterministic sequence whose points fill a unit hypercube more uniformly than random draws, measured by star discrepancy \(D^*_N\)
Coprimality #coprimality — two integers sharing no common factor greater than 1; ensures Halton sequences in different dimensions never synchronize
Owen scrambling #owen-scrambling — random digit permutations within each base that preserve low-discrepancy while removing deterministic bias






Random Monte Carlo gives \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\) convergence regardless of dimension. With 100 draws, different seeds produce different elasticity estimates. Regular grids require \(O(10^D)\) points. In 5 dimensions, adequate coverage demands 100,000 grid points. Halton sequences achieve approximately \(O(\log(N)^D / N)\) convergence: 100 Halton draws match roughly 1000 random draws in accuracy.



Assign the first \(D\) primes as bases, one per dimension. For base \(b\), represent each integer \(n\) in base \(b\), then reflect the digits about the decimal point.
For base 2: \(n=1\) gives 0.5, \(n=2\) gives 0.25, \(n=3\) gives 0.75, \(n=4\) gives 0.125, \(n=5\) gives 0.625. Each level fills gaps left by previous levels, tracing a binary tree of the unit interval.
For base 3: \(n=1\) gives 0.333, \(n=2\) gives 0.667, \(n=3\) gives 0.111, and so on.



Because the bases share no common factors, the sequences across dimensions never align at the same \(n\). When base 2 places a point at 0.5 in dimension 1, base 3 is at 0.333 in dimension 2. Each new draw lands in a maximally distant region of the preference cube. This guarantees uniform joint coverage without requiring explicit construction of a multidimensional grid.



Without scrambling, Halton draws are deterministic: the same “consumer types” appear in every MCMC iteration. Owen scrambling applies random digit permutations within each base. The space-filling property is preserved because permuting digits within a base still fills each sub-interval uniformly. Multiple MCMC chains can use independent scramblings. Bias from specific fixed types is eliminated.



Halton draws live on \([0,1]^D\). The inverse Normal CDF maps them to actual preference parameters:
\[\alpha_i = \alpha_{\text{pop}} + \sigma_\alpha \cdot \Phi^{-1}(v_i)\]
A Halton value of 0.5 produces the median consumer. A value of 0.95 produces a consumer 1.64 standard deviations above the mean. The uniform space-filling on \([0,1]\) becomes representative coverage of the Normal distribution.




Halton sequence in base \(b\): for integer \(n\) with base-\(b\) representation \(n = \sum_{k=0}^{m} d_k b^k\), the Halton value is \(H_b(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} d_k b^{-(k+1)}\).
Share integral approximation: \(s_{jm} \approx \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{\exp(x_j\beta_r - \alpha_r p_j + \xi_j)}{1 + \sum_k \exp(x_k\beta_r - \alpha_r p_k + \xi_k)}\)
Convergence: \(|I - I_N| = O\left(\frac{(\log N)^D}{N}\right)\) versus \(O(N^{-1/2})\) for random Monte Carlo.




[[BLP as Ecological Reverse-Engineering]] — Halton draws are the computational mechanism enabling distributional inference from aggregate data
[[Effective Sample Size as Implicit Regularization]] — the number of Halton draws \(R\) and the effective sample size \(n\) are two distinct knobs controlling different aspects of approximation quality

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text: Halton sequences achieve near-\(O(1/N)\) convergence for numerical integrals in moderate dimensions by exploiting coprimality of prime bases. Each new draw fills the largest remaining gap in the unit hypercube. This makes them vastly more efficient than pseudo-random Monte Carlo for computing mixed-logit share integrals.
crumbs: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text: BLP demand estimation requires evaluating integrals of the form \(s_{jm} = \int P(\text{choose } j \mid \theta) \, dF(\theta)\). With \(D\) random coefficients, this is a \(D\)-dimensional integral with no closed form. The computational method for approximating this integral determines both accuracy and feasibility of estimation.
crumbs: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Low-discrepancy sequence #low-discrepancy — a deterministic sequence whose points fill a unit hypercube more uniformly than random draws, measured by star discrepancy \(D^*_N\)
Coprimality #coprimality — two integers sharing no common factor greater than 1; ensures Halton sequences in different dimensions never synchronize
Owen scrambling #owen-scrambling — random digit permutations within each base that preserve low-discrepancy while removing deterministic bias
crumbs: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Random Monte Carlo gives \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\) convergence regardless of dimension. With 100 draws, different seeds produce different elasticity estimates. Regular grids require \(O(10^D)\) points. In 5 dimensions, adequate coverage demands 100,000 grid points. Halton sequences achieve approximately \(O(\log(N)^D / N)\) convergence: 100 Halton draws match roughly 1000 random draws in accuracy.



Assign the first \(D\) primes as bases, one per dimension. For base \(b\), represent each integer \(n\) in base \(b\), then reflect the digits about the decimal point.
For base 2: \(n=1\) gives 0.5, \(n=2\) gives 0.25, \(n=3\) gives 0.75, \(n=4\) gives 0.125, \(n=5\) gives 0.625. Each level fills gaps left by previous levels, tracing a binary tree of the unit interval.
For base 3: \(n=1\) gives 0.333, \(n=2\) gives 0.667, \(n=3\) gives 0.111, and so on.



Because the bases share no common factors, the sequences across dimensions never align at the same \(n\). When base 2 places a point at 0.5 in dimension 1, base 3 is at 0.333 in dimension 2. Each new draw lands in a maximally distant region of the preference cube. This guarantees uniform joint coverage without requiring explicit construction of a multidimensional grid.



Without scrambling, Halton draws are deterministic: the same “consumer types” appear in every MCMC iteration. Owen scrambling applies random digit permutations within each base. The space-filling property is preserved because permuting digits within a base still fills each sub-interval uniformly. Multiple MCMC chains can use independent scramblings. Bias from specific fixed types is eliminated.



Halton draws live on \([0,1]^D\). The inverse Normal CDF maps them to actual preference parameters:
\[\alpha_i = \alpha_{\text{pop}} + \sigma_\alpha \cdot \Phi^{-1}(v_i)\]
A Halton value of 0.5 produces the median consumer. A value of 0.95 produces a consumer 1.64 standard deviations above the mean. The uniform space-filling on \([0,1]\) becomes representative coverage of the Normal distribution.
crumbs: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration

title: Halton Sequences and Quasi-Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Halton sequence in base \(b\): for integer \(n\) with base-\(b\) representation \(n = \sum_{k=0}^{m} d_k b^k\), the Halton value is \(H_b(n) = \sum_{k=0}^{m} d_k b^{-(k+1)}\).
Share integral approximation: \(s_{jm} \approx \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \frac{\exp(x_j\beta_r - \alpha_r p_j + \xi_j)}{1 + \sum_k \exp(x_k\beta_r - \alpha_r p_k + \xi_k)}\)
Convergence: \(|I - I_N| = O\left(\frac{(\log N)^D}{N}\right)\) versus \(O(N^{-1/2})\) for random Monte Carlo.

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox.html
title: Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox
text:
In hierarchical Bayesian models, the population mean can look “wrong” by classical standards while the model produces correct substantive quantities. In BLP demand estimation, \(\alpha_\text{pop} = -0.30\) appears too small to generate realistic elasticities. City-specific draws \(\alpha_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_\text{pop}, \tau_\alpha)\) produce own-price elasticities of \(-2.6\) to \(-3.5\), matching the literature. The population mean is not the quantity to benchmark against single-level estimates.



Nevo (2000) reports price coefficients \(\alpha \approx -0.8\) to \(-2.5\) (in dollars) from GMM estimation of BLP on the cereal dataset. A Bayesian hierarchical implementation with 8 city-level random effects produces \(\alpha_\text{pop} \approx -0.30\) (in cents). At first glance, this looks three orders of magnitude off. The resolution lies in understanding what the population mean represents in a hierarchical model.




Population mean (\(\alpha_\text{pop}\)) #population-mean — the centre of the random effects distribution; in a hierarchical model, it is the mean across groups, not the coefficient that enters any specific group’s likelihood
Partial pooling #partial-pooling — the hierarchical mechanism that shrinks group-level estimates toward the population mean; the degree of shrinkage depends on group sample size relative to prior precision
Elasticity #elasticity — \(\epsilon_{jj} = (p_j / s_j) \int \alpha_i \, s_{ij}(1-s_{ij}) \, dF(\alpha_i, \beta_i)\); depends on price level, share level, and the full distribution of heterogeneous coefficients, not just \(\alpha_\text{pop}\)






A pooled (non-hierarchical) BLP model estimated by GMM gives \(\alpha \approx -1.8\) to \(-2.5\). This parameter enters the utility function directly and, through the share integral, produces elasticities in the \(-2.8\) to \(-3.5\) range. The Bayesian hierarchical model gives \(\alpha_\text{pop} \approx -0.30\). Naively comparing these numbers suggests the hierarchical model is underestimating price sensitivity by a factor of six or more.



\(\alpha_\text{pop}\) is not the analogue of the pooled \(\alpha\). It is the mean of a distribution. Individual cities draw \(\alpha_r \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha_\text{pop}, \tau_\alpha)\) with \(\tau_\alpha \approx 0.068\). These city-specific draws range from roughly \(-0.15\) to \(-0.45\). Elasticities are computed using city-specific coefficients, not the population mean. The nonlinear transformation from utility coefficients to elasticities amplifies the spread.
The pooled model’s \(\alpha\) is a compromise: it tries to fit all cities with a single coefficient and lands on a value that works “on average.” The hierarchical model separates the population mean from city-level variation. The population mean is pulled toward zero by partial pooling. The city-specific draws fan out to cover the range that the pooled model captures with a single point.



The right comparison is not \(\alpha_\text{pop}\) vs. Nevo’s \(\alpha\). It is the implied elasticities vs. Nevo’s elasticities. Mean own-price elasticity from the hierarchical model: \(-3.17\). Median: \(-3.23\). Range: \([-3.52, -2.60]\). Nevo Table IV: \(-2.8\) to \(-3.5\). The hierarchical model’s range is tighter, which is exactly what partial pooling predicts: it regularizes the extremes.



In any hierarchical model, the population-level parameter is a hyperparameter governing the distribution of group-level effects. It should not be compared directly to a single-level estimate. The single-level estimate conflates between-group and within-group variation. The hierarchical model separates them. The population mean governs between-group variation. The group-level draws govern within-group behaviour. Substantive quantities (elasticities, marginal effects, predictions) should be computed from the group-level draws, not the population mean.





[[Effective Sample Size as Implicit Regularization]] — \(n\) regularizes the likelihood; partial pooling regularizes the coefficients; both make the model “looser” in defensible ways
[[Non-Collapsibility in Hierarchical Demand Models]] — non-collapsibility means that aggregating over heterogeneous coefficients changes the apparent effect size; this is a related but distinct phenomenon
[[Ecological Fallacy and BLP’s Inversion of Inference]] — the population mean paradox is a micro-level instance of the macro insight: aggregate quantities do not straightforwardly map to individual-level parameters
[[Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models]] — the Normal likelihood approximation interacts with the hierarchical structure; both are pragmatic compromises





With only 8 cities, how reliably can the model separate \(\alpha_\text{pop}\) from \(\tau_\alpha\)? Is the population mean identified or just prior-driven?
Does the paradox sharpen or dissolve as the number of groups grows? With 47 cities, does \(\alpha_\text{pop}\) move closer to the pooled estimate?
Is there a general formula relating the pooled single-level estimate to the hierarchical population mean and group-level variance?
crumbs: Hierarchical Pooling and the Population Mean Paradox

objectID: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects.html
href: notes/certain_things/Public/Statistics/Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects.html
title: Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects
text:
When a baseline treatment propagates through a multi-stage process with time-varying confounders affected by prior treatment, standard regression gives biased estimates of the total causal effect. Marginal structural models recover the total effect by weighting rather than conditioning.



A treatment assigned at baseline (e.g. freemium vs. paid) affects intermediate behaviours (engagement, feature adoption), which in turn predict downstream outcomes (conversion, churn). These intermediates are simultaneously mediators and time-varying confounders. Conditioning on them blocks part of the causal pathway. Not conditioning leaves confounding unaddressed. This is the structure that makes naive regression inadequate.




Time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment #time-varying-confounder — a variable \(L(t)\) that is shaped by past treatment and predicts future outcomes. Conditioning on it induces collider bias; ignoring it leaves confounding.
Total effect #total-effect — the full downstream consequence of baseline treatment assignment, flowing through all pathways including mediated ones. The policy-relevant estimand for binary decisions like “offer freemium or not.”
Controlled direct effect #controlled-direct-effect — the effect of treatment if mediators were fixed at a reference level. Requires the interventional mediation analysis machinery.
Inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights #iptcw — weights that simultaneously adjust for baseline confounding and time-varying confounding without conditioning on intermediates.






At baseline: confounders \(W\) affect both treatment \(A\) and outcomes. Post-baseline: time-varying behaviours \(L(t)\) are affected by \(A\) and by prior \(L\), and predict future transitions (conversion, churn). The causal path \(A \to L(t) \to Y\) is the mechanism by which treatment works. Conditioning on \(L(t)\) blocks this path. The DAG also includes a direct path \(A \to Y\) not through \(L(t)\).



Cox regression with time-varying covariates \(L(t)\) estimates the effect of \(A\) conditional on \(L(t)\). This removes the indirect effect through \(L\), yielding something closer to the controlled direct effect than the total effect. For the policy question (“should we offer freemium?”), the total effect is what matters. The indirect effect through changed behaviour is the whole point of the intervention.



Fit inverse-probability-weighted models where the weights adjust for both baseline confounding (\(W\)) and the time-varying confounding from \(L(t)\), without conditioning on \(L(t)\) in the outcome model. The weights create a pseudo-population where treatment is independent of both \(W\) and \(L(t)\), and the resulting survival curves have a total-effect interpretation.
In the competing risks setting (conversion vs. churn), the weights serve double duty: adjusting for baseline confounding of treatment assignment and handling time-varying confounding from intermediate engagement variables. The output is causal cause-specific hazards that combine into causal cumulative incidence functions.



The causal effect of baseline assignment on events 18 months later is genuinely attenuated. Post-baseline events (product changes, competitor actions, economic conditions) intervene. The survival curve framework handles this naturally: the gap between \(S(t \mid A=1)\) and \(S(t \mid A=0)\) shrinks over time. This reflects the causal truth, not a methodological failure. The cumulative incidence at later time points still carries the trace of the early effect, because early conversions are “locked in.”





[[Two-Stage Survival Models for Freemium Economics]] — the applied context that motivates MSMs for multi-stage processes
[[Non-Collapsibility of Hazard Ratios]] — MSMs target survival curves rather than hazard ratios, avoiding the non-collapsibility problem
[[Hernán’s Target Trial Framework for Survival Outcomes]] — the target trial framework clarifies when MSMs are needed versus simpler approaches
[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — g-computation is the alternative to IPTW for total effects with time-varying confounding
[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — MSMs operationalise the interventionist view while the time-varying structure gestures toward process





How sensitive are MSM estimates to misspecification of the weight model? Practical diagnostics for weight model adequacy remain underdeveloped.
Can doubly robust methods for time-varying treatments achieve meaningful gains over IPTW alone in survival settings?
The principal stratum decomposition (always-converters, induced converters, never-converters) operates on a different conceptual level from MSMs. Can the two be combined?

title: Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models
text:
The Normal likelihood on log-share-ratios in BLP estimation is a deliberate approximation that trades theoretical correctness for computational tractability. For typical market data, the approximation is accurate and the computational savings are decisive. This pragmatism extends to temporal structure: with few time periods, iid assumptions are more honest than misspecified dynamics.



Berry (1994) proposed transforming market shares to log-share-ratios and fitting a Normal likelihood. The theoretically correct likelihood is multinomial: shares are proportions that sum to one, and the multinomial enforces this budget constraint while capturing negative correlations between products. The Normal approximation drops both properties. Why accept this?




Berry inversion #berry-inversion — transforming market shares \(s_j\) to log-share-ratios \(\log(s_j/s_0)\) to obtain a linear-in-parameters equation
Budget constraint #budget-constraint — the requirement that predicted shares sum to 1, automatically satisfied by multinomial but not by the Normal approximation
Information criteria validity #information-criteria — WAIC and LOO require a correctly specified likelihood to be interpretable for model comparison






The multinomial likelihood enforces the share-summing constraint and captures negative correlations between products. It enables valid information criteria. It costs roughly 10x more computation and produces worse MCMC mixing.
The Normal approximation on log-share-ratios ignores the constraint and treats share observations as independent. For products with moderate shares (say, 1-20%), the approximation is accurate. The Berry (1994) variance formula captures the leading-order heteroskedasticity. Most applied BLP work uses this approximation.
The choice is pragmatic, not principled. The modeler accepts a small bias in exchange for large computational gains. This is a recurring pattern in structural econometrics: the “true” model is too expensive to estimate, so researchers adopt approximations whose error is small relative to other sources of uncertainty (structural shocks, instrument validity, functional form).



The same pragmatism governs temporal modeling. With two quarters of data, one cannot identify AR(1) persistence, factor structures, or seasonal effects in the structural error \(\xi_{jt}\). Imposing a misspecified AR(1) can be worse than treating markets as iid. The iid assumption is the honest choice when temporal dynamics are unidentified.
A misspecified AR(1) or random walk introduces bias without providing genuine information. The model should match the complexity the data can support. With few time periods, that complexity is zero.



The Normal approximation breaks down for very small shares (below 0.1%) or very large shares (above 50%). The log transformation amplifies errors near zero. The independence assumption fails when a dominant product’s share moves. title: Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models
text: Berry (1994) proposed transforming market shares to log-share-ratios and fitting a Normal likelihood. The theoretically correct likelihood is multinomial: shares are proportions that sum to one, and the multinomial enforces this budget constraint while capturing negative correlations between products. The Normal approximation drops both properties. Why accept this?

title: Pragmatic Likelihood Choice in Structural Models
text:
The multinomial likelihood enforces the share-summing constraint and captures negative correlations between products. It enables valid information criteria. It costs roughly 10x more computation and produces worse MCMC mixing.
The Normal approximation on log-share-ratios ignores the constraint and treats share observations as independent. For products with moderate shares (say, 1-20%), the approximation is accurate. The Berry (1994) variance formula captures the leading-order heteroskedasticity. Most applied BLP work uses this approximation.
The choice is pragmatic, not principled. The modeler accepts a small bias in exchange for large computational gains. This is a recurring pattern in structural econometrics: the “true” model is too expensive to estimate, so researchers adopt approximations whose error is small relative to other sources of uncertainty (structural shocks, instrument validity, functional form).



The same pragmatism governs temporal modeling. With two quarters of data, one cannot identify AR(1) persistence, factor structures, or seasonal effects in the structural error \(\xi_{jt}\). Imposing a misspecified AR(1) can be worse than treating markets as iid. The iid assumption is the honest choice when temporal dynamics are unidentified.
A misspecified AR(1) or random walk introduces bias without providing genuine information. The model should match the complexity the data can support. With few time periods, that complexity is zero.



The Normal approximation breaks down for very small shares (below 0.1%) or very large shares (above 50%). The log transformation amplifies errors near zero. The independence assumption fails when a dominant product’s share moves. The Dirichlet-Multinomial might offer a middle ground: it enforces the budget constraint with less computational cost than full multinomial integration.

title: Separability as the Potential Outcomes Alternative to Cross-World Counterfactuals
text:
The separability framework (Robins, Richardson, Stensrud) redefines mediation estimands so that no quantity requires nesting two interventions. It decomposes the treatment into independently manipulable components rather than decomposing the causal mechanism. The cost is a strong substantive assumption about the treatment’s structure.



The natural direct effect (NDE) requires the cross-world quantity \(Y(1, M(0))\): the outcome under treatment with the mediator held at its natural value under control. No single experiment can produce this quantity. The potential outcomes school objects not that the NDE is uncomputable but that it has no experimental referent. Separability offers a way to define direct and indirect effects without cross-world reasoning.




Cross-world counterfactual #cross-world — a quantity like \(Y(a, M(a'))\) that nests two incompatible intervention regimes; no single randomisation can identify it without structural assumptions
Separable treatment components #separability — decomposing treatment \(X\) into \((X_M, X_Y)\) where \(X_M\) is the component affecting the mediator and \(X_Y\) is the component affecting the outcome directly
Modularity #modularity — the structural assumption that intervening on one equation leaves others unchanged; the process-model alternative to separability






Decompose treatment \(X\) into two components: \(X_M\) (the part that affects mediator \(M\)) and \(X_Y\) (the part that affects outcome \(Y\) directly). Define:
\[\text{Separable Direct Effect} = E[Y(X_Y=1, X_M=0)] - E[Y(X_Y=0, X_M=0)]\]
\[\text{Separable Indirect Effect} = E[Y(X_Y=0, X_M=1)] - E[Y(X_Y=0, X_M=0)]\]
Each estimand involves a single-world intervention. You imagine a trial where the direct and mediated components can be administered independently. No nesting is required.



Separability requires that the treatment actually decomposes into independent components. This is an empirical claim about the intervention, not a modelling choice. For a drug with anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular effects that could be administered separately, separability is plausible. For exercise, psychological therapy, or policy interventions, you cannot cleanly separate “the part that works through the mediator” from “the part that works directly.” The treatment is unitary.



A structural equations model (Aalen, Pearl, dynamic path analysis) places the decomposition at the level of the mechanism, not the treatment. The model specifies how \(X\) affects \(M\) and how \(M\) affects \(Y\), then reads off direct and indirect contributions from the coefficient paths. This inherits the modularity assumption: intervening to change \(M\) leaves the \(M \to Y\) mechanism intact. Modularity is a structural assumption about the data-generating process. Separability is a substantive assumption about the treatment. The two approaches trade one untestable commitment for another.



Separability wins when the treatment genuinely decomposes and you want estimands with clean experimental interpretations. Process models win when the treatment is unitary but you need to know which pathway carries the effect and how that pathway evolves over time. A weighted marginal structural model with separability gives a single number. A time-varying coefficient model gives a trajectory. The trajectory is what produces actionable recommendations like “intervene on the mediator after day 100.”





[[G-Computation as the Bridge Between Process and Estimand]] — g-computation propagates through nonlinearities to produce marginal estimands from structural parameters
[[Processual vs Interventionist Causation in Survival Analysis]] — the philosophical framing: process models ask “how does it work?” while PO models ask “what would happen if?”
[[Marginal Structural Models for Multi-Stage Causal Effects]] — IPW is the PO school’s tool for handling temporal confounding, complementing separability for the estimand definition
[[Aalen’s Dynamic Path Analysis and Dependence-Production Boundary]] — the process-model alternative where decomposition lives in the structural equations





Can separability and process decomposition ever be shown to agree? Under what conditions do the separable direct effect and the NDE from a structural model converge?
For survival outcomes with time-varying mediators, does separability even have a natural formulation? The mediator’s time-profile makes “the component of treatment that acts on M” time-indexed.
Is there a middle ground: a partial separability assumption that requires decomposition only at certain time points?
crumbs: Separability as the Potential Outcomes Alternative to Cross-World Counterfactuals

title: Consideration Set Mixed Logit in PyMC Marketing
text:
This contribution extends the existing MixedLogit class with a two-stage consideration-then-choice structure. The core insight is that consumers do not evaluate every available alternative before deciding — they first form a consideration set (which products are even on the table) and only then choose among the products they actually considered. The implementation can be found in pymc-marketing here.


Stage 1 — Consideration:
\[
\pi_{nj} = \sigma\!\left(\gamma_{0j} + \sum_k \gamma_{zjk} \cdot \tilde{z}_{njk} + \eta_n\right)
\]
where \(\tilde{z}_{njk}\) are mean-centred consideration instruments satisfying an exclusion restriction: they must be structurally separate from the utility covariates. At \(\tilde{z} = 0\), \(\pi = 0.5\) — only deviations from population-average screening drive consideration.
Stage 2 — Choice:
\[
P(j \mid n) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\log \pi_{nj} + V_{nj}\right)
\]
The bridge formula \(U^{\text{avail}}_{nj} = V_{nj} + \log \pi_{nj}\) integrates consideration directly into the utility index, so the mixed logit likelihood structure from the parent class is preserved without modification.
This is the discrete choice analogue of the key/query separation in transformer attention: the consideration instruments \(Z\) play the role of the query while the utility covariates \(X\) play the role of the value.




Exclusion restriction: \(Z\) instruments must not appear in \(V_{nj}\). This identifies the consideration stage separately from the preference stage.
Mean-centring: At average screening behaviour (\(\tilde{z} = 0\)) the consideration probability is exactly \(0.5\), so the utility intercept \(\alpha_j\) absorbs baseline alternative-specific effects. When consideration_intercept=True, \(\gamma_{0j}\) and \(\alpha_j\) compete to explain baseline effects — use informative priors or constrain one set.
Random consideration (random_consideration=True) adds a per-individual intercept \(\eta_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{consider}})\), capturing unobserved heterogeneity in “visibility” across all alternatives.




from pymc_marketing.customer_choice.consideration_set_logit import (
    ConsiderationSetMixedLogit,
    ConsiderationInstruments,
)

instruments: ConsiderationInstruments = {
    "Z_tilde": Z_tilde,             # (N, J) mean-centred, or (N, J, K_z)
    "z_instrument_names": ["adspend", "shelf_position"],
}

model = ConsiderationSetMixedLogit(
    choice_df=df,
    utility_equations=[
        "brand_a ~ price_a + quality_a | income",
        "brand_b ~ price_b + quality_b | income",
        "brand_c ~ price_c + quality_c | income",
    ],
    depvar="choice",
    covariates=["price", "quality"],
    consideration_instruments=instruments,
    consideration_intercept=False,   # alpha_j absorbs baseline consideration
    random_consideration=True,       # per-individual consideration heterogeneity
)

idata = model.fit(target_accept=0.97, tune=2000)
The class inherits the full MixedLogit interface: Wilkinson-style formula specification, non-centered parameterisation, panel data support, control-function endogeneity correction, apply_intervention, and sample_posterior_predictive.




Numerically stable log-sigmoid: \(\log(\sigma(x)) = x - \operatorname{softplus}(x)\), avoiding the catastrophic cancellation in \(\log(\sigma(x) + \varepsilon)\) for large negative \(x\).
Multi-instrument support: \(Z\) can be 2-D \((N, J)\) for a single instrument per alternative or 3-D \((N, J, K_z)\) for multiple instruments, with named coordinates surfaced in the posterior.
Dimension-switch guard: switching \(Z\) from 2-D to 3-D after the model is built raises a clear ValueError, preventing silent model mismatches on apply_intervention.

title: Bayesian BLP Demand Estimation in PyMC Marketing
text:
The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995) model is the canonical structural demand model for aggregate market-share data — the kind that comes from Nielsen scanner panels, IRI retailer data, or any setting where you observe product-level shares across markets rather than individual purchase decisions. It accounts for price endogeneity, allows consumer heterogeneity through random coefficients, and produces structurally identified cross-price elasticities.
The classical BLP approach solves a contraction mapping to recover mean utilities and then uses GMM with instruments. This contribution drops both in favour of a fully Bayesian joint posterior over all parameters, following Jiang, Manchanda & Rossi (2009, QME) and Yang, Chen & Allenby (2003). The result is honest uncertainty quantification, hierarchical pooling across regions at essentially no extra cost, and full posterior elasticities without delta-method approximations. The implementation can be found in pymc-marketing here and extended to replicate the Nevo (2000) cereal market application here.


Mean utility for product \(j\) in market \(m\):
\[
\delta_{jm} = \alpha_r p_{jm} + x_{jm}^\top \beta_r + \xi_j + \tilde{\xi}_{jm}
\]
where \(\alpha_r\), \(\beta_r\) are region-level price and characteristic coefficients, \(\xi_j\) is a product fixed effect (absorbed demand quality), and \(\tilde{\xi}_{jm}\) is the residual market-specific shock.
Consumer-level utility with random coefficients:
\[
u_{ijm} = \delta_{jm} + \sum_{d} \sigma_d \cdot \nu_{id} \cdot c_{jmd} + \varepsilon_{ijm}
\]
The consumer taste shocks \(\nu_{id}\) are integrated out using Owen-scrambled Halton draws, giving predicted market shares \(\hat{s}_{jm}\) without solving a contraction mapping.
Likelihood (Berry 1994 log-share ratio):
\[
\log s_{jm} - \log s_{0m} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\log \hat{s}_{jm} - \log \hat{s}_{0m},\; \sigma^2_{jm}\right)
\]
where the delta-method variance \(\sigma^2_{jm} = \left(\frac{1}{n_m s_{jm}} + \frac{1}{n_m s_{0m}}\right)\) scales with the per-market sample size \(n_m\).



Instruments \(z_{jm}\) identify \(\alpha\) under endogeneity via the conditional decomposition of \((η_{jm}, \tilde{\xi}_{jm})\):
\[
p_{jm} = \pi_{0j} + \pi_z \cdot z_{jm} + \eta_{jm}
\qquad
\tilde{\xi}_{jm} = \underbrace{\frac{\gamma}{\sigma_\eta}}_{\rho \cdot \sigma_\xi / \sigma_\eta} \eta_{jm} + \omega \cdot \varepsilon_{jm}
\]
Sampling on the slope-residual coordinates \((\gamma, \omega)\) rather than \((\rho, \sigma_\xi)\) breaks the multiplicative ridge that pins diagonal-mass NUTS at the depth cap.



from pymc_marketing.customer_choice.bayesian_blp import BayesianBLP

model = BayesianBLP(
    market_data=panel_df,          # long-format: (market, product, share, price, ...)
    characteristics=["quality", "calories", "sugar"],
    instruments=["cost_iv", "rival_price_iv"],

title: Bayesian BLP Demand Estimation in PyMC Marketing
text:
Mean utility for product \(j\) in market \(m\):
\[
\delta_{jm} = \alpha_r p_{jm} + x_{jm}^\top \beta_r + \xi_j + \tilde{\xi}_{jm}
\]
where \(\alpha_r\), \(\beta_r\) are region-level price and characteristic coefficients, \(\xi_j\) is a product fixed effect (absorbed demand quality), and \(\tilde{\xi}_{jm}\) is the residual market-specific shock.
Consumer-level utility with random coefficients:
\[
u_{ijm} = \delta_{jm} + \sum_{d} \sigma_d \cdot \nu_{id} \cdot c_{jmd} + \varepsilon_{ijm}
\]
The consumer taste shocks \(\nu_{id}\) are integrated out using Owen-scrambled Halton draws, giving predicted market shares \(\hat{s}_{jm}\) without solving a contraction mapping.
Likelihood (Berry 1994 log-share ratio):
\[
\log s_{jm} - \log s_{0m} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\log \hat{s}_{jm} - \log \hat{s}_{0m},\; \sigma^2_{jm}\right)
\]
where the delta-method variance \(\sigma^2_{jm} = \left(\frac{1}{n_m s_{jm}} + \frac{1}{n_m s_{0m}}\right)\) scales with the per-market sample size \(n_m\).

title: Bayesian BLP Demand Estimation in PyMC Marketing
text:
Instruments \(z_{jm}\) identify \(\alpha\) under endogeneity via the conditional decomposition of \((η_{jm}, \tilde{\xi}_{jm})\):
\[
p_{jm} = \pi_{0j} + \pi_z \cdot z_{jm} + \eta_{jm}
\qquad
\tilde{\xi}_{jm} = \underbrace{\frac{\gamma}{\sigma_\eta}}_{\rho \cdot \sigma_\xi / \sigma_\eta} \eta_{jm} + \omega \cdot \varepsilon_{jm}
\]
Sampling on the slope-residual coordinates \((\gamma, \omega)\) rather than \((\rho, \sigma_\xi)\) breaks the multiplicative ridge that pins diagonal-mass NUTS at the depth cap.

title: MaxDiff Conjoint Analysis in PyMC Marketing
text:
MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) is the workhorse of conjoint analysis. Rather than asking respondents to rate items on a scale — which produces noisy, anchoring-biased data — it presents subsets of items and asks which is most preferred and which is least preferred. This forces genuine discrimination and yields interval-scaled utilities that are comparable across respondents.
This contribution implements the Louviere sequential best-worst model with optional hierarchical Bayesian respondent heterogeneity (HB-MaxDiff), two modes of identifying item utilities (item intercepts or part-worths from attributes), and a fully generative prediction path. The implementation can be found in pymc-marketing here.


The sequential best-worst likelihood factors as:
\[
P(\text{best}_t = b, \, \text{worst}_t = w \mid \text{subset}_t)
= \underbrace{\frac{e^{U_b}}{\sum_{k \in S_t} e^{U_k}}}_{\text{best pick}}
\cdot \underbrace{\frac{e^{-U_w}}{\sum_{k \in S_t \setminus \{b\}} e^{-U_k}}}_{\text{worst pick from remainder}}
\]
Two separate pm.Categorical observed distributions encode this in the PyMC graph — one for best, one for worst — so sample_posterior_predictive yields best_pick and worst_pick draws directly.



In the default item-intercept mode the population utility for item \(i\) is \(\beta_i\), with the reference item pinned to zero for identification. With random_intercepts=True, each respondent draws item-level deviations:
\[
\beta^r_i = \beta_i + \sigma_i \cdot z^r_i, \quad z^r_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)
\]
This gives individual-level WTP estimates via the posterior of \(\beta^r_i\), which is the defining feature of HB-MaxDiff.



When items are described by measurable attributes (brand, price, quality) rather than arbitrary labels, passing item_attributes and a utility_formula switches the model into part-worths mode:
\[
U_i = X_i^\top \beta_{\text{feat}}
\]
This extrapolates naturally to new items via their attributes without requiring them to have appeared in any training task.



from pymc_marketing.customer_choice.maxdiff import MaxDiffMixedLogit

# Item-intercept mode with respondent heterogeneity
model = MaxDiffMixedLogit(
    task_df=task_df,         # long-format: (respondent_id, task_id, item_id, is_best, is_worst)
    items=["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date", "elderberry"],
    random_intercepts=True,  # HB-MaxDiff: per-respondent item utilities
    reference_item="date",   # pinned to 0 for identification
    non_centered=True,
)

idata = model.fit()

# Generative prediction on a new task design (coherent joint best/worst draw)
sim = model.predict_choices(new_task_df, new_respondents="population")

# Part-worths mode: utilities from item attributes
model_pw = MaxDiffMixedLogit(
    task_df=task_df,
    items=items,
    item_attributes=item_attrs_df,    # DataFrame indexed by item name
    utility_formula="~ 0 + C(brand) + price + quality",
    random_attributes=["price"],       # random coefficient on price
)

# Score hypothetical new items without retraining
new_shares = model_pw.score_new_items(new_sku_attributes)



sample_posterior_predictive is valid for in-sample posterior predictive checks: it conditions the worst pick on the observed best position, so the joint draw is intentionally incoherent for generative use. For counterfactual or out-of-sample simulation, use predict_choices or apply_intervention — these sample best first, then sample worst conditioned on the freshly drawn best, producing the correct generative joint.




Full LKJ covariance (full_covariance=True): replaces independent per-item scales with a full Cholesky covariance \(\Sigma = LL^\top\) estimated via pm.LKJCholeskyCov. Captures correlated item utilities (e.g. premium brands cluster together) at the cost of \(O(I^2)\) parameters.
Ragged subset support: tasks may show different numbers of items. The preprocessing step pads to \(K_{\max}\) positions using the reference item as a sentinel and a boolean mask marks real positions, so the masked softmax handles variable-size subsets without data duplication.
Batched prediction: predict_choices accepts a draw_batch_size to cap peak memory on large posteriors, while guaranteeing bit-identical output to the unbatched path via pre-drawn uniforms.

title: Causal Locutions as Norms Under Construction
text:
Causal vocabulary is unlike settled modal vocabulary such as “copper conducts”: researchers are still instituting the norms governing “X caused Y” by contesting which DAGs and identification conditions are licensed. This live contestation favors Brandom’s anti-representationalist semantics over a picture where causal facts were fixed all along and only our access to them was unsettled.



Standard Kant-Sellars cases treat modal vocabulary as already in stable use, with philosophy explaining its semantics after the fact. Causal vocabulary in statistics is different. Pearl’s do-calculus, Rubin’s potential outcomes, and Robins’ structural models are rival proposals for what licenses a causal claim at all. The disagreement is not just about which graph fits the data. It is about what “caused” should mean.




Norm institution #brandom — the historical process by which a vocabulary earns its inferential role, rather than describing a pre-existing domain
Myth of Jones #sellars — Sellars’s story of how mentalistic vocabulary entered a language through its inferential utility, not through detection of mental facts
DAG contestation #causal-inference — disagreement over which causal graph, adjustment set, or identification strategy correctly represents a system
Practical mastery prior to discursive mastery #brandom — non-linguistic causal know-how (expecting a glass to break when dropped) that precedes any explicit theory of causation






Within an already-fixed DAG, d-separation and do-calculus are a straightforward explicitation of commitments implicit in the graph plus the Markov assumption. This part behaves like ordinary modal vocabulary. The harder case is the choice among rival DAGs. A social-normative process settles that choice, if anything does: researchers propose graphs, contest them on grounds of confounding or implausible independence, and adjudicate with intervention experiments. This is closer to Sellars’s myth of Jones, where a vocabulary earns its keep through inferential utility rather than discovery.



If “X caused Y” tracked a determinate, mind-independent relation, causal semantics should be fixed in advance of methodology. Instead the methodology and the semantics are worked out together: identification conditions, exchangeability assumptions, and admissible adjustment sets are all in motion at once. This is better explained by norms-and-practices-first: entitlement-conferring practice comes first, and what the vocabulary is about gets constituted by what the practice eventually licenses. Pearl’s framework was adopted because it made explicit inferences practitioners already wanted to draw, not because someone detected do-calculus facts directly.



Brandom’s project bundles several claims that this case does not equally support. Causal inference vindicates the anti-representationalist core most directly. A picture where causal facts are fixed in advance predicts that semantics settles before methodology does. Instead the two are worked out together: identification conditions, exchangeability assumptions, and admissible adjustment sets are all in motion at once.
The case also supports Sellars’s myth-of-Jones claim, that a vocabulary earns its keep through inferential utility rather than discovery. Pearl’s framework was adopted because it made explicit inferences practitioners already wanted to draw, not because anyone detected do-calculus facts directly. This is unusually strong evidence because it is a documented, observable case rather than a philosophical reconstruction of prehistory.
The strong Kant-Sellars thesis is a separate claim: no descriptive vocabulary is possible without modal vocabulary already in play. Causal inference’s contested history does not establish this. It shows that one region of modal vocabulary, causal locutions, is practice-first. It says nothing about whether purely observational predicates could exist without inferential connections to other claims. That stronger claim rests on Brandom’s separate regress argument about what fixes the content of an observational predicate, not on the causal case.



A defender of representationalism can redescribe the same history without conceding the point: the causal facts were determinate all along, and only our epistemic access was unsettled. On this view, DAG contestation is ordinary scientific disagreement about measurement, no different from contested instruments in physics. This redescription has to explain why the contestation is about what the vocabulary licenses, not merely which instrument reads correctly. That is a real cost, but the move remains available.



Brandom can hold that practical causal know-how, expecting a dropped glass to break, recoiling from fire, is already operative before any explicit causal vocabulary exists. This continues Sellars’s point that even basic observation reports presuppose inferential commitments the reporter cannot make explicit. On this reading, Pearl, Rubin, and Robins are not instituting causal normativity from nothing. They are articulating a practical-inferential capacity that was already operative but badly understood. The slow correction of causal theory is the explicitation of a complex implicit structure, not norm-creation ex nihilo.
This move also blocks the representationalist redescription. The determinacy these theories are answerable to is not a freestanding causal fact. It is the determinate-enough shape of our practical engagement with interventions, which later theory gets right or wrong by reference to that practical shape rather than to a mind-independent relation.



Brandom needs practical mastery itself to be normative, governed by a social practice of holding people to their expectations about interventions, prior to any propositional or DAG-theoretic form. A skeptic can ask whether this is genuine normative structure or just regularity-tracking behavior dressed in normative vocabulary.





[[Bayesian Posterior Predictives as Brandomian Explicitation]] — the companion case where the modal vocabulary (statistical counterfactuals) is comparatively settled
[[Brandom’s Inferentialism and Hegelian Conceptual Content]] — the general framework; this note is the hard test case for it
[[Causal Identification in Multi-State Survival Models]] — a concrete domain where DAG-level contestation (which intermediate variables confound vs. mediate) plays out in practice





Is there any empirical case, beyond causal inference, that could evidence the strong Kant-Sellars thesis rather than just the weaker practice-first claim?
What would count as decisive evidence that practical mastery is normative rather than mere regularity-tracking?
Does the historicist argument generalize beyond causal vocabulary to other contested scientific modal idioms (probability itself, mechanism in biology)?
Can principal stratification and partial identification be read as a further site of norm institution, where the field is still deciding what a well-defined estimand even is?

The case also supports Sellars’s myth-of-Jones claim, that a vocabulary earns its keep through inferential utility rather than discovery. Pearl’s framework was adopted because it made explicit inferences practitioners already wanted to draw, not because anyone detected do-calculus facts directly. This is unusually strong evidence because it is a documented, observable case rather than a philosophical reconstruction of prehistory.
The strong Kant-Sellars thesis is a separate claim: no descriptive vocabulary is possible without modal vocabulary already in play. Causal inference’s contested history does not establish this. It shows that one region of modal vocabulary, causal locutions, is practice-first. It says nothing about whether purely observational predicates could exist without inferential connections to other claims. That stronger claim rests on Brandom’s separate regress argument about what fixes the content of an observational predicate, not on the causal case.



A defender of representationalism can redescribe the same history without conceding the point: the causal facts were determinate all along, and only our epistemic access was unsettled. On this view, DAG contestation is ordinary scientific disagreement about measurement, no different from contested instruments in physics. This redescription has to explain why the contestation is about what the vocabulary licenses, not merely which instrument reads correctly. That is a real cost, but the move remains available.



Brandom can hold that practical causal know-how, expecting a dropped glass to break, recoiling from fire, is already operative before any explicit causal vocabulary exists. This continues Sellars’s point that even basic observation reports presuppose inferential commitments the reporter cannot make explicit. On this reading, Pearl, Rubin, and Robins are not instituting causal normativity from nothing. They are articulating a practical-inferential capacity that was already operative but badly understood. The slow correction of causal theory is the explicitation of a complex implicit structure, not norm-creation ex nihilo.
This move also blocks the representationalist redescription. The determinacy these theories are answerable to is not a freestanding causal fact. It is the determinate-enough shape of our practical engagement with interventions, which later theory gets right or wrong by reference to that practical shape rather than to a mind-independent relation.



Brandom needs practical mastery itself to be normative, governed by a social practice of holding people to their expectations about interventions, prior to any propositional or DAG-theoretic form. A skeptic can ask whether this is genuine normative structure or just regularity-tracking behavior dressed in normative vocabulary.

title: Bayesian Posterior Predictives as Brandomian Explicitation
text:
A fitted Bayesian model encodes implicit constraints on possible observations. Posterior predictive sampling under interventions makes those constraints explicit, mirroring how modal vocabulary articulates inferential commitments already present in empirical claims rather than describing separate modal facts.



Brandom’s reading of Sellars holds that modal vocabulary (“necessarily,” “if this were copper, it would conduct”) does not track modal facts. It makes explicit the inferential licenses already governing ordinary empirical claims. I wanted to test this against applied Bayesian workflow: fit a model on observed data, then use posterior predictive sampling to generate counterfactual or future states.




Explicitation #brandom — converting an implicit inferential commitment into an explicit, assessable claim
Material inference #inferentialism — an inference licensed by the content of the concepts involved, not by logical form alone (“this is copper” licenses “this conducts”)
Posterior predictive distribution #bayesian — the distribution over future or counterfactual observations implied by a fitted model, conditional on observed data






A posterior, once fit, encodes a constraint structure over possible observations that was already implicit in the prior and likelihood given the data. Sampling counterfactual outcomes under a changed covariate or intervention extracts a commitment that was latent in the joint distribution. No one needs to observe the counterfactual outcome for the model to be committed to a distribution over it. This matches the modal case: no one needs to observe the counterfactual to be committed, by an already-accepted material inference, to what would happen if the antecedent held.



Brandom’s modal vocabulary is metalinguistic: it talks about inferential licenses connecting claims, not about the world. Posterior predictive draws stay in the object language; they are claims about what y would be, not claims about the license connecting x-claims to y-claims. The genuine metalinguistic analogue is the model itself, its parameters and functional form, since that is what compresses the inferential license. A credible interval on a causal contrast is the better analogue of an explicit modal claim. It states: given the data and model, were x set to x’, y would shift by this much with this much confidence. The sampling step is closer to the inferential transition than to the modal claim it grounds.



Brandom’s project explains how modal vocabulary is possible at all, without metaphysical danglers. The Bayesian workflow takes “empirical regularity constrains possible realizations” as a starting methodological assumption (exchangeability, choice of likelihood, choice of prior). It does not explain the possibility of that assumption. The Bayesian case is a regional, formal instance of the explicitating pattern. It illustrates the move without vindicating the transcendental claim that descriptive and modal vocabularies are conceptually interdependent in all discursive practice.



Brandom’s account needs a score-keeping practice: a social practice of holding people to the commitments and entitlements their modal claims carry. The natural statistical candidate is posterior predictive checking and model criticism. Checking whether a model’s explicit counterfactual predictions hold up is structurally like holding an asserter to what their modal claim entails. This gives a three-part structure: implicit regularity, explicit predictive claim, and a normative practice of checking and revising that claim.





[[Brandom’s Inferentialism and Hegelian Conceptual Content]] — the general inferentialist framework this note applies to a specific domain
[[Causal Locutions as Norms Under Construction]] — the harder case where the modal vocabulary itself is unsettled, not just applied
[[Thinking about Statistics]] — broader reflections on what statistical modeling is doing conceptually





What disciplines model criticism as a genuine normative practice, rather than mere goodness-of-fit checking?
Does treating the model’s parameters as the metalinguistic layer, rather than the predictive draws, change how we should interpret prior sensitivity?

title: Notes on Good Data Science
text:
Engineers talk of the mythical 10x engineer. Data scientists have their own fable: the “unicorn” who is simultaneously computer scientist, project manager, statistician and software engineer. These chimeric creatures exist, but they are not what their job descriptions would suggest. The data scientist is an ambiguously valuable professional hire, so it’s worth a little time trying to say where the value lies.
When I think of good data scientists I don’t think of a laundry list of software they claim to use, I think of accordion players. I think of the capacity to stretch across domains and go deep into any of them. This is not merely the classic T-shaped professional, with some breadth and a specialism. The ask for a data-scientist, like the statisticians before them, is to play in everyone’s backyard. To absorb domain context and go deep where your stakeholders can’t, derive insight and value, define the problem and build the solution… and then do it all over again in the next domain.
